title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
About this lecture
By the end of P3 our plant has water, minerals and sugar. But a plant cannot move. It must decide when to germinate, which way to grow, whether to branch, when to flower and when to let a leaf die, using only what it can sense where it stands. How does a plant turn light, gravity and season into these decisions? Today we follow one plant from seed to senescence and ask, at each stage, which signal is in charge.

Signals: the chain from cue to response, and the main plant hormones.
Seed: dormancy, germination and the ABA : gibberellin balance.
Light as information: photoreceptors, and phytochrome as a red/far-red switch.
Growing the right way: phototropism, gravitropism and apical dominance.
Flowering: day length, night breaks, florigen and vernalisation.
The end of the cycle: double fertilisation and senescence.


Frame the lecture as a life cycle: seed, seedling, shoot, flower, seed again, and finally an ageing leaf. At each stage the plant makes a decision, and the question is always the same: what does it sense, what carries the signal, and what does the signal change? Link back to P3: carbon and nutrients are the raw material; today is about the control of how that material is used. P5 then uses the same signalling machinery for stress and defence.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
From cue to response


Cue → receptor → signal transduction → response

Every response needs a receptor: a cue the plant cannot perceive has no effect.
Fast (seconds to minutes): existing proteins change. A touched Mimosa leaf folds.
Slow (hours to weeks): gene expression changes. A flower forms.
The same signal can give different responses in different tissues.



Photos: Bluemoose, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons: open and touched

Many of the signals inside the plant are hormones. Which ones?

This is the framework for every example in the lecture: whenever we meet a response, ask what the cue is (light, gravity, temperature, a hormone), what the receptor is, and whether the change is in existing proteins (ion fluxes, protein activity) or in gene expression. The photo is the fast case: touch triggers ion fluxes and water loss from motor cells in the pulvinus at the leaflet base, and the leaflets fold within seconds; no genes are involved. Stomatal closing is the other fast example. Point out the last bullet: auxin promotes elongation in shoots but inhibits it in roots at the same concentration, so the response depends on the responding cell, not only on the signal. The next slide lists the hormones.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
The plant hormones









Hormone
Made in / moves by
Main effects
Example




Auxin (IAA)
Shoot apex, young leaves; polar transport downwards
Cell elongation, tropisms, apical dominance, root initiation
Rooting powder for cuttings


Cytokinin
Mainly roots; xylem
Cell division, bud outgrowth, delays senescence
Leaf discs stay green


Gibberellin (GA)
Young tissues, embryo
Stem elongation, bolting, breaks seed dormancy
Tall vs dwarf pea (Mendel)


Abscisic acid (ABA)
Leaves and roots under water deficit
Stomatal closure, seed dormancy
Seeds stay dormant in the fruit


Ethylene
Most tissues; a gas
Climacteric fruit ripening, abscission, triple response
One ripe banana ripens the rest


Brassinosteroids
Most tissues
Cell expansion
Mutants are dark-green dwarfs


Strigolactones
Roots
Inhibit bud outgrowth
Mutants are bushy



Jasmonic acid and salicylic acid control defence; we meet them in P5.

Students must be able to match hormone and effect (exercise 1.1). Go through the example column, because concrete cases are easier to recall than lists: rooting powder is synthetic auxin; ethylene from one ripe fruit triggers ripening in its neighbours in climacteric fruits such as banana, tomato and apple, but not in non-climacteric fruits such as citrus or grape. Strigolactones are included because they appear on the apical dominance slide. Transition: how do we find out what a hormone does? Mostly from mutants.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Reading a hormone mutant


Spray gibberellin on two dwarf pea mutants:



Mutant
+ GA
Defect




A
normal height
biosynthesis (Mendel’s le)


B
stays dwarf
perception or signalling



Triple response: dark-grown seedlings + ethylene give a short, thick hypocotyl and an exaggerated hook. etr1 (receptor mutant) + ethylene stays long and thin.
Rule: rescued by the hormone → defect in making it.


Photo: Dehaan, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons


This is the logic of hormone genetics and appears in exercises 1.4 and 1.5. The photo shows the kind of phenotype we start from: a dwarf mutant beside wild type (here intermediate wheatgrass; the photo alone does not tell us which hormone is involved, which is exactly why we do the spraying experiment). A biosynthesis mutant is rescued by the hormone; a receptor or signalling mutant is not. The Green Revolution semi-dwarf wheats (Rht genes) are GA-insensitive, which is the second class. The triple response screen found the ethylene receptor ETR1: mutants that ignore ethylene look like untreated seedlings; the hormone is present but the receptor cannot pass on the signal. Transition: we start the life cycle with the seed, where two of these hormones are in direct opposition.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
section: The seed: dormant or just waiting?
text:
The seed: dormant or just waiting?









Quiescent
Dormant




Definition
Will germinate as soon as conditions allow
Will not germinate even in water, O₂ and warmth


Example
Dry seeds in a packet; seeds in dry soil
Fresh seeds that need months of dry storage


Released by
Water
After-ripening (dry storage), stratification (moist cold), light




Dormancy stops a seed germinating in the wrong season, for example in autumn just before winter.
Stratification is why many temperate seeds germinate in spring.

What holds a dormant seed back?

Dormancy is an internal block; quiescence is only a lack of water or warmth. Stratification is why many temperate seeds germinate in spring after a winter in moist soil, not in autumn. Transition: the block is set by a balance between two hormones.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
section: ABA versus gibberellin: the balance decides
text:
ABA versus gibberellin: the balance decides



ABA maintains dormancy; gibberellin promotes germination.
ABA-deficient maize mutants show vivipary: seeds germinate on the cob.
GA-deficient mutants do not germinate unless GA is supplied.
Germination (radicle emergence) is scored at a stated time: 12 of 20 seeds by day 5 = 60%.



Photo: Gaiacoyote, CC0, Wikimedia Commons


The two mutant phenotypes show the ABA : GA balance from both sides (exercise 4.2). The photo shows vivipary in an overripe tomato: the seeds have germinated inside the fruit and the seedlings push out through the skin. Normally ABA in the seeds and the osmotic pull of the fruit flesh keep them dormant; when that block fails, as in ABA-deficient or ABA-insensitive mutants, the seeds germinate where they sit. The germination percentage needs a denominator and a time point (exercise 4.3); non-germinated seeds may be dormant, slow or dead. Transition: once germination starts, what does gibberellin actually do in the seed?

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Germination: gibberellin mobilises the reserves



The starchy endosperm is dead. The living aleurone layer around it makes the enzymes.
Embryo signals with GA; aleurone transcribes α-amylase.
ABA blocks this, so a dormant grain keeps its reserves.
Malting: barley germinated with added GA, for brewing sugar.




But many small seeds also check something outside: is there light?

This is the best-understood hormone response in a seed and is the order asked in exercise 1.3: GA from embryo, induction in the aleurone, secretion, hydrolysis, uptake via the scutellum. Follow the numbers in the figure. It is also a clear example of a slow, gene-expression response from the first slide. ABA antagonism ties back to the ABA : GA balance. Transition: small seeds such as lettuce have few reserves and should only germinate near the surface, which they detect with light.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
section: Light is information as well as energy
text:
Light is information as well as energy








Photoreceptor
Light absorbed
Example responses




Phytochrome
Red / far-red
Seed germination, shade avoidance, photoperiod


Cryptochrome
Blue / UV-A
Inhibits hypocotyl elongation; entrains the circadian clock


Phototropin
Blue / UV-A
Phototropism, chloroplast movement, stomatal opening


UVR8
UV-B
UV-protective responses (e.g. flavonoid sunscreens)




A seedling responds to a light flash far too dim to support photosynthesis. These receptors read the colour, direction and timing of light.

What does a seedling do when it has no light at all?

Distinguish light as energy (P3) from light as a signal. The match between photoreceptor, wavelength and response is exercise 3.4. Phytochrome gets three slides because it underlies germination, shade avoidance and the night-break experiments in flowering.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Etiolation: growing in the dark



In darkness a seedling is etiolated: long, pale, hooked, small leaves.
All reserves go into elongation until the shoot reaches light.
Light triggers de-etiolation: the hook opens, leaves expand, chlorophyll forms, elongation slows.



Photo: Chiswick Chap, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

The red/far-red receptor is the key to germination and to flowering. How does it work?

Etiolation is a strategy: a buried seedling cannot photosynthesise, so it spends its reserves on getting to the light. The photo compares bluebell shoots that grew under an opaque cover (long, yellow) with uncovered ones (short, green): same plants, same soil, only light differs. Phytochromes and cryptochromes both drive de-etiolation; that is the red- and blue-light inhibition of hypocotyl elongation in the table on the previous slide.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Phytochrome: a red/far-red switch






Pr
Pfr




Absorbs
red, ~660 nm
far-red, ~730 nm


Light converts it to
Pfr
Pr


Active?
no
yes


Made as?
yes
no




The last light decides the state.
Pfr enters the nucleus and changes gene expression.
In darkness Pfr slowly reverts or is degraded.





Students should be able to fill this table from memory (exercise 3.1). The key idea is a switch with two stable states, each converted to the other by the light it absorbs. The spectra show why red light never gives 100 % Pfr: Pfr also absorbs a little at 660 nm, so continuous red reaches about 85 % Pfr, while far-red, which Pr hardly absorbs, leaves only a few per cent. Phytochrome is made as inactive Pr, which is why a seed in darkness has no active phytochrome. The last bullet matters for photoperiod: the plant can use the decline in Pfr during the night. The next slide shows the classic experiment that proved photoreversibility.

The lettuce seed experiment


Imbibed lettuce seeds, brief light flashes, then darkness:

Photo: Rasbak, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons


The last flash decides. This photoreversibility identified phytochrome (Borthwick and Hendricks, 1950s).
Why it matters: a buried seed sees no light and stays dormant until the soil is disturbed.

Light under a canopy has a different colour. What does phytochrome tell the plant there?

The photo shows what “germinate” means in this experiment: lettuce seeds on moist paper with the radicle out and covered in root hairs; the seed coat is still on some of the cotyledons. Work the sequence column by column; exercise 3.2 extends it to five flashes. The ecological meaning: small-seeded weeds germinate after ploughing because the soil is turned and seeds get a flash of light. Transition to shade: phytochrome does not just detect light versus dark, it detects the ratio of red to far-red.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
section: Try it: flash the lettuce seeds
text:
Try it: flash the lettuce seeds




Live version of the lettuce-seed table. The buttons give a brief, saturating red or far-red flash; the chart shows the fraction of phytochrome as active Pfr after each flash (about 85 % after red, about 3 % after far-red), and “Incubate 2 days in darkness” shows how many of 20 seeds germinate. Start with “dark” and incubate: almost none germinate, because phytochrome is made as Pr. Then let the room choose sequences, for example R FR R FR R FR R: ask them to predict before you incubate. Points to draw out: only the last flash matters; Pfr never reaches 100 % because Pfr also absorbs some red light; the result is all-or-nothing per seed but the dish gives a percentage, as in exercise 4.3. The buttons under “Lecture sequences” load the rows of the table. The seed pattern is fixed, so a rerun looks the same. Reset clears the flashes.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Shade avoidance



Chlorophyll absorbs red light but transmits and reflects far-red.
Under a canopy, the red : far-red ratio falls (sunlight ~1.2; deep shade ~0.2).
Less red → less Pfr. The plant reads this as “neighbours above me”.








Shade-avoidance response
Benefit




Faster stem and petiole elongation
Leaves reach light before the competitor’s


Leaves angled upwards
Less self-shading


Less branching
Resources go into height


Earlier flowering
Seeds are set before resources run out




The cost: thin, weak stems and less root growth. Dense crops lose yield to this.



Photo: Jugrü, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons


The photo compares trees of the same species growing alone (left: broad, low-branched crowns) and in a dense stand (right: tall, slender, unbranched trunks with the leaves only at the top); beech above, birch below. The stand trees show the shade-avoidance syndrome from the table at the scale of a whole forest. Exercise 3.3. Emphasise that the plant responds to reflected far-red from neighbours even before it is actually shaded, which is an early warning. The cost row connects to agriculture: crop breeders have selected plants with weaker shade avoidance to allow dense planting. Transition: phytochrome reads colour; the direction of light is read by a different receptor and causes the shoot to bend.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Phototropism: bending towards light





Coleoptile, lit from one side
Bends?




Untreated
yes


Tip removed, or opaque cap
no


Tip in a transparent cap
yes


Opaque collar below the tip
yes


Tip replaced on a gelatin block
yes




Light is perceived at the tip; a diffusible signal moves down.



Photo: Dennis Brown, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

What is the signal, and why does the shoot bend?

The table summarises Darwin (1880, caps and collars) and Boysen-Jensen (1913, gelatin block); Went (1928) then collected the signal in agar blocks and named it auxin. Each row asks: where is light perceived, and can the signal pass through gelatin? This is exercises 2.1 and 2.2. The photo shows the everyday version: onion seedlings grown indoors all lean towards the window.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
The Cholodny–Went model



Phototropin at the tip senses blue light from one side.
Auxin is moved to the shaded side, then down to the growing zone.
Shaded cells elongate faster: the shoot bends towards the light.




The same auxin redistribution explains a response to gravity.

Exercise 2.2. The model has two parts: lateral redistribution at the tip, then basipetal (downward) polar transport to the elongation zone. The lit side does not lose auxin by destruction; auxin is moved across by PIN efflux carriers. Transition: in gravitropism auxin also moves to one side, but in roots it has the opposite effect.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Gravitropism: the root grows down


Root turned horizontal:

Columella cells of the root cap sense gravity: starch-filled amyloplasts (statoliths) sediment to the lower side.
Auxin is redirected to the lower side.
In roots, high auxin inhibits elongation: the root bends down.

Shoot: auxin also goes to the lower side but promotes elongation: the shoot bends up.



Same signal, same redistribution, opposite outcome: the response depends on the tissue.

Exercise 2.3. The root cap is the sensor: remove it and the root still grows but no longer bends. The contrast between root and shoot is the clearest demonstration of the first slide’s point that the response depends on the responding tissue’s sensitivity to auxin. The next slide shows the shoot half in a real plant.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Gravitropism in a shoot



These Kalanchoe stems fell over under their own weight.
Each tip has turned upwards again.
Auxin on the lower side made the lower flank grow faster.
The old, horizontal part of the stem has stopped growing, so it stays bent: only the growing zone responds.



Photo: Trio3D, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons


The photo shows shoot gravitropism in an ordinary house plant: Kalanchoe blossfeldiana stems bent over the rim of the pot under their own weight, and each growing tip has curved back up. The bend is confined to the young part near each tip; the older stem does not straighten, because mature cells can no longer elongate. Ask the room which side of each bend has more auxin (the lower side) and whether the same auxin level would make a root bend up or down (down). Transition: auxin flowing down the shoot also decides whether side branches grow.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
section: Apical dominance: should the plant branch?
text:
Apical dominance: should the plant branch?



Pea shoot treatment
Lateral buds




Intact
Inhibited


Apex removed
Grow out


Apex removed + auxin paste on stump
Inhibited


Apex removed + plain lanolin on stump
Grow out


Intact + cytokinin on a bud
Grows out




Auxin from the apex replaces the apex (Thimann and Skoog, 1934).
Auxin does not enter the bud. It acts indirectly: it lowers cytokinin supply to the bud and raises strigolactone synthesis.
Gardeners use this: pinching out the tip makes a bushier plant.

The shoot is now built. When does it stop making leaves and make flowers?

Exercise 1.2. The lanolin-only control is essential: it shows that the paste itself does nothing, so the effect is due to auxin. The indirect mechanism is the modern view; the old idea that auxin enters the bud and inhibits it directly does not fit the transport data. Transition to flowering: the biggest developmental decision of an annual plant.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Flowering: measuring the night



Short-day plants (SDP) flower when the night is longer than a critical night length (chrysanthemum, soybean, poinsettia).
Long-day plants (LDP) flower when it is shorter (Arabidopsis, spinach, wheat).
The plant measures the uninterrupted dark period: an hour of darkness in the day changes nothing.



Photo: Carl Davies, CSIRO, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

What happens if we interrupt the night instead of the day?

The names are historical: they refer to day length, but experiments showed that night length is what is measured. With a critical night length of 11 h, 16 h light / 8 h dark makes LDP flower; 8 h light / 16 h dark makes SDP flower; and 8 h light with 1 h dark in the middle plus a 16 h night still makes SDP flower, because the night is unchanged (exercise 5.1). Arabidopsis in the photo is the model long-day plant: grown in long days in a growth cabinet it flowers within a few weeks. Transition: a brief light flash in the middle of the night has a large effect, and the colour of that flash tells us which receptor reads the night.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Night breaks reveal phytochrome


8 h light / 16 h dark, brief flash mid-night:

Red makes Pfr and splits the long night into two short ones: SDP stop, LDP flower.
Far-red right after reverses it: phytochrome is the receptor.
Growers light chrysanthemums at night to delay flowering.




The flash is sensed in the leaves. How does the message reach the apex?

Exercise 5.1 c and d. Connect to the lettuce seed slide: the same last-flash rule, applied to a night instead of a seed. Students often think the red flash adds “day”; stress that it only matters because it breaks the dark period. Read the figure row by row and ask for the longest uninterrupted dark period each time: 8, 16, 8 and 16 h.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Try it: the photoperiod clock




Live version of the photoperiod table and figure. The clock shows one 24-hour cycle with noon at the top; the bar below shows the night as the plant measures it, with the critical night length (11 h, as in the lecture) as a dashed line. The two plants show whether a short-day and a long-day plant flower. Run through the “Lecture cases” buttons in order and ask the room to predict each one first: 16 L / 8 D, 8 L / 16 D, + red break, + red, far-red, + dark in day. Then slide the day length slowly from 8 to 16 h: both plants switch at 13 h of light (an 11 h night). Then add a red break and move “Flash at” towards dusk: once one fragment of the night is longer than 11 h again, the SDP flowers despite the break; this is why growers place the night break near the middle. Far-red alone has no effect, because phytochrome is already Pr at night. Reset restores the start.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
section: Florigen: a protein from leaf to apex
text:
Florigen: a protein from leaf to apex



Grafting (1930s): an induced leaf sends a signal, named florigen.
In Arabidopsis florigen is the protein FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT): FT–GFP made in leaves is found at the apex (Corbesier et al., 2007).
The leaf perceives, the phloem transports, the apex responds.




Some plants need a second condition before they can respond to day length.

Exercise 5.2. CONSTANS protein accumulates in the leaf phloem companion cells only when long days give light at the end of the day, which is how day length is converted into a molecular signal. FT is small enough to move through plasmodesmata into sieve tubes and travels with the assimilate flow from P3. At the apex it pairs with the transcription factor FD to switch on floral identity genes such as APETALA1. Transition: some plants need a winter before they can respond to day length.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Vernalisation: remembering winter



Vernalisation: prolonged cold (weeks at ~0–10 °C) gives the competence to flower. Examples: winter wheat, winter-annual Arabidopsis.
The plant does not flower in the cold. It flowers later, in warm, long days.
The cold is perceived by the shoot apex.
In Arabidopsis, cold represses FLC, a repressor of flowering. FLC stays off through later cell divisions: an epigenetic memory of winter.
The memory is reset in each generation: seeds need cold again.



Photo: Nigel Mykura, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons




Plant
Cold received
Outcome in spring long days




Winter wheat sown in autumn
Yes
Flowers, sets grain


Winter wheat sown in spring
No
Stays vegetative




Exercise 5.3 is a true/false set on these bullets; the common misconceptions are that cold triggers flowering directly and that the vernalised state is inherited. The photo shows winter wheat in an English field in winter: sown in autumn, it overwinters as a short leafy seedling, receives its weeks of cold in the field, and only flowers in the long days of the following summer. The point of vernalisation is to prevent flowering in autumn, when days are short in the run-up to winter; flowering waits for the spring after a winter has passed. Transition: once the flower opens and is pollinated, the next generation begins.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Double fertilisation: building the seed





Structure
From
Ploidy




Embryo
sperm 1 + egg
2n


Endosperm
sperm 2 + central cell
3n


Seed coat
integuments (maternal)
2n


Fruit wall
ovary wall (maternal)
2n




The endosperm is the food store of the barley grain.
Developing seeds are strong sinks (P3).




Where do those nutrients come from at the end of the season?

Exercise 5.4. The pollen tube delivers two sperm cells and both fertilise: double fertilisation. The central cell has two polar nuclei, which is why the endosperm is triploid. Close the loop to the start of the lecture: the endosperm made here is the starch store mobilised by gibberellin in the next generation. The seed coat and fruit are maternal tissue, not the next generation. The ploidy column is the usual exam check. The sink bullet links back to phloem transport in P3 and leads into senescence: the old leaves become the nutrient source for the seeds.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Senescence: recycling the leaf



Senescence is a regulated, programmed process, not passive decay.
Chlorophyll and proteins (including Rubisco) are broken down first, so the leaf yellows.
Nutrients are remobilised through the phloem to seeds and young leaves.
N, P and K are phloem-mobile and are exported. Ca is phloem-immobile and stays in the leaf.




Hormone
Effect on senescence




Cytokinin
Delays it


Ethylene, ABA, jasmonic acid
Promote it




Tobacco expressing a cytokinin-synthesis gene from a senescence promoter keeps its leaves green much longer (Gan and Amasino, 1995).



Photo: Stanature, CC0, Wikimedia Commons


Exercise 6.1. The photo shows four leaves from one young oak tree in autumn, in order of senescence: green (chlorophyll intact), yellow (chlorophyll broken down, revealing the carotenoids, with the last green along the veins), and two brown leaves whose cells have died after the nutrients were exported. The phloem-mobility rule comes from P2: calcium moves in the xylem only, so it cannot be exported from an old leaf, and calcium deficiency appears in young tissue. A yellow leaf alone does not show senescence; deficiency or stress also yields yellowing, so tissue age and growth conditions must be known. The Gan and Amasino experiment is a neat feedback loop: senescence switches on cytokinin production, which delays senescence. It also introduces the idea of a stage-specific promoter, which returns in P5.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Signal chain
cue → receptor → transduction → fast (protein) or slow (gene expression) response


Hormones
auxin, cytokinin, GA, ABA, ethylene, brassinosteroids, strigolactones


Hormone mutants
rescued by the hormone → biosynthesis defect; not rescued → perception/signalling


Dormancy
ABA maintains it; GA breaks it; quiescence is only lack of water or warmth


Barley aleurone
GA → α-amylase → starch to sugar; ABA blocks


Phytochrome
Pr (660 nm) ⇄ Pfr (730 nm); Pfr active; last flash decides


Shade avoidance
low R:FR → less Pfr → elongation, earlier flowering


Tropisms
auxin to the shaded / lower side; promotes shoot, inhibits root elongation


Apical dominance
apical auxin lowers cytokinin, raises strigolactone at buds


Photoperiod
plants measure the uninterrupted night; a red night break splits it


Florigen
FT protein: leaf → phloem → apex


Vernalisation

Senescence
cytokinin delays; N, P, K remobilised via phloem; Ca stays



Next (P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology): the same signals, ABA, jasmonic acid and salicylic acid among them, let a plant survive drought, salt and attack. And knowing the genes lets us change them.
Tutorial · Exercises · Quiz

Read the table as the life cycle: signal framework and hormones, then seed, seedling, growth direction, branching, flowering, the next seed and the ageing leaf. P5 reuses three ideas from today: ABA as a water-stress signal, hormone pathways as switches that can be turned on by an attacker, and promoters that express a gene in one tissue or condition.

title: P4 exercises — Signals, growth and reproduction
text: The questions follow the tutorial and slides. Answer each question before opening its answer.

title: P4 exercises — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Plant hormones

1.1
Match each hormone to the effect that best describes it: auxin, cytokinin, gibberellin, abscisic acid (ABA), ethylene, brassinosteroid.








Effect




A
A gas that promotes ripening of climacteric fruits and leaf abscission


B
Promotes cell division in shoot meristems and delays leaf senescence


C
Promotes stomatal closure during drought and maintains seed dormancy


D
Promotes stem elongation (bolting) and breaks seed dormancy


E
Moves by polar transport from the shoot tip; maintains apical dominance and promotes root formation on cuttings


F
A steroid that promotes cell expansion; deficient mutants are dark-green dwarfs









Answer





A: ethylene. B: cytokinin. C: ABA. D: gibberellin. E: auxin. F: brassinosteroid.





1.2
Predict whether the lateral buds of a pea shoot grow out or stay inhibited after each treatment.

intact plant
shoot apex removed (decapitated)
shoot apex removed and auxin (IAA) in lanolin paste applied to the cut stump
shoot apex removed and plain lanolin applied to the cut stump
intact plant with cytokinin applied directly to a lateral bud







Answer






Inhibited. b. Grow out. c. Inhibited: auxin replaces the apex.
Grow out: lanolin alone has no effect. e. Grows out: cytokinin promotes bud outgrowth.

Auxin moving down the stem does not enter the bud. It acts indirectly, by lowering cytokinin supply to the bud and raising strigolactone synthesis.





1.3
Put the steps of starch mobilisation in a germinating barley grain in order.

α-amylase is secreted into the starchy endosperm
the embryo releases gibberellin
sugars are absorbed by the scutellum and supply the growing embryo
gibberellin reaches the aleurone layer and induces α-amylase gene expression
starch is hydrolysed to sugars







Answer





b → d → a → e → c. ABA antagonises this response by inhibiting the gibberellin-induced expression of α-amylase.





1.4
Two dwarf pea mutants are sprayed with gibberellin. Mutant A grows to normal height. Mutant B stays dwarf. Which mutant is most likely defective in gibberellin biosynthesis, and which in gibberellin perception or signalling?






Answer





Mutant A: biosynthesis. The added hormone replaces what the plant cannot make. Mutant B: perception or signalling. The plant cannot respond to the hormone even when it is supplied.





1.5
Etiolated (dark-grown) Arabidopsis seedlings are exposed to ethylene.

Name the three features of the triple response.
What do ethylene-treated seedlings of the ethylene-insensitive mutant etr1 look like?







Answer






Shorter hypocotyl (and root), thicker (radially swollen) hypocotyl, and an exaggerated apical hook.
Like untreated dark-grown seedlings: long, thin hypocotyls with a normal apical hook. The ETR1 receptor cannot pass on the ethylene signal.

title: P4 exercises — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Tropisms

2.1
A coleoptile is lit from one side with blue light. Complete the sentences.

The light is detected by the photoreceptor ______.
Auxin is redistributed towards the ______ side.
Cells on the ______ side elongate faster.
The coleoptile therefore bends ______ the light.







Answer






Phototropin. b. Shaded. c. Shaded. d. Towards.

This is the Cholodny–Went model: lateral auxin transport causes unequal growth on the two sides of the organ.





2.2
Grass coleoptiles are lit from one side after each treatment. Predict whether each coleoptile bends towards the light.

untreated
tip removed
tip covered with an opaque cap
tip covered with a transparent cap
opaque collar around the region below the tip, tip exposed
tip cut off and replaced on a thin gelatin block







Answer






Bends. b. No bending. c. No bending. d. Bends. e. Bends. f. Bends.

The light is perceived at the tip, and a signal that can diffuse through gelatin (auxin) moves down to the growing region below.





2.3
A vertically growing root is turned horizontal.

Which cells perceive gravity, and which organelles act as statoliths?
On which side does auxin accumulate?
Which side elongates faster, and in which direction does the root bend?







Answer






Columella cells of the root cap. Starch-filled amyloplasts sediment to the lower side of the cell.
The lower side.
The upper side elongates faster, because high auxin concentrations inhibit elongation in roots. The root bends downwards.

A seedling grows under a dense leaf canopy.

Is the red : far-red ratio higher or lower than in direct sunlight? Why?
How does this change the proportion of phytochrome in the Pfr form?

Answer






Lower. Chlorophyll absorbs red light but transmits and reflects far-red light.
The proportion of Pfr falls.
Any two of: faster stem and petiole elongation, upward leaf movement, reduced branching, earlier flowering.

title: P4 exercises — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Germination and dormancy

4.1
Classify each seed as dormant or quiescent.

Dry seeds stored in a packet.
Freshly harvested seeds do not germinate on moist paper at 20 °C, but do after several months of dry storage.
Seeds in dry soil germinate after the first rain.
Seeds germinate only after several weeks of moist chilling.







Answer






Quiescent. b. Dormant (released by after-ripening). c. Quiescent.
Dormant (released by cold stratification).






4.2
Predict the germination behaviour of:

an ABA-deficient mutant
a gibberellin-deficient mutant







Answer






Reduced dormancy. Seeds may germinate while still on the mother plant (vivipary).
Seeds fail to germinate unless gibberellin is supplied.

The ABA : gibberellin balance regulates dormancy: ABA maintains it, and gibberellin promotes germination.





4.3
Four dishes each contain 20 seeds. By day 5, radicles have emerged from 12 and 14 seeds in the two control dishes, and from 16 and 18 seeds in the two treated dishes. Calculate the germination percentage of each dish and the mean for each group.






Answer





Control: 60% and 70%, mean 65%. Treated: 80% and 90%, mean 85%.

A short-day plant (SDP) and a long-day plant (LDP) both have a critical night length of 11 h. Predict whether each plant flowers under each 24 h cycle.

16 h light / 8 h dark
8 h light / 16 h dark

The length of the uninterrupted night is the deciding factor. A red night break divides the long night into two short ones. Far-red reverses the red effect, so phytochrome perceives the night break. Darkness during the day has no effect.





5.2
In Arabidopsis under long days, name:

the organ that perceives the photoperiod
the mobile protein that signals floral induction
the tissue through which it moves
the site where it acts to start flower formation







Answer






Leaves. b. FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT). c. Phloem. d. Shoot apical meristem, where FT with the transcription factor FD activates floral meristem identity genes.






5.3
True or false? Correct any false statements.

Vernalisation makes a plant flower while it is still in the cold.
Vernalisation is perceived by the shoot apex.
In Arabidopsis, vernalisation represses the flowering repressor FLC.
The vernalised state is passed on to the plant’s seeds.







Answer






False. Prolonged cold gives the competence to flower. Flowering itself usually happens later, under warmer, inductive conditions.
True.

title: P4 exercises — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Senescence

6.1

Name the hormone that delays leaf senescence and two hormones that promote it.
Which of these nutrients are efficiently remobilised from a senescing leaf to the seeds: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium?
Through which tissue are remobilised nutrients exported from the leaf?







Answer






Cytokinin delays senescence. Ethylene, ABA and jasmonic acid promote it (any two).
Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Calcium is immobile in the phloem and stays in the leaf.
Phloem.

E2.2
With no flash, move the day length slider (steps of 0.5 h). What is the longest day length at which the SDP still flowers? What is the night length then?






Answer





13 h of light, giving an 11 h night, exactly the critical night length. At 13.5 h of light the night is 10.5 h, the SDP stays vegetative and the LDP flowers. Both plants switch at the same day length; they respond in opposite directions to the same measured night.

Press “+ red break” (8 h day, 16 h night, flash at 50 %). Move “Flash at” in steps of 5 %. Over which range of flash positions does the SDP stay vegetative?

A night break works only if neither fragment reaches the critical night length, which is why growers place it near the middle of the night.

Yes, the SDP flowers (longest dark period 16 h). At night phytochrome is already mostly in the inactive Pr form, so far-red has almost no Pfr to convert; the night is not interrupted.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
About this lecture
At noon a sunlit leaf takes up CO₂ and exports sugar. At midnight the same leaf gives off CO₂. Its roots never see light, yet they grow, take up ions and feed fungal partners day and night. How does a leaf turn light into sugar, and how does that sugar pay for the whole plant? In P2 we opened the stomata and paid ~500 water molecules for every CO₂ molecule fixed. Today we follow that CO₂ into the chloroplast and out to the roots.

Light reactions: light, water and electron transport make ATP, NADPH and O₂.
Calvin–Benson cycle: ATP and NADPH fix CO₂ into sugar, and what it costs.
Rubisco’s flaw: photorespiration, and the C4 and CAM solutions.
Measuring photosynthesis: light-response curves and units.
Transport: sources, sinks and pressure flow in the phloem.
Using the sugar: respiration, fermentation and nitrogen assimilation.


The running example is one CO₂ molecule entering a leaf through an open stoma (P2) and ending up in a root, either respired or built into an amino acid. The lecture follows it in order: energy capture, fixation, the problems of fixation in hot dry conditions, measurement, transport, and use. The opening observation (a leaf releasing CO₂ at night) is explained by the light-response curve.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
One equation, two stages
6\,\text{CO}_2 + 12\,\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\,\text{O}_2 + 6\,\text{H}_2\text{O}

Linked by ATP and NADPH: one stage makes them, the other spends them.



Photo: and3k and caper437, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Start with the light reactions: where does the O₂ come from?

Exercise 1.1 is this table. The overall equation hides two separate machines, one in the membrane and one in the soluble stroma, joined by an energy currency. Point to the micrograph: the dark stacked lines are the thylakoid membranes (grana), where the light reactions run; the paler background is the stroma, where the Calvin–Benson cycle runs. The jobs: the light reactions convert light energy to chemical energy, the cycle uses that energy to reduce CO₂. The extra water on both sides of the equation is deliberate: it shows that all 12 O atoms of the released O₂ come from water, which is the next slide.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
Capturing light and splitting water



Chlorophyll absorbs blue (~430 nm) and red (~660 nm) and reflects green.
An antenna of hundreds of pigments funnels energy to a reaction centre: P680 (photosystem II), P700 (photosystem I).
At photosystem II, water is split:

2\,\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + 4\,\text{H}^+ + 4\,e^-

The O₂ comes from water, not CO₂ (¹⁸O-labelled water, Ruben and Kamen, 1941).



Photo: Kristian Peters – Fabelfroh, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Where do the electrons from water go?

Exercise 1.2. The photo shows living leaf cells of a moss, one cell layer thick, so the chloroplasts are visible without sectioning: each green disc is one chloroplast, and each holds the thylakoid membranes of the previous slide. The classic error is that O₂ comes from CO₂. The isotope experiment settles it: label the water and the O₂ is labelled; label the CO₂ and it is not. CO₂ supplies the carbon of the sugar. The electrons replace those lost by P680, and the H⁺ is released into the thylakoid lumen. Full sunlight is about 2000 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, the x-axis unit of the light-response curve later in the lecture.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
Linear electron flow



Light lifts electrons twice: at photosystem II and at photosystem I (the “Z-scheme”).
Between them, electrons flow downhill: plastoquinone (PQ) → cytochrome b₆f → plastocyanin (PC).
b₆f pumps H⁺ into the lumen.
Ferredoxin (Fd) and FNR reduce NADP⁺ to NADPH.




Result: O₂, NADPH and a proton gradient. How does the gradient make ATP?

Exercise 1.3 asks for this order: H₂O → PSII → PQ → cyt b₆f → PC → PSI → Fd → NADP⁺. Students do not need redox potentials, but should know the sequence and that two photosystems act in series; the vertical axis of the figure is electron energy, not a measured scale. Point out the two sources of lumen protons: water splitting at PSII and the cytochrome b₆f complex. The chain is structurally similar to the mitochondrial electron transport chain students know from A2.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
section: ATP synthase and cyclic electron flow
text:
ATP synthase and cyclic electron flow



Lumen pH ~5, stroma pH ~8: a 1000-fold H⁺ gradient.
ATP synthase: H⁺ flows lumen → stroma; ATP is made in the stroma.
Linear flow gives ~1.3 ATP per NADPH; the cycle needs 1.5.

The stroma now holds ATP and NADPH. What does the Calvin–Benson cycle do with them?

Exercises 1.4 and 1.5. The mechanism is the same chemiosmotic principle as in mitochondria (A2), with the membrane orientation reversed: protons are pumped into the lumen and flow out into the stroma. Cyclic flow (PSI → ferredoxin → back to the cytochrome b₆f complex, dashed arrow) pumps protons without passing electrons to NADP⁺, so it adds ATP without making NADPH or O₂. That fixes the ATP:NADPH mismatch; the 1.5 ratio is derived on the next-but-one slide.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
The Calvin–Benson cycle: three phases



Carboxylation: Rubisco adds CO₂ to ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP), giving two 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA).
Reduction: ATP and NADPH reduce 3-PGA to triose phosphate.
Regeneration: five of every six triose phosphates rebuild three RuBP.




Count the cost: how much ATP and NADPH does one sugar take?

Exercise 2.1 asks for the phases in order and the enzyme. Walk around the figure with three CO₂ so the carbon balances: 3 × 5 C + 3 C = 18 C in six triose phosphates; 15 C regenerate RuBP and 3 C leave as one net triose phosphate. Rubisco is the enzyme from P1 encoded by two genomes, and the most abundant protein on Earth.

ATP : NADPH = 9 : 6 = 3 : 2 (1.5).
Per CO₂: 3 ATP and 2 NADPH.


Not a “dark reaction”

The cycle needs ATP and NADPH from the light reactions.
Several of its enzymes (including Rubisco, via Rubisco activase) are switched on by light and off in darkness.
In the dark, the cycle stops within minutes.


Rubisco has a second problem: it does not only react with CO₂.

Exercise 2.2 (18 ATP and 12 NADPH, ratio 3:2) and 2.3a. The name “dark reactions” means only that the cycle does not absorb photons itself; it runs in the light and stops in darkness because its substrates run out and its enzymes are deactivated. This explains the opening observation in part: at night the leaf fixes no CO₂ and only respiration remains.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
Rubisco’s flaw: photorespiration



Rubisco is slow (~3 reactions s⁻¹) and can use O₂ instead of CO₂, giving 2-phosphoglycolate, which the cycle cannot use.
Salvage runs through chloroplast → peroxisome → mitochondrion, and releases CO₂ already fixed.
25 °C, air: ~1 oxygenation per 3 carboxylations; ~25 % less C3 photosynthesis.
Photorespiration ≠ respiration.




When does Rubisco make this mistake more often?

Exercises 2.3b–d and 2.4. Rubisco evolved when the atmosphere had almost no O₂, so discrimination against O₂ was not needed. Photorespiration is a salvage pathway: it recovers three of every four carbons in 2-phosphoglycolate but loses one as CO₂, releases NH₃ that must be refixed, and costs ATP and NADPH. Leaves contain so much Rubisco (up to half of their soluble protein) because it is slow. Stress the distinction from mitochondrial respiration, which is a common exam error: photorespiration starts with Rubisco and recycles 2-phosphoglycolate; respiration oxidises sugar to make ATP.

What increases photorespiration?

The problem is worst in hot, dry, bright conditions: exactly when P2’s stomata close to save water.

Some plants have evolved a fix: raise the CO₂ concentration at Rubisco.

Exercise 2.5. Connect directly to P2: ABA closes stomata in drought, the CO₂ inside the leaf is used up, and Rubisco increasingly fixes O₂. So the water-saving response worsens the carbon problem. Greenhouse growers raise CO₂ to about 1000 ppm partly for this reason. Transition to the CO₂-concentrating mechanisms.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
C4: separating fixation in space



Mesophyll: PEP carboxylase fixes HCO₃⁻ into oxaloacetate (4C), then malate. It ignores O₂.
Malate moves to the bundle sheath and releases CO₂ next to Rubisco at ~10× the air concentration.
Regenerating PEP costs 2 ATP per CO₂: 5 instead of 3.


Kranz anatomy; maize, sugarcane, sorghum.



Photo: Kelvinsong, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Desert succulents use the same enzymes but separate the steps in time.

Exercises 3.4 (advantage and cost) and part of 3.1. Kranz is German for wreath: in the section, find a vein and the ring of large bundle-sheath cells around it, with mesophyll cells outside. C4 is a pump that concentrates CO₂ at Rubisco, paid for in ATP. Advantage: almost no photorespiration, so higher photosynthesis and water-use efficiency in warm, bright conditions. Cost: 5 ATP per CO₂ instead of 3, so C4 is no better in cool or shaded conditions. C4 plants are only about 3 % of species but carry out about a quarter of land photosynthesis, mostly tropical grasses. The Calvin–Benson cycle and Rubisco are still there; C4 only changes how CO₂ is delivered.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
CAM: separating fixation in time


Night, stomata open: PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ → malate, stored as malic acid in the vacuole. Acidity rises.
Day, stomata closed: malate is decarboxylated and Rubisco fixes the CO₂ using light energy. Acidity falls.

Cool night air: very little water lost per CO₂.
Slow growth: the vacuole limits storage.
Fingerprint: acid at dawn, not at dusk.



Photo: Markus Leupold-Löwenthal, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Side by side: C4 separates the two steps in space, CAM in time.

Exercise 3.3: the acidity rhythm is the CAM fingerprint; Kranz anatomy is the C4 fingerprint. CAM solves the water problem from P2 by opening stomata only when evaporation is low. The cost is capacity: the night’s CO₂ store sets the day’s photosynthesis. Pineapple is the main CAM crop; others are prickly pear (Opuntia), Agave and many orchids. Again, Rubisco is still present and does the final fixation.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
section: C4 and CAM: space versus time
text:
C4 and CAM: space versus time



Both use PEP carboxylase first, to make malate, and Rubisco last.
C4: two cell types, both steps by day.
CAM: one cell, steps at night and by day.
Both raise CO₂ at Rubisco, so photorespiration stays low.





This figure is the one-sentence summary of the last two slides: the same two enzymes, separated either between cells (C4) or between night and day (CAM). Ask students where the stomata are open in each case and why that matters for water loss; the next slide puts numbers on it.

How do we measure how fast a leaf is fixing carbon?

Exercises 3.1 and 3.2. The water row links the three pathways back to P2’s transpiration ratio. Students should classify the six crops in 3.2 from this table. Transition from mechanism to measurement: a gas-exchange instrument measures the net CO₂ flux of a leaf.

The light-response curve

Dark respiration: 2 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹.
Compensation point: 50 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
Gross at 200 = 6 + 2 = 8.




Net = gross − respiration. Below compensation the leaf loses carbon: midnight.

Exercise 4.1. Units: light in µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, net CO₂ in µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ (positive = net uptake). Slopes: 50 → 200 is 6/150 = 0.04 CO₂ per photon; 200 → 800 is 3/600 = 0.005, so the curve saturates. The curve answers the opening observation: in darkness only respiration remains, so net exchange is negative. At low light, rate is limited by light; at high light, by CO₂ supply and Rubisco capacity, so extra photons add little. Shade leaves have lower compensation points and lower respiration than sun leaves. Assume respiration is unchanged in light to get gross photosynthesis. The plotted curve is a smooth fit through the four table points.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
section: Try it: a leaf under changing light, CO₂ and heat
text:
Try it: a leaf under changing light, CO₂ and heat




Live version of the light-response curve, for a sun leaf (a standard leaf photosynthesis model, so the numbers are larger than the shade-leaf table on the previous slide). Drag the round handle along the curve or use the Light slider; the readout gives net and gross photosynthesis, dark respiration, the CO₂ released by photorespiration and what limits the rate. Suggested sequence, about 5 minutes. (1) Tick “Zoom in on low light”: find the compensation point and the respiration line, then untick. (2) Press “Keep this curve”, then “Hot, dry”: the curve drops, photorespiration rises (more O₂ per CO₂) and respiration doubles; this is P2’s closed stomata meeting Rubisco’s flaw. (3) Press “1000 ppm” (greenhouse): photorespiration falls and the plateau rises. (4) Switch to “C4 leaf (maize)” and repeat “Hot, dry”: C4 keeps most of its rate because PEP carboxylase concentrates CO₂. (5) Press “Cool, 12 °C” for both C3 and C4: now C3 wins, because C4 pays 2 extra ATP per CO₂ and its enzymes are cold-sensitive. Ask the room to predict each change before you press. Reset restores the start. The figure on the previous slide is the static fallback for PDF.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
section: From a rate to an amount
text:
From a rate to an amount


A leaf of 0.02 m² takes up CO₂ at 6 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ for 10 min:
6\ \frac{\mu\text{mol}}{\text{m}^2\,\text{s}} \times 0.02\ \text{m}^2 \times 600\ \text{s} = 72\ \mu\text{mol CO}_2
72\times10^{-6}\ \text{mol} \times 44\ \text{g mol}^{-1} = 3.2\times10^{-3}\ \text{g} = 3.2\ \text{mg CO}_2

Multiply by area and by time in seconds; the m⁻² and s⁻¹ cancel.
Carry the units through every step; most errors are in minutes → seconds.



Photo: Viséan, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

That carbon is made in the leaf. How does it reach a root or a fruit?

The photo shows where such numbers come from: a portable gas-exchange system (LI-6800) clamped onto a maize leaf in a field trial. The chamber encloses a known leaf area, sets light and CO₂, and measures the CO₂ and water-vapour difference between incoming and outgoing air, so it reports net photosynthesis directly in µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹; the light-response curve on the previous slides is made with such an instrument. Exercise 4.2. This is the same unit logic as the transpiration calculation in P2. Show the cancellation of units explicitly. Transition to transport: carbon fixed in a leaf is exported as sucrose through the phloem from P1.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
Sources and sinks



Source: exports sugar. Sink: imports it.
The phloem carries mainly sucrose.
Roles change with development.




Organ
Role




Mature, illuminated leaf
source


Developing fruit, root tip
sink


Young, expanding leaf
sink


Tuber sprouting in spring
source





Photo: Bmerva, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

What pushes sap from a source to a sink?

Exercises 5.1 and 5.3. The sprouting tuber in the photo is the important case: a storage organ that was a sink last summer becomes a source when its starch is mobilised for the new shoots. Source and sink describe current carbon flow, not organ type. A young leaf is a sink until it is roughly half expanded, then becomes a source. Chloroplasts store starch during the day and break it down at night to keep sucrose export going.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
Pressure flow in the phloem



Sucrose is loaded into sieve tubes (often H⁺-coupled).
Ψs falls; water enters from the xylem.
Pressure rises at the source (~1 MPa).
Sap moves by bulk flow, ~1 m h⁻¹.
Sucrose is unloaded at the sink; water leaves.




Water potential (P2) running a second transport system.

Exercise 5.2 asks for this order. This is the Münch pressure-flow model. It reuses every idea from P2: Ψs = −cRT drives water entry, Ψp builds up, and flow goes from high to low pressure. Loading uses the proton gradient from P2. Direction is set by where sources and sinks are, so phloem can move sap up or down, unlike xylem. Next: how do we know the sap is under pressure?

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
section: Evidence: aphids tap the sieve tubes
text:
Evidence: aphids tap the sieve tubes



An aphid’s mouthparts (stylet) enter one sieve element.
Cut the stylet: sap keeps flowing out for hours, pushed by the pressure inside.
The sap is mostly sucrose, often 0.3–1 M.
Aphids excrete surplus sugar as honeydew drops.



Photo: Lamiot, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Then what does the sink do with the sugar?

The aphid stylet technique is the classic evidence for the pressure-flow model: the aphid does not pump, the sap is forced into its gut by the sieve-tube pressure, and a severed stylet bleeds pure phloem sap that can be collected and analysed. The sap is a concentrated sucrose solution with amino acids and ions, so aphids take in far more sugar than they need and excrete the rest as honeydew, which ants collect. The photo shows a colony on a nasturtium stem: every aphid has its stylet in a sieve element. Transition: the sink uses the sugar, either in respiration or as carbon skeletons.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget

Using the sugar: respiration










Stage

Electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation
inner mitochondrial membrane
ATP, H₂O (O₂ is the final acceptor)



Aerobic: ~30 ATP per glucose.

Flooded roots: fermentation

No O₂ → electron transport stops → NADH accumulates.
Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue.
Products in roots: ethanol and CO₂ (some lactate).
Only 2 ATP per glucose: ~15× less.



Every living cell respires, in light and in darkness: roots for ion uptake (P2), growth and maintenance.

Respiration also supplies the carbon skeletons that turn nitrate into amino acids.

Exercises 6.1 and 6.2. This links to P2’s waterlogging chain: without O₂, the root’s ATP supply drops about fifteen-fold, so the H⁺-ATPase and ion uptake fail. Ethanol accumulation is also toxic. Respiration is not just the reverse of photosynthesis: it provides ATP and the intermediates used to build amino acids and other compounds.

Reducing nitrate to ammonium takes 8 electrons: from photosynthesis (ferredoxin) or respiration (NADH).

So nitrogen uptake (P2) depends on carbon metabolism, and photosynthesis depends on nitrogen in Rubisco and chlorophyll.

Back to the leaf and the root we started with.

Exercise 6.3 asks for the order and the enzymes. The GS/GOGAT cycle is how almost all inorganic nitrogen enters organic molecules in plants, including ammonium from photorespiration and from rhizobia (P2). Emphasise the two-way dependence: carbon pays for nitrogen assimilation, and nitrogen builds the photosynthetic machinery.

Tutorial · Exercises · Quiz

Read the table as the path of one CO₂ molecule: captured by the light reactions’ products in the Calvin–Benson cycle, sometimes lost to photorespiration, concentrated by C4 and CAM, measured as a net rate, exported through the phloem, and used in respiration and nitrogen assimilation. title: P3 exercises — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
The Calvin–Benson cycle and photorespiration

2.1
Name the three phases of the Calvin–Benson cycle in order, and the enzyme that catalyses the first.






Answer





Carboxylation → reduction → regeneration of ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP). Carboxylation is catalysed by Rubisco (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase), which adds CO₂ to RuBP to form two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate.





2.2
Fixing 3 CO₂ into one net triose phosphate requires 9 ATP and 6 NADPH.

How much ATP and NADPH are needed to fix 6 CO₂, the carbon of one hexose?
What is the ATP : NADPH ratio required?







Answer






18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
3 : 2 (1.5 ATP per NADPH).






2.3
True or false? Correct any false statements.

The Calvin–Benson cycle runs all night because it is a “dark reaction”.
Rubisco can react with O₂ as well as CO₂.
Photorespiration is the same process as mitochondrial respiration.
Photorespiration releases CO₂ that has already been fixed.







Answer






False. The cycle needs ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, and several of its enzymes are activated in light; it stops soon after darkness begins.
True.
False. Photorespiration starts with Rubisco oxygenation and recycles 2-phosphoglycolate; mitochondrial respiration oxidises sugars to make ATP.
True. CO₂ is released in the mitochondria when glycine is converted to serine.






2.4
Name the three organelles involved in the photorespiratory pathway.






Answer





Chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion.





2.5
State whether each change increases or decreases the rate of photorespiration relative to carboxylation in a C3 leaf.

Higher leaf temperature
Stomatal closure during drought
Higher atmospheric CO₂ concentration







Answer






Increases (the solubility of CO₂ falls more than that of O₂, and Rubisco’s specificity for CO₂ decreases).
Increases (the CO₂ concentration inside the leaf falls).
Decreases.

Oxaloacetate (4 C), stored as malate


Separation of initial fixation and Calvin cycle
None
Spatial: mesophyll and bundle-sheath cells
Temporal: night and day


Stomata open mainly
Day
Day
Night


Photorespiration
High in warm conditions
Low
Low



In all three, the CO₂ is finally fixed by Rubisco in the Calvin–Benson cycle.





3.2
Classify each plant as C3, C4 or CAM: maize, wheat, pineapple, sugarcane, rice, prickly pear cactus (Opuntia).






Answer





C3: wheat, rice. C4: maize, sugarcane. CAM: pineapple, Opuntia.





3.3
Which observation is characteristic of a CAM plant?

Bundle-sheath cells packed with chloroplasts
Acidity of the leaf tissue rises during the night and falls during the day
Stomata open only at midday
Rubisco is absent







Answer






Malic acid accumulates in the vacuole at night and is decarboxylated during the day to supply CO₂ to Rubisco. Option a describes C4 (Kranz) anatomy.






3.4
Name the advantage and the cost of the C4 CO₂-concentrating mechanism.






Answer





Advantage: high CO₂ around Rubisco in the bundle sheath suppresses photorespiration, giving higher photosynthesis and water-use efficiency in warm, bright conditions. Cost: extra ATP (2 ATP per CO₂) to regenerate PEP from pyruvate.

text:
Light-response curves and units

4.1
The net CO₂ exchange of one leaf is measured at four light levels. Positive values are net uptake.



Light (µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹)
Net CO₂ exchange (µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹)

What is the rate of respiration in darkness?
What is the light compensation point?
Calculate the increase in net CO₂ uptake per additional µmol photons between 50 and 200, and between 200 and 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
Assuming respiration is unchanged in light, what is gross photosynthesis at 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹?







Answer






2 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹.
50 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, where net exchange is zero.
6 / 150 = 0.04 µmol CO₂ per µmol photons; 3 / 600 = 0.005 µmol CO₂ per µmol photons. The response saturates at high light.
6 + 2 = 8 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹.






4.2
A leaf of area 0.02 m² takes up CO₂ at a constant net rate of 6 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹ for 10 min.

Calculate the total net CO₂ uptake in µmol.
Convert it to mg CO₂ (M(CO₂) = 44 g mol⁻¹).







Answer






6 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ × 0.02 m² × 600 s = 72 µmol CO₂.
72 × 10⁻⁶ mol × 44 g mol⁻¹ = 3.2 × 10⁻³ g = 3.2 mg CO₂.

title: P3 exercises — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
Sources, sinks and phloem transport

5.1
Classify each organ as a source or a sink.

Mature, illuminated leaf
Developing fruit
Root tip
Young, expanding leaf
Potato tuber sprouting in spring







Answer






Source. b. Sink. c. Sink. d. Sink. e. Source (stored starch is mobilised to supply the new shoot).






5.2
Put the steps of the pressure-flow model of phloem transport in order:

hydrostatic pressure rises in the sieve tubes at the source
sucrose is loaded into the sieve-element–companion-cell complex
sucrose is unloaded at the sink and water leaves the sieve tubes
water enters the sieve tubes from the xylem by osmosis
sap moves by bulk flow towards the sink







Answer





b → d → a → e → c.





5.3
Name the main sugar transported in the phloem of most plants and the main storage carbohydrate in chloroplasts.






Answer





Sucrose is transported in the phloem; starch is stored in chloroplasts.

6.2
Roots of a flooded plant switch to fermentation.

Why can glycolysis continue during fermentation?
Name the main fermentation products in plant roots.
About how many ATP are formed per glucose by fermentation, compared with complete aerobic oxidation?







Answer






Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ from NADH, which glycolysis requires.
Ethanol and CO₂ (and some lactate).
2 ATP per glucose by fermentation, compared with about 30 ATP by aerobic respiration.






6.3
Put the steps of nitrate assimilation in order and name the enzyme for each step: ammonium → glutamine; nitrite → ammonium; nitrate → nitrite; glutamine + 2-oxoglutarate → glutamate.






Answer






Nitrate → nitrite: nitrate reductase (cytosol).
Nitrite → ammonium: nitrite reductase (plastid).
Ammonium + glutamate → glutamine: glutamine synthetase (GS).
Glutamine + 2-oxoglutarate → 2 glutamate: glutamate synthase (GOGAT).

The reducing power, ATP and carbon skeletons (2-oxoglutarate) come from photosynthesis and respiration, so nitrogen assimilation depends on carbon metabolism.

title: P3 exercises — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
Explore: Light-response curve
The demo plots net CO₂ uptake of one sun leaf against light, for a C3 leaf (wheat) or a C4 leaf (maize). Use the Light slider (or drag the round handle) to read the curve; the table gives net and gross photosynthesis, dark respiration, the CO₂ released by photorespiration, the light compensation point and what limits the rate. The scenario buttons (“Hot, dry”, “1000 ppm”, “Cool, 12 °C”) change CO₂, temperature and stomata but keep the light where it is. Press Reset before each question.




E1.1
Start values: C3 leaf, 420 ppm CO₂, 25 °C, light 600 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.

Read off net uptake, gross photosynthesis and dark respiration. Show that the three numbers are consistent.
What limits the rate at this light: light or Rubisco?
Move the light to 0. What is the net uptake now, and why is it negative?







Answer






Net 14.7, gross 15.9 and respiration 1.2 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. Net = gross − respiration: 15.9 − 1.2 = 14.7.
Light. At 2000 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ the limit switches to Rubisco (net about 16), where the curve flattens.
−1.2 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. In darkness there is no photosynthesis, but mitochondrial respiration continues and releases CO₂.






E1.2
Tick “Zoom in on low light”. Read off the light compensation point of the C3 leaf at 25 °C, then press “C4 leaf (maize)” and read it again. Which leaf has the lower compensation point, and by about how much?






Answer





C3: 25 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. C4: 23 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. The two are almost the same: at 25 °C both leaves have the same dark respiration (1.2), and at low light the C4 leaf’s extra ATP cost per CO₂ roughly cancels the C3 leaf’s loss to photorespiration.





E1.3
Reset (C3, light 600) and press “Hot, dry” (38 °C, stomata nearly closed).

Read off net uptake, the CO₂ released by photorespiration (with the number of O₂ fixed per CO₂) and dark respiration. Compare with E1.1.
Now press “C4 leaf (maize)” and “Hot, dry” again. What is the net uptake of the C4 leaf?
Which enzyme explains the difference between b and a?







Answer






Net uptake falls from 14.7 to 1.5 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. Photorespiration rises from 2.7 to 5.4 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ (O₂/CO₂ from 0.29 to 1.10), and respiration rises from 1.2 to 3.0. Closed stomata lower the CO₂ inside the leaf, and heat raises Rubisco’s oxygenation relative to carboxylation.
13.8 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹, about nine times the C3 leaf.
PEP carboxylase. It does not react with O₂ and binds CO₂ (as HCO₃⁻) at low concentration, so the C4 leaf concentrates CO₂ around Rubisco in the bundle sheath and photorespiration stays near zero (0.3).






E1.4
Reset and press “1000 ppm” (a greenhouse with CO₂ enrichment), light 600.

Read off net uptake and photorespiration of the C3 leaf.
Press “C4 leaf (maize)”. Does raising CO₂ from 420 to 1000 ppm increase the net uptake of the C4 leaf at this light?







Answer






Net 18.9 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ (up from 14.7); photorespiration 1.3 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ (down from 2.7; O₂/CO₂ 0.12). More CO₂ wins the competition with O₂ at Rubisco’s active site.
No: it stays at 29.7 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹, because the C4 leaf already concentrates CO₂ and is light-limited at 600. This is why CO₂ enrichment benefits C3 crops more than C4 crops.






E1.5
Reset and press “Cool, 12 °C” (light 600). Read off net uptake for the C3 leaf, then press “C4 leaf (maize)” and “Cool, 12 °C”. Which leaf takes up more CO₂, and what limits the C4 leaf?






Answer





C3: 10.1 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. C4: 6.0 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. The C3 leaf wins. The C4 leaf is limited by enzyme capacity: its enzymes are cold-sensitive, and it pays 2 extra ATP per CO₂, which is not worth it when photorespiration is already low in the cold (C3 O₂/CO₂ is only 0.15 at 12 °C). This is why C4 grasses dominate warm regions and C3 grasses cool ones.



Continue with the self-check quiz.

title: Optional R: repeat one familiar analysis
text:
What you need
Use the downloaded student project with physiology.Rproj, data/ and optional-computing/ kept in their supplied relative positions. R and RStudio with the Intro Computing packages readr, dplyr, ggplot2, knitr and rmarkdown are needed to run and render. Set up packages before the session using the supported Intro Computing instructions; do not put installation commands in an analysis report. HTML rendering also needs Pandoc, supplied by RStudio or Quarto in the teaching environment.
The source files are analysis.R and respirometry.Rmd. The input is animal-respirometry.csv, documented in the data dictionary. These values are simulated.

title: Optional R: repeat one familiar analysis
text:
Read before running
The function in analysis.R imports and checks the table, calculates a background-corrected amount, divides by time and mass, summarises groups and plots each animal. Its checks suit this deliberately complete teaching dataset; a real dataset needs protocol-specific checks and explicit handling of missing or unexpected readings.
The calculation is the same one already used by hand:
oxygen_used_umol <- (initial - final - blank) * water_volume_l
rate_umol_min_g <- oxygen_used_umol / duration_min / mass_g
Each row is one animal, so grouped counts are animal counts here. That would not automatically be true for repeated measurements from one animal.

title: Optional R: repeat one familiar analysis
text:
Run from the project root
Open physiology.Rproj and create a source script or use the supplied script as a reference. In the R console, starting at the project root, run:
source("optional-computing/analysis.R")
analysis <- analyse_respirometry("data/animal-respirometry.csv")
analysis$rates
analysis$summary
analysis$plot
Locate A01 and A02 in the output. Their rates should be 0.18 and 0.20 µmol O₂ min⁻¹ g⁻¹. Group means should be 0.20 and 0.325. Explain why the mean is higher in the warmer simulated group, and why this alone does not show better growth or performance.

R Markdown evaluates relative input paths from that document’s folder, so the report uses ../data/animal-respirometry.csv and sources analysis.R beside it. The project-root commands above instead use data/.... These are two descriptions of the same file from different working directories.
The complete report produces a self-contained HTML file next to the .Rmd. Read its design, calculation and limitations, not only its figure. Restart R and Knit again without creating console objects first. Keep the source, function, dictionary and input with the HTML if sharing the work.

text:

Copy the report before changing it. Add one sentence explaining the independent unit and one identifying an assumption you would need to check in a real experiment. title: Physiology glossary
text:
Use these short definitions to orient yourself, then return to the relevant unit for the mechanism and its limits. Terms describe a process in context; similar words do not always imply the same mechanism in plants and animals.







Term
Working meaning




Acclimation
A change in an individual’s phenotype in response to conditions during its lifetime


Adaptation
A heritable feature shaped by evolution that contributes to function in a particular environment


Action potential
A regenerative change in membrane voltage produced by changes in ion conductance


Active transport
Transport coupled to an energy source that can move a substance against its electrochemical gradient


Apoplast
Plant cell-wall and extracellular continuum outside the plasma membranes


Assimilation
Incorporation of a resource into organic material; specify carbon, nitrogen or another resource


Autotroph
An organism using inorganic carbon as a major carbon source; the energy source must also be specified


Chemical potential
A quantity describing a substance’s tendency to move or react under given conditions


Compensation point
Conditions at which opposing fluxes balance; specify the measured net flux


Conductance
Ease of movement of a particular current or flux through a pathway


Control
A comparison or reference condition used to help interpret an experimental change


Differentiation
Development of specialised cell properties and functions


Diffusion
Net movement down a chemical-potential gradient arising from molecular motion


Electrochemical gradient
Combined chemical and electrical driving force acting on an ion


Endothermy
Substantial use of metabolic heat to maintain body temperature


Ectothermy
Predominant reliance on external heat sources for body heat balance


Experimental unit
The smallest unit independently assigned to a treatment in the design


Feedback
A response that influences the process or variable that generated the response


Filtration
Pressure-driven movement of fluid and permeable solutes across a barrier


Gross photosynthesis
Photosynthetic carbon fixation before subtracting the losses specified by the measurement/model


Homeostasis
Dynamic regulation of internal variables within a functional range


Hormone
A signalling substance whose effect depends on receptors, context and concentration


Hydraulic conductivity
Ease of water movement through a pathway for a specified driving gradient


Meristem
A plant region with cells that maintain the capacity for division and contribute to growth


Metabolism
The connected chemical transformations that sustain living systems


Net gas exchange
The measured balance of opposing gas fluxes under the stated conditions


Osmosis
Water movement across a selectively permeable membrane driven by a water-potential difference


Osmolarity
Total concentration of osmotically active particles per litre of solution


Osmoregulation
Regulation of body fluid water and solute relationships


Phloem
Vascular tissue involved in transport of assimilates and other substances between sources and sinks


Photoperiod
Duration of light in a daily cycle; responses often depend on associated night duration


Photosynthate
Organic product of photosynthesis, including carbohydrates


Plasticity
Ability of a genotype to produce different phenotypes under different conditions


Receptor
A molecule that detects a signal and participates in initiating a response


Replicate
A repeat whose level of independence must be specified; technical repeats differ from independent experimental units


Respiration
Metabolic processes that transfer energy from substrates; distinguish cellular respiration from ventilation


Senescence
Regulated age- or context-associated changes leading toward loss of function and often resource remobilisation


Sink
A tissue or organ importing assimilates for use or storage under the stated conditions


Source
A tissue or organ supplying assimilates for export under the stated conditions


Standard deviation
A measure of spread among observations; not itself uncertainty in a group mean


Stoma
An epidermal pore regulated by guard cells, contributing to gas exchange and water loss


Symplast
Cytoplasmic continuum of plant cells connected by plasmodesmata


Transpiration
Loss of water vapour from plant surfaces, principally through stomata in many leaves


Turgor
Hydrostatic pressure of cell contents against the wall


Ventilation
Bulk movement of respiratory medium across an exchange surface


Water potential
Water’s potential energy per unit volume relative to a reference, useful for predicting its movement


Xylem
Vascular tissue that conducts water and solutes and contributes structural support



The tutorials introduce these ideas through examples. For background and more detailed definitions, see OpenStax Biology 2e and the reading guide.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
text:
About this lecture
In A3, blood carried O₂ from the gills or lungs to every cell. But the same blood must also keep its water and ion content stable, and the thin, enlarged surfaces that exchange gases also let water and ions through. A goldfish lives in almost pure water, a cod in water three times saltier than its blood, and a kangaroo rat in a desert where it never drinks. All three keep their plasma near 300 mOsm L⁻¹. How?

The physics: osmolarity, osmotic water movement and tonicity.
Life in water: conformers and regulators; freshwater and marine fish; sharks.
The tool: the transporting epithelial cell.
The mammalian kidney: filtration, reabsorption and secretion; what each nephron segment does; clearance.
Saving water: the medullary gradient and ADH.
Getting rid of nitrogen: ammonia, urea and uric acid; the insect solution.


The single picture for today: plasma held near 300 mOsm in three very different environments. The goldfish is flooded with water and loses salt; the cod loses water and gains salt; the kangaroo rat loses water by evaporation and must excrete nitrogen without wasting water. The lecture first gives the physical rules that decide which way water moves, then the cellular tool (the polarised epithelium) that every solution is built from, then the mammalian kidney in detail, and finally the problem of nitrogen waste, which ties water balance to metabolism. The link back to A3: gills and lungs are designed to be permeable, so they are also the main route of unwanted water and ion movement.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: The problem: three animals, one target
text:
The problem: three animals, one target





mOsm L⁻¹

Kangaroo rat

~5 (fresh water)

desert air, food
