Gills are built for O₂ (A3): large and thin, so equally leaky to water and ions.
Each animal must balance input = output for water and for each ion.



Photo: George Harrison, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

To predict which way water moves, we first have to count dissolved particles.

Set up the running examples; the photo is a giant kangaroo rat; kangaroo rats never drink and get their water from the metabolism of dry seeds. Point out that the problem is created by the solution to the gas-exchange problem: a surface built for diffusion of O₂ cannot be made impermeable to water. The plasma values are typical; the exact number is not the point, the direction of the difference from the surroundings is. Remind students of the A1 idea of dynamic balance: a constant plasma osmolarity is a balance of continuous fluxes in and out.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
text:
Osmolarity counts particles
Osmolarity = molar concentration × number of particles each formula unit releases in solution (unit: Osm L⁻¹ or mOsm L⁻¹).



Solution (ideal, fully dissociated)
Particles
Osmolarity




0.10 mol L⁻¹ glucose
1
100 mOsm L⁻¹


0.10 mol L⁻¹ NaCl (Na⁺ + Cl⁻)
2
200 mOsm L⁻¹


0.10 mol L⁻¹ Na₂SO₄ (2 Na⁺ + SO₄²⁻)
3
300 mOsm L⁻¹


0.10 mol L⁻¹ glucose + 0.10 mol L⁻¹ NaCl
1 + 2
300 mOsm L⁻¹




Osmolarity depends on the number of particles, not their mass or size: one albumin molecule (66 kDa) counts the same as one urea molecule (60 Da).
Reference values: fresh water 1–10, plasma ~290–300, seawater ~1,000 mOsm L⁻¹.

So which way does water move between two solutions?

Work through the table: the only skill is to count how many particles each formula unit releases. Mixtures simply add. Make the mass point explicitly, because students instinctively weigh solutes. The reference values are worth memorising; they are used throughout the lecture. Real solutions are not perfectly ideal (NaCl behaves as about 1.8 particles), but the ideal count is what we use for all calculations in this course.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: Water moves towards the higher osmolarity
text:
Water moves towards the higher osmolarity

Across a membrane permeable to water but not solute, water moves from the lower to the higher osmolarity.
Compared with body fluids of 300 mOsm L⁻¹, a medium is

hyposmotic if lower (fresh water): water tends to enter the animal;
isosmotic if equal: no net osmotic water movement;
hyperosmotic if higher (seawater): water tends to leave the animal.

The driving force is the osmotic pressure \pi = cRT. A difference of 300 mOsm L⁻¹ at 37 °C gives \pi \approx 7.6 atm.
An opposing hydrostatic pressure can stop net water flow before the concentrations become equal (as in a plant cell pressing on its wall, P2).

But does osmolarity alone predict whether a cell swells or shrinks?

The three terms are always relative: say “hyperosmotic to what”. The numerical osmotic pressure shows that osmosis is a strong force: 7.6 atmospheres is more than the pressure at 70 m depth in water. Hydrostatic pressure is the counter-force: water flow stops when the pressure difference equals the osmotic pressure difference. Students meet this again in capillaries and in plant turgor. The transition question sets up tonicity: osmolarity counts all particles, but some particles cross membranes.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
text:
Tonicity: only trapped solutes count
Tonicity describes the effect of a solution on cell volume. Only solutes that cannot cross the membrane exert a lasting osmotic effect.


Red blood cells (inside 300 mOsm L⁻¹; urea crosses, NaCl does not):



Bath (mOsm L⁻¹)
Tonicity
Cells




NaCl 300
isotonic
keep volume


NaCl 200
hypotonic
swell


NaCl 400
hypertonic
shrink


NaCl 150 + urea 150
hypotonic
swell



Urea equilibrates; only the 150 of NaCl counts. Isosmotic does not mean isotonic.


Micrographs: Zephyris, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons


The micrographs show the three outcomes in real red cells: crenated (spiky) in hypertonic solution, biconcave discs in isotonic, swollen spheres in hypotonic. The last row of the table is the important one: total osmolarity matches the cell, yet the cells swell, because urea is a penetrating solute. Its concentration equalises across the membrane, so it adds nothing to the difference. The rule: tonicity depends only on non-penetrating solutes. A solution of pure urea at 300 mOsm is isosmotic and strongly hypotonic, and the cells burst. This idea returns with sharks, which use urea as a body-fluid osmolyte.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: Try it: tonicity and the red cell
text:
Try it: tonicity and the red cell




Live version of the tonicity table. The cell starts with 300 mOsm of trapped solute; the left panel shows the bath (blue dots NaCl, gold dots urea) and the right panel the cell volume over time. It opens on the trap case, NaCl 150 + urea 150: the bath is isosmotic, yet the cell swells as urea diffuses in and water follows, ending at about 1.7 times its volume. Then click the presets in order: NaCl 300 (nothing happens), NaCl 200 (swells), NaCl 400 (shrinks within a moment and crenates; water moves fast). Ask the room to predict “Urea 300” before clicking: isosmotic, but the cell bursts, because none of the solute is trapped. Finally untick “Membrane lets urea through” with the 150 + 150 bath: now urea acts like NaCl and the cell keeps its volume, which shows that tonicity is a property of the solution and the membrane together. The time axis is schematic; in real red cells water equilibrates in well under a second.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
text:
Conformers and regulators



Osmoconformers: body fluids follow the medium. Mussels, sea stars and many crabs are ~1,000 mOsm L⁻¹ in seawater. They may still regulate single ions (crabs keep Mg²⁺ low).
Osmoregulators hold their own osmolarity: bony fishes, freshwater invertebrates, all land animals.
Stenohaline: narrow salinity range (goldfish). Euryhaline: wide range (salmon, eels).




Bony fishes are regulators. So what must a freshwater and a marine teleost do?

Conforming is cheap because there is no osmotic gradient to fight, but the cells must tolerate whatever the medium does. Regulating costs energy but gives cells a stable environment. The ion point corrects a common error: “conformer” refers to total osmolarity, not to every solute. Euryhaline fish such as salmon switch their gill transport direction when they migrate, which leads straight into the comparison on the next slide.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: Freshwater and marine teleosts: opposite problems
text:
Freshwater and marine teleosts: opposite problems



Fresh water: fish hyperosmotic to the medium. Gains water, loses salt; drinks little; much dilute urine; gill cells take up NaCl; ions also from food.
Seawater: fish hyposmotic. Loses water, gains salt; drinks seawater; little urine, about isosmotic; gill cells secrete NaCl; kidney removes Mg²⁺ and SO₄²⁻.
Same organs, direction of transport reversed. The gill cells that move ions are ionocytes.




Marine sharks live in the same sea as the cod, but solve it differently.

Go through each row as a consequence of the first row: once you know whether the fish is hyper- or hyposmotic to its medium, everything else follows. The marine teleost drinks to replace water lost osmotically, but drinking seawater adds salt; the gill ionocytes then secrete the NaCl and the kidney removes the divalent ions the gills cannot handle. The freshwater fish faces the reverse: it gets rid of the excess water as copious dilute urine and recovers ions actively at the gills and from food. Exercise 2.1 asks for this comparison; every row of it is on the figure.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: Sharks: becoming slightly saltier than the sea
text:
Sharks: becoming slightly saltier than the sea



Plasma NaCl stays low, but sharks and rays retain urea (~350 mmol L⁻¹) and TMAO.
Total ~1,050 vs sea ~1,000 mOsm L⁻¹: water moves slightly in, so sharks do not drink.
Gills are almost impermeable to urea; TMAO counteracts urea’s effect on proteins.
NaCl that leaks in is secreted by the rectal gland (~2× plasma NaCl).



Photo: Doug Costa, NOAA/SBNMS, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

Both fishes depend on cells that move ions in one direction. How does one cell do that?

The photo is the spiny dogfish, the shark on which most of this physiology (including the rectal gland) was worked out. The shark is a partial conformer: it matches the sea in total osmolarity using an organic solute rather than salt. Urea is normally a waste product and denatures proteins at these concentrations; TMAO is the counteracting osmolyte. This links forward to the nitrogen-waste section: the shark is ureotelic and turns its waste product into an osmolyte. The rectal gland is the shark’s equivalent of the teleost gill ionocyte. The transition: gills, rectal gland, gut and kidney all depend on the same basic cell design.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
text:
The transporting epithelial cell



Apical membrane faces the lumen: Na⁺ channels, Na⁺–glucose cotransporter, aquaporins.
Basolateral membrane faces the blood: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP), K⁺ channels.
The pump keeps cell Na⁺ low and the inside negative, so Na⁺ enters passively at the apical side.
Water is never pumped. It follows solute, through aquaporins and between cells.




The mammalian kidney is a long tube built from cells like this.

This is the cell that does all the work in the gill, the gut and every nephron segment. The key logic: only one step uses ATP directly, the basolateral pump. Everything else runs downhill on the gradient it creates. Without knowing which membrane each protein sits in, you cannot predict the direction of net transport; that is why polarity matters (exercise 3.2c). Correct the common error “the kidney actively pumps water”: no water pump exists; water follows solute.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: The nephron: one tube, four processes
text:
The nephron: one tube, four processes



Filtration: plasma water and small solutes pass from the glomerulus into Bowman’s capsule.
Reabsorption: tubular fluid → blood.
Secretion: blood → tubular fluid.
Excretion: what finally leaves in the urine.

A filtered molecule has left the blood, not the body. A human kidney has about one million nephrons.



Step one is filtration. What does the filter let through, and how much?

Give the route first (exercise 4.1 asks for it) and then the four processes with their directions. Students most often confuse secretion with excretion: secretion is a transport step into the tubule; excretion is the final output. Several nephrons drain into each collecting duct. The figure shows the real arrangement: the loop dips into the medulla and returns to the cortex next to its own glomerulus, and the collecting duct runs down through the medulla again, which matters for the concentrating mechanism later.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
text:
Filtration: a large, coarse filter


Barrier (blood → capsule): fenestrated capillary endothelium, basement membrane, filtration slits between podocytes. Water, ions, glucose, amino acids and urea pass; blood cells and albumin do not.



Pressure
mmHg




Glomerular capillary blood
+55


Bowman’s capsule fluid
−15


Plasma protein (oncotic)
−30


Net filtration
+10





Micrograph: Ed Uthman, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

GFR ≈ 125 mL min⁻¹ = 180 L day⁻¹; urine ≈ 1.5 L day⁻¹, so more than 99 % of filtered water is reabsorbed.
With so much filtered and returned, how do we calculate what is excreted?

In the micrograph the basement membranes stain magenta: the knot in the middle is the glomerular capillary tuft, the clear space around it is Bowman’s space, where filtrate collects, and the profiles around are tubules. The filter is non-selective for small solutes: it does not choose between glucose and urea. Selection happens afterwards, in the tubule. Filtration is bulk flow driven by blood pressure, the same Starling balance as in A3 capillaries, but with an unusually high capillary pressure. The numbers are striking: the whole plasma volume (about 3 L) is filtered about 60 times a day. Filtering everything and taking back what is needed lets the kidney get rid of any unwanted small molecule, even one it has never met before.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: The renal balance: amounts per minute
text:
The renal balance: amounts per minute
\text{filtered load} = \text{GFR} \times P
\text{excretion} = \text{filtered load} - \text{reabsorption} + \text{secretion}
\text{urine concentration} = \text{excretion} \div \text{urine flow}
Worked example: GFR = 0.12 L min⁻¹, plasma concentration P = 4 mmol L⁻¹, reabsorption 0.40 mmol min⁻¹, secretion 0.04 mmol min⁻¹, urine flow 0.001 L min⁻¹.

Filtered load = 0.12 × 4 = 0.48 mmol min⁻¹
Excretion = 0.48 − 0.40 + 0.04 = 0.12 mmol min⁻¹
Urine concentration = 0.12 ÷ 0.001 = 120 mmol L⁻¹

Halving urine flow doubles the concentration but not the amount excreted.
Which parts of the tubule do the reabsorbing?

Insist on units: every term in the balance is an amount per time, never a concentration. The third line converts back to a concentration. The last line is a common exam trap: concentrated urine can come from less water, not more solute. Students practise the same calculation with different numbers in exercise 5.1.

About 25 % of filtered Na⁺ is taken up in the loop, ~5 % in the distal tubule and ~2–5 % in the collecting duct.
The bulk is recovered early and unregulated; the final adjustment is late and hormonally controlled.

How can we measure from outside what the tubule does to a substance?

This table is the core of the nephron for the exam (exercise 4.2). Read it top to bottom as the story of one litre of filtrate: the proximal tubule takes back two thirds isosmotically; the loop separates salt from water, so fluid leaving the thick ascending limb is hyposmotic (about 100 mOsm), whatever the body’s water state; the distal tubule and collecting duct make the regulated final adjustments. The last column foreshadows the concentrating mechanism: the descending limb reaches 1,200 mOsm at the bottom of the loop.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: Clearance: what the tubule does, measured from outside
text:
Clearance: what the tubule does, measured from outside


Clearance = volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute: C = \frac{U \times V}{P} (U urine concentration, V urine flow, P plasma concentration)

Inulin is filtered only, so C_\text{inulin} = GFR: 30 mg mL⁻¹ × 2 mL min⁻¹ ÷ 0.5 mg mL⁻¹ = 120 mL min⁻¹.
C < GFR: net reabsorption.
C > GFR: net secretion.




Why is the glucose clearance zero, and when does it stop being zero?

Clearance is a virtual volume, so its unit is mL min⁻¹. Inulin defines GFR because everything filtered ends up in the urine and nothing else does. The comparison rule then lets us infer tubular handling from a urine sample and a blood sample. PAH is secreted so efficiently that almost all of it is removed in one pass, so its clearance approximates renal plasma flow. Creatinine is the clinical substitute for inulin because the body makes it continuously. Exercises 5.2 and 5.3 use exactly this logic.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: The transport maximum: glucose in diabetes
text:
The transport maximum: glucose in diabetes



Na⁺–glucose cotransporters saturate at T_m ≈ 2.0 mmol min⁻¹.
Threshold = T_m ÷ GFR = 2.0 ÷ 0.125 = 16 mmol L⁻¹.
At 24 mmol L⁻¹: filtered 3.0, reabsorbed 2.0, excreted 1.0 mmol min⁻¹.
Glucose in urine (glycosuria) takes water with it: the large urine volume and thirst of untreated diabetes mellitus.




The kidney recovers solutes. How does it recover water and make urine more concentrated than plasma?

Fasting plasma glucose is about 5 mmol L⁻¹, well below the threshold, so normally no glucose is excreted. Because nephrons differ in their individual Tm, glucose begins to appear in human urine from about 10 mmol L⁻¹, somewhat before the calculated threshold. Link back to A2: insulin failure raises plasma glucose; here we see the renal consequence. The osmotic diuresis bridges to water handling: urine volume depends on how much water follows the solutes, which is the subject of the next slides.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: Try it: glucose in the kidney
text:
Try it: glucose in the kidney




Live version of the transport-maximum plot, using the renal balance from two slides back. The bar at the top is one minute of filtered glucose, split into the part returned to the blood (green) and the part lost in the urine (gold). Start at Fasting (5 mmol/L): everything is reabsorbed and the clearance is zero. Drag plasma glucose up slowly and ask the room where glucose will first appear; it is at the red threshold line, Tm/GFR = 16 mmol/L. “Untreated diabetes” (20 mmol/L) excretes 0.5 mmol/min. Then ask: what happens to glycosuria if GFR falls, as in diabetic kidney disease? Click “Diabetes + low GFR”: the filtered load drops below Tm and the glucose disappears from the urine even though plasma glucose is just as high, which is why urine glucose is a poor test in kidney disease. The clearance readout shows that clearance stays below GFR whatever you do, because glucose is reabsorbed and never secreted. The sharp corner is a simplification: real nephrons differ in Tm, so the curve is rounded (“splay”).

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
text:
Building the medullary gradient



The thick ascending limb pumps NaCl into the medulla but lets no water follow.
The descending limb is water-permeable: water leaves, and the fluid inside concentrates to match.
Opposite flow in the two limbs (countercurrent multiplication) stacks small steps into 300 → ~1,200 mOsm L⁻¹. Recycled urea adds to the inner medulla.
Longer loops, larger gradient. Max urine: beaver ~500, human ~1,200, kangaroo rat ~5,000 mOsm L⁻¹.




The gradient is there. What decides whether the collecting duct uses it?

The essential trick is differential permeability: one limb moves salt without water, the other moves water without salt. Each step only needs a modest difference (about 200 mOsm between ascending limb and interstitium); the countercurrent arrangement stacks these steps along the length of the loop. The vasa recta blood vessels follow the same hairpin shape, so they supply the medulla without washing the gradient away. The comparative numbers return to the running example: the kangaroo rat’s long loops let it make urine about four times as concentrated as ours.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: ADH: a feedback loop that opens the water valve
text:
ADH: a feedback loop that opens the water valve



Sensor: osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a 1–2 % rise in plasma osmolarity.
Messenger: ADH (antidiuretic hormone, vasopressin), made in the hypothalamus, released from the posterior pituitary.
Effector: ADH binds V2 receptors on collecting-duct cells; cAMP causes aquaporin-2 to be inserted in the apical membrane.
Water leaves the duct into the hyperosmotic medulla.
Thirst is triggered in parallel.







flowchart TB
  A["Dehydration:<br/>plasma osmolarity rises"] --> B["Hypothalamic<br/>osmoreceptors"]
  B --> C["ADH released from<br/>posterior pituitary"]
  C --> D["Aquaporin-2 inserted<br/>in collecting duct"]
  D --> E["Water reabsorbed;<br/>small volume of concentrated urine"]
  E -->|"plasma osmolarity falls:<br/>less ADH (negative feedback)"| A







How much difference does ADH make to urine volume?

This is the A1 negative-feedback loop with real parts: compare it with the temperature loop component by component. ADH does not change GFR and does not create water; it changes the water permeability of the last segment, so that the gradient built by the loop can be used. Without ADH the collecting duct is nearly impermeable and the dilute fluid from the distal tubule (about 100 mOsm) passes through as dilute urine. A fall in blood volume or pressure also increases ADH release. Exercise 6.1 asks for this sequence.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: What ADH is worth: the minimum urine volume
text:
What ADH is worth: the minimum urine volume


Urine volume = solute to excrete ÷ urine osmolarity
A person must excrete 900 mOsm of solute a day:

maximum ADH, 1,200 mOsm L⁻¹: 0.75 L day⁻¹;
no ADH, 100 mOsm L⁻¹: 9 L day⁻¹;
at the kangaroo rat’s 5,000 mOsm L⁻¹: 0.18 L day⁻¹.

Diabetes insipidus: ADH missing (central) or ignored by the kidney (nephrogenic): a large volume of dilute urine and great thirst.



Much of that solute load is nitrogen from protein. In which form should it leave?

This turns the concentrating mechanism into a number. The same solute load needs twelve times more water without ADH. The kangaroo rat row shows why the long loop matters for a desert animal that gets most of its water from metabolism of dry seeds. Exercise 6.2 has the same calculation with a different solute load. Transition: urea is the largest single component of that solute, so the choice of nitrogenous waste is part of the water budget.

Nitrogenous waste: a water–energy trade-off

Urea

Animals
Ammonotelic: teleosts, tadpoles, most aquatic invertebrates

Ammonia is cheap but toxic; it can only be used where water flushes it away, usually by diffusion across the gills.
A frog switches from ammonia to urea at metamorphosis, when it leaves the water.
Uric acid saves the most water but costs the most energy.

Why do all animals that develop in a shelled egg make uric acid?

Amino-acid breakdown produces ammonia; the question is whether to excrete it as is or convert it first. Read the table as a trade-off between water and energy. The tadpole-to-frog switch is the clearest example that the choice follows the water supply, not the taxonomic group. Exercise 7.2 asks students to classify animals; the rule is habitat plus lineage, with the three examples in the table.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: Uric acid: the egg and the bird
text:
Uric acid: the egg and the bird


The shelled (cleidoic) egg is closed: wastes stay inside until hatching.

Urea would stay dissolved and reach toxic levels.
Uric acid precipitates: neither toxic nor osmotically active.

The adult bird keeps the same waste:

Uric acid leaves as a white paste of urates, mixed with faeces in the cloaca: little water is lost with it.
Light and water-saving: useful for flight and for dry habitats.



Photo: AmbroseHem, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

Insects also make uric acid, but have no nephrons. How do they excrete it?

The cleidoic egg is the classic argument: a closed system cannot dilute or remove a soluble waste, so the embryo stores its nitrogen as an insoluble solid. Birds and most reptiles keep uric acid as adults. The photo is a chicken dropping: the white part is urates (uric acid and its salts) from the kidneys, the brown part is faeces from the intestine; both leave together through the cloaca. Because uric acid is excreted as a semi-solid paste, the water lost per gram of nitrogen is small (about 10 mL, from the table). Exercise 7.2 links the waste to habitat and development.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
text:
Insects: Malpighian tubules



No filtration: tubules secrete K⁺; water and solutes (with uric acid) follow, isosmotic to haemolymph.
The tubules empty into the hindgut.
The rectum reabsorbs water, ions and useful solutes; uric acid precipitates and leaves with dry faeces.



Photo: Adrian J. Hunter, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Same tasks as the nephron, built from secretion instead of filtration.

In the photo of a dissected cockroach, the arrow marks the tuft of fine Malpighian tubules where midgut meets hindgut; each tubule is a blind-ended tube bathed in haemolymph. The insect excretory system is a useful contrast with the nephron: the primary urine is made by active secretion of K⁺ rather than by pressure filtration, but the later steps are the same logic, a large flow of fluid followed by selective recovery. A desert locust’s rectum can extract nearly all the water, leaving dry pellets. Exercise 7.4 asks for this sequence.

Read the table as the story: physical rules, aquatic solutions, the transporting cell, the kidney’s accounting, the concentrating mechanism and the nitrogen trade-off. Return once more to the three opening animals: the goldfish uses dilute urine and gill uptake, the cod drinks and secretes salt, the kangaroo rat uses long loops and ADH. The preview of A5 picks up the ADH loop: it needed a sensor, a controller and a messenger, and A5 is about exactly those.

title: A4 exercises — Water, ions and excretion
text:
Osmotic concentration and tonicity

1.1
Calculate the osmolarity (mOsm L⁻¹) of each solution. Treat the solutions as ideal and the salts as fully dissociated.

0.15 mol L⁻¹ glucose
0.15 mol L⁻¹ NaCl
0.10 mol L⁻¹ CaCl₂
0.10 mol L⁻¹ NaCl + 0.10 mol L⁻¹ urea

300 mOsm L⁻¹ (Na⁺ + Cl⁻: 2 particles per formula unit).
300 mOsm L⁻¹ (Ca²⁺ + 2 Cl⁻: 3 particles per formula unit).
300 mOsm L⁻¹ (200 from NaCl + 100 from urea).






1.2
An animal’s body fluids have an osmolarity of 300 mOsm L⁻¹. For each external medium, state whether the medium is hyperosmotic, isosmotic or hyposmotic to the body fluids, and the direction in which water tends to move across a water-permeable body surface.

10 mOsm L⁻¹ (fresh water)
300 mOsm L⁻¹
1,000 mOsm L⁻¹ (seawater)







Answer






Hyposmotic; water tends to enter the animal.
Isosmotic; no net osmotic water movement.
Hyperosmotic; water tends to leave the animal.






1.3
Red blood cells (intracellular osmolarity 300 mOsm L⁻¹) are placed in each solution. State whether the cells swell, shrink or keep their volume. The membrane is permeable to urea but effectively impermeable to NaCl.

300 mOsm L⁻¹ NaCl
150 mOsm L⁻¹ NaCl
600 mOsm L⁻¹ NaCl
300 mOsm L⁻¹ urea







Answer






Keep their volume (isotonic).
Swell (hypotonic).
Shrink (hypertonic).
Swell, and eventually burst. Urea enters the cells until its concentration is equal on both sides, so it exerts no lasting osmotic effect. The cells’ own trapped solutes then draw water in. The solution is isosmotic but hypotonic.






1.4
True or false? Correct any false statements.

Two solutions with the same osmolarity always have the same effect on cell volume.
Osmolarity depends on the number of dissolved particles, not on their mass.
An osmoconformer keeps every internal ion at the same concentration as seawater.
A hydrostatic pressure can stop net osmotic water movement before the solute concentrations on the two sides become equal.







Answer






False. Tonicity depends only on solutes that cannot cross the membrane, so isosmotic solutions can differ in tonicity (see 1.3 d).
True.
False. An osmoconformer matches the total osmotic concentration of its medium but may still regulate individual ions.
True.

text:
Epithelial transport

In a typical transporting epithelial cell:

On which membrane, apical or basolateral, is the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase located?
How many Na⁺ and K⁺ ions does it move per ATP, and in which directions?
Why is the pump needed for Na⁺ to enter the cell passively across the other membrane?







Answer






The basolateral membrane.
3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into the cell per ATP hydrolysed.
By removing Na⁺, the pump keeps intracellular Na⁺ low (and the inside negative). This creates an inward electrochemical gradient for Na⁺ across the apical membrane, which channels and cotransporters use.

The kidney reabsorbs water by active transport of water molecules.

False. No pump transports water. Water follows osmotic gradients set up by active solute transport.

False. You also need to know whether each transporter is on the apical or basolateral membrane.

title: A4 exercises — Water, ions and excretion
text:
Renal calculations

5.1
For a freely filtered solute, the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is 0.10 L min⁻¹ and the plasma concentration is 5 mmol L⁻¹. Reabsorption is 0.40 mmol min⁻¹ and secretion is 0.02 mmol min⁻¹. Urine flow is 0.002 L min⁻¹.

Calculate the filtered load.
Calculate the excretion rate.
Calculate the urine concentration of the solute.
Urine flow is halved while the excretion rate stays the same. What is the new urine concentration?







Answer






Filtered load = GFR × plasma concentration = 0.10 L min⁻¹ × 5 mmol L⁻¹ = 0.50 mmol min⁻¹.
Excretion = 0.50 − 0.40 + 0.02 = 0.12 mmol min⁻¹.
Urine concentration = excretion ÷ urine flow = 0.12 ÷ 0.002 = 60 mmol L⁻¹.
0.12 ÷ 0.001 = 120 mmol L⁻¹. The concentration doubles although the amount excreted per minute is unchanged.






5.2
The renal clearance of a substance is \(C = U \times V / P\), where \(U\) is its urine concentration, \(V\) the urine flow and \(P\) its plasma concentration. Inulin is infused into a subject. Plasma inulin is 0.20 mg mL⁻¹, urine inulin is 25 mg mL⁻¹ and urine flow is 1.0 mL min⁻¹.

Calculate the inulin clearance.
Why does inulin clearance equal the GFR?







Answer






\(C = 25 \times 1.0 / 0.20 = 125\) mL min⁻¹.
Inulin is freely filtered and is neither reabsorbed, secreted nor metabolised by the tubule. All filtered inulin is therefore excreted, and the volume of plasma cleared per minute equals the volume filtered per minute.






5.3
The GFR is 125 mL min⁻¹. Four freely filtered substances have the clearances below. For each, state whether the tubule shows net reabsorption, net secretion or neither.

Glucose: 0 mL min⁻¹
Urea: 60 mL min⁻¹
Substance X: 125 mL min⁻¹
Para-aminohippuric acid (PAH): 600 mL min⁻¹







Answer






Net reabsorption (complete).
Net reabsorption (partial).
Neither, like inulin.
Net secretion.

Clearance below the GFR means net reabsorption; clearance above the GFR means net secretion.

0.125 L min⁻¹ × 5 mmol L⁻¹ = 0.625 mmol min⁻¹.
None. The filtered load is below \(T_m\), so all of it is reabsorbed.
Filtered load = 0.125 × 20 = 2.5 mmol min⁻¹. Excretion = 2.5 − 2.0 = 0.5 mmol min⁻¹.






5.5
A human kidney filters 180 L of plasma per day and produces 1.5 L of urine per day. What percentage of the filtered water is reabsorbed?






Answer





(180 − 1.5) / 180 × 100 = 99.2 %.

title: A4 exercises — Water, ions and excretion
text:
Concentrating the urine

6.1
Put the steps in order for the response to dehydration.

Aquaporin-2 water channels are inserted into the apical membrane of collecting-duct cells.
Plasma osmolarity rises.
ADH binds to V2 receptors on collecting-duct cells.
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the change.
Water moves from the collecting duct into the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium, and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced.
ADH is released from the posterior pituitary.
Plasma osmolarity falls and ADH release decreases.







Answer





b → d → f → c → a → e → g. Step g is the negative feedback.





6.2
A person must excrete 600 mOsm of solute per day. The maximum urine osmolarity in humans is about 1,200 mOsm L⁻¹.

What is the minimum daily urine volume?
A person who lacks ADH (diabetes insipidus) produces urine of 100 mOsm L⁻¹. What is their daily urine volume for the same solute load?







Answer






600 mOsm ÷ 1,200 mOsm L⁻¹ = 0.5 L day⁻¹.
600 mOsm ÷ 100 mOsm L⁻¹ = 6 L day⁻¹.






6.3
True or false? Correct any false statements.

Tubular fluid leaving the thick ascending limb is hyposmotic to plasma.
ADH increases urine concentration mainly by reducing the GFR.
Without ADH, the collecting duct has low water permeability and the urine stays dilute.
Urea contributes to the osmotic gradient of the inner medulla.
Desert rodents that produce very concentrated urine tend to have relatively long loops of Henle.







Answer






True (about 100 mOsm L⁻¹), because NaCl is removed without water.
False. ADH increases the water permeability of the collecting duct, so more water is reabsorbed into the medulla.
True.
True.
True. A longer loop (and a thicker medulla) builds a larger corticomedullary gradient.

7.2
Classify each animal as ammonotelic, ureotelic or uricotelic.

goldfish
human
chicken
tadpole
adult frog
desert locust







Answer






Ammonotelic. b. Ureotelic. c. Uricotelic. d. Ammonotelic.
Ureotelic. f. Uricotelic.






7.3
Why is uric acid, rather than urea, the nitrogenous waste of embryos that develop inside a shelled (cleidoic) egg?






Answer





The egg is a closed system: wastes cannot leave it. Uric acid is insoluble, so it precipitates and is stored in solid form, where it is neither toxic nor osmotically active. Urea would stay dissolved and accumulate to toxic concentrations.





7.4
Put the steps of urine formation in an insect in order.

Water, ions and useful solutes are reabsorbed in the rectum.
K⁺ is actively secreted into the lumen of the Malpighian tubules.
Dry waste, including precipitated uric acid, is eliminated with the faeces.
Water and solutes, including uric acid, follow into the tubule lumen.
The tubule fluid empties into the hindgut.







Answer





b → d → e → a → c. The Malpighian tubules produce a fluid isosmotic to the haemolymph by secretion, not by filtration; the hindgut recovers water.

title: A4 exercises — Water, ions and excretion
text:
Explore: Tonicity and cell volume
A red cell with 300 mOsm L⁻¹ of trapped solute sits in a bath of NaCl, which cannot cross the membrane, and urea, which can. Set the bath with the sliders or presets and watch the cell volume over time; the readout gives the total and the non-penetrating osmolarity outside and the final cell volume.




E1
The demo opens with NaCl 150 + urea 150 mOsm L⁻¹. Read off the total osmolarity outside, the non-penetrating osmolarity, the verdict and the final cell volume.






Answer





Total 300 mOsm L⁻¹, non-penetrating 150 mOsm L⁻¹, “isosmotic, but hypotonic”, final volume 1.67×. Urea diffuses into the cell and water follows, so only the NaCl counts for tonicity.





E2
Press NaCl 200 and then NaCl 400. Give the final cell volume for each and say whether each bath is hypotonic, isotonic or hypertonic.






Answer





NaCl 200: 1.35×, hypotonic (the cell swells). NaCl 400: 0.83×, hypertonic (the cell shrinks and crenates). With only non-penetrating solute, osmolarity and tonicity agree.





E3
Press Urea 300. Which is the outcome?

The cell keeps its volume, because the bath is isosmotic.
The cell shrinks, because urea draws water out.
The cell swells until it bursts.







Answer






The bath is isosmotic (300 mOsm L⁻¹) but its non-penetrating osmolarity is 0, so it is as hypotonic as pure water: urea and water both enter until the cell bursts (haemolysis).






E4
Press NaCl 150 + urea 150 and untick Membrane lets urea through. Give the final cell volume and the verdict. What does the comparison with E1 show?

Tonicity depends on the solution alone.
Tonicity depends on the solution and on the permeability of the membrane.







Answer





Final volume 1.00×, “isosmotic and isotonic”. b: the same bath is hypotonic to a urea-permeable cell and isotonic to a urea-impermeable one.





E5
Tick the urea box again and set NaCl 300 + urea 300 mOsm L⁻¹ with the sliders. Before running it, predict the final volume: smaller than 1, 1.00, or larger than 1? Then check the verdict and the final volume.






Answer





1.00×, “hyperosmotic, but isotonic” (total 600, non-penetrating 300 mOsm L⁻¹). The cell shrinks briefly while water leaves faster than urea enters, then recovers as urea equilibrates.

title: A4 exercises — Water, ions and excretion
text:
Explore: Glucose transport maximum
The kidney filters glucose at a rate GFR × plasma glucose and reabsorbs it up to a transport maximum, Tm. Change plasma glucose, GFR and Tm with the sliders or presets; the bar shows one minute of filtered glucose split into reabsorbed (green) and excreted (gold), and the readout gives the rates and the glucose clearance.




E6
Press Fasting. Read off the threshold, the filtered load, the excreted glucose and the glucose clearance.






Answer





Threshold 16.0 mmol L⁻¹ (= Tm ÷ GFR = 2 ÷ 0.125 L min⁻¹). Filtered load 0.63 mmol min⁻¹ (0.125 × 5), all reabsorbed: excreted 0.00 mmol min⁻¹, clearance 0 mL min⁻¹.





E7
Press Untreated diabetes (plasma glucose 20 mmol L⁻¹). Read off the filtered, reabsorbed and excreted glucose and the clearance.






Answer





Filtered 2.50, reabsorbed 2.00 (= Tm), excreted 0.50 mmol min⁻¹. Clearance 0.50 ÷ 20 mmol L⁻¹ = 0.025 L min⁻¹ = 25 mL min⁻¹, below the GFR of 125, because glucose is reabsorbed.





E8
Press Diabetes + low GFR (GFR 60 mL min⁻¹, plasma glucose still 20 mmol L⁻¹). Read off the threshold and the excreted glucose. Which statement is correct?

Glucose disappears from the urine because the patient’s diabetes is now controlled.
Glucose disappears from the urine because the filtered load (1.20 mmol min⁻¹) is now below Tm.
Glucose excretion doubles because less of the filtrate is reabsorbed.







Answer





Threshold 33.3 mmol L⁻¹, excreted 0.00 mmol min⁻¹. b: with a low GFR, less glucose is filtered than the tubule can take back, so a negative urine test does not rule out high plasma glucose in kidney disease.





E9
Press Fasting, then set Tm to 1.0 mmol min⁻¹, as with a drug that blocks tubular glucose transporters. Read off the new threshold. Then set plasma glucose to 10 mmol L⁻¹ and read off the excreted glucose.






Answer





Threshold 8.0 mmol L⁻¹ (1.0 ÷ 0.125). At 10 mmol L⁻¹: filtered 1.25, reabsorbed 1.00, excreted 0.25 mmol min⁻¹. Halving Tm halves the threshold, so glucose appears in the urine at a plasma concentration that was previously fully reabsorbed.





E10
Set plasma glucose to 30 mmol L⁻¹, GFR to 180 mL min⁻¹ and Tm to 2.0 mmol min⁻¹. Read off the clearance. Can any combination of the sliders make the glucose clearance larger than the GFR?






Answer





Clearance 113 mL min⁻¹ (excreted 3.40 mmol min⁻¹ ÷ 30 mmol L⁻¹), below the GFR of 180. No: glucose is only filtered and reabsorbed, never secreted, so the excreted amount can never exceed the filtered load and clearance stays below GFR.



Continue with the self-check quiz.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
About this lecture
An amoeba takes oxygen straight from the pond water around it. A mitochondrion deep in a mouse’s thigh muscle is millimetres from the nearest air. How does an animal body get oxygen and food to every cell, and keep conditions around those cells stable? That question runs through the whole animal half of the course, and today we set up the tools to answer it.

Organisation: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems, and the internal environment that cells actually live in.
The physical problem: surface area, volume and diffusion distance. These explain why large animals need special exchange surfaces and transport.
The building materials: the four primary tissue types, and how to recognise them in a section.
Keeping it stable: homeostasis and feedback control.
Many solutions: response, acclimation and adaptation, with an insect and a mammal compared.


The single picture for today: one cell, deep inside a body, that needs oxygen and nutrients and needs stable surroundings. Everything in the lecture is a step towards explaining how a body achieves that. Organisation tells us where the cell sits; geometry tells us why that is a problem; tissues are the materials for the solution; feedback keeps the solution working; and comparison shows that animals have solved it in more than one way. The following units (A2–A5) each take one part of this problem: energy, gas exchange and circulation, water and ions, and control.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
section: The problem: one cell versus a whole animal
text:
The problem: one cell versus a whole animal



Amoeba (~0.5 mm): O₂ diffuses a few µm from the pond water to its mitochondria.
Mouse (~80 mm): O₂ travels ventilation → lungs → blood → tissue, up to several mm; cells sit in interstitial fluid.
Every cell needs O₂ and fuel in, CO₂ and wastes out, and suitable temperature and ions.
Most mouse cells never touch the outside world.



Photo: SmallRex, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

So what does a mouse body consist of, and where do its cells actually live?

Start with the contrast rather than with definitions. The amoeba is a single cell in direct contact with its environment; diffusion over a few micrometres is fast enough. The mouse is a hundred times longer, and its muscle cells are far from air. This raises two questions that the rest of the lecture answers: how is the body organised (next slides), and why does size create a problem (geometry slides).

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
Levels of organisation



Cell: the smallest living unit.
Tissue: similar cells plus extracellular material, with one function.
Organ: several tissues working together, e.g. the intestine.
Organ system: organs with a shared task, e.g. the digestive system.
Organism.

Each level has properties that the level below lacks: a single muscle cell cannot pump blood, but cardiac muscle in a heart can.




Walk through the figure from the cell outwards using the intestine as the example, because we return to it later in the lecture when we look at tissues. Emphasise that the organ-system boundaries are a convenience: digestion depends on circulation and nerves too. The point for the story: the mouse solves its problem by building specialised tissues and organs. Next question: where are the cells, relative to the outside?

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
The internal environment



Body cells are bathed in interstitial fluid, not in the outside world.
Blood plasma exchanges with interstitial fluid across capillary walls.
The gut lumen is continuous with the exterior: food in the gut is still outside the body.
To enter the body, a substance must cross an epithelium.

Claude Bernard (1865): the milieu intérieur.



The internal environment must be supplied from outside, across exchange surfaces.

This is the key reframing: cells live in interstitial fluid, and that fluid is what the body has to keep supplied and stable. A glucose molecule in the gut lumen has not yet been absorbed; it must cross the intestinal epithelium, enter the blood, leave the capillary and cross the muscle cell membrane. Students practise this route in exercise 1.4. The next question is: why can’t the outer surface of the body simply do all the exchange, as in the amoeba?

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
section: Why size is a problem: surface area and volume
text:
Why size is a problem: surface area and volume


For a cube with side L:
A = 6L^2, \qquad V = L^3, \qquad \frac{A}{V} = \frac{6}{L}



L
A
V
A/V




1 mm
6 mm²
1 mm³
6 mm⁻¹


2 mm
24 mm²
8 mm³
3 mm⁻¹


4 mm
96 mm²
64 mm³
1.5 mm⁻¹




Demand (metabolism) scales roughly with volume.
Supply across the body surface scales with area.
Double the size: 4× the area must serve 8× the volume.





Work the table on the board. The cube is a toy, but it makes the scaling argument exact: area goes as length squared, volume as length cubed, so the ratio falls as 1/L. Metabolic demand comes from the volume of living tissue; supply through the surface comes from area. A larger animal therefore has less surface per unit of tissue to supply. That is half the problem. The other half is distance.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
section: Why size is a problem: diffusion distance
text:
Why size is a problem: diffusion distance


Time to diffuse a distance x: \quad t \approx \dfrac{x^2}{2D}
For O₂ in water, D \approx 2 \times 10^{-9} m² s⁻¹:



Distance
Time




10 µm (one cell)
~0.03 s


1 mm
~4 min


1 cm
~7 h




10× the distance → 100× the time.
Diffusion is fast enough within a cell, and far too slow across a body.




So how does a large animal get O₂ to a cell that is centimetres from the air?

This is the decisive number. Diffusion over a cell width takes a few hundredths of a second; over a centimetre it takes hours. The squared dependence is what matters: students can check 10 µm versus 1 mm (100× the distance, 10 000× the time). This is why no animal more than about a millimetre thick relies on diffusion through its body surface alone. Pose the question at the bottom and let them suggest answers before the next slide.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
section: Try it: how big can diffusion alone go?
text:
Try it: how big can diffusion alone go?




Live version of the last two slides. The animal is a ball of tissue in air-saturated water that gets O₂ only by diffusion from its surface; colour shows the O₂ level, dark means none. Start at Reset (0.5 mm radius): every cell gets O₂ and the centre still has about 80 %. Drag the radius up slowly and ask the room to call out when the centre runs out; at about 1.1 mm an anoxic core appears, and the “5 mm ball” preset is mostly anoxic. Point to the readouts: A/V falls as 3/r and the diffusion time to the centre grows as r², exactly as on the previous slides. Then press “Mouse tissue”: the same 0.5 mm ball with a mammalian metabolic rate already has a dead core, because the largest size scales as 1/√(rate). “Flatworm” shows the way out by shape: a thin sheet stays supplied whatever its length and width. Use this to ask: what else could the animal do? That leads into the three solutions on the next slide. Numbers: D = 2 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹, surface O₂ 0.27 mM, uniform O₂ use; the largest radius is √(6DC/M).

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
Three solutions



Enlarge the exchange surface: alveoli (~100 m² in a human lung), gill lamellae, intestinal villi.
Make the barrier thin: the air–blood barrier in a lung is < 1 µm.
Use bulk flow over long distances. Ventilation moves air or water to the surface; circulation moves blood around the body.

Diffusion still covers the last few µm, capillary to cell.


Photo: Yale Rosen from USA, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

Building these solutions needs specialised materials: the tissues.

Every exchange organ students will meet in A2–A4 and P2 is a combination of these three solutions. Make the link explicit: the lung is (1) and (2), the circulation is (3), and the capillary bed brings bulk flow to within diffusion range of every cell. Transition: to build a thin, folded surface, a pump and a set of tubes, the body uses four kinds of tissue.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
The four primary tissue types









Tissue
Defining feature
Main functions
Example




Epithelial
Sheets of tightly joined cells; little matrix
Boundaries, exchange, secretion, protection
Lining of gut, alveoli, skin


Connective
Cells scattered in abundant extracellular matrix
Support, binding, transport
Tendon, bone, cartilage, blood


Muscle
Elongated cells with contractile proteins
Force and movement
Skeletal muscle, heart, gut wall


Nervous
Neurons with long processes, plus glia
Signalling and integration
Brain, nerves



Every organ is built from these four. We now take them one at a time.

This overview slide is the map for the next four slides. Students should be able to reproduce the “defining feature” column, because that is what they use to recognise tissue in a section: is it a sheet of cells, cells in matrix, elongated contractile cells, or cells with long processes?

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
section: Epithelium: the exchange surface and the barrier
text:
Epithelium: the exchange surface and the barrier



Simple squamous (one thin layer): short diffusion distance, so suited for exchange (alveoli, capillaries).
Stratified squamous (many layers): suited for protection (skin, oesophagus).
Simple columnar (tall cells): suited for absorption and secretion (intestine).
Each cell has an apical side (facing the lumen) and a basal side (on the basement membrane). Different transport proteins on each side make directional transport possible.





Connect back to “three solutions”: the thin barrier of solution 2 is a simple squamous epithelium. Apical/basal polarity is the basis of every absorbing and secreting epithelium in the course: the gut in A2, the gill and kidney in A4, and plant epidermis by analogy in P1. Shape plus number of layers is the naming system.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
Epithelia in the microscope


Simple squamous, seen from above: one layer of flat, polygonal cells.

Photo: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

Stratified squamous, oesophagus in section: many layers, flattening upwards.

Photo: Nva1991, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons


These are the two extremes from the previous slide, as students will see them in the histology practical. The left image is a whole mount seen from above, so the single layer appears as a mosaic of flat cells with their nuclei; in a section it would be a thin line of cells with flattened nuclei, as in the alveolar wall. The right image is a section through the oesophagus: count the cell layers, notice that the basal cells are cuboidal and crowded and that cells flatten as they move up towards the lumen. The pale tissue underneath is connective tissue, which carries the blood vessels; the epithelium itself has none. Ask: which of these would you expect in an alveolus, and which on the inside of the mouth?

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
section: Connective tissue: defined by its matrix
text:
Connective tissue: defined by its matrix



Cells are scattered in an extracellular matrix; the matrix sets the properties.




Tissue
Matrix → property




Tendon
parallel collagen → tensile strength


Cartilage
collagen in a firm gel → resilience


Bone
mineralised collagen → rigidity


Blood
fluid plasma → transport




It also carries the blood vessels that supply epithelia.



Photo: Doc. RNDr. Josef Reischig, CSc., CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons


In the cartilage image, point out how little of the area is cells: each chondrocyte sits in a small cavity (lacuna) surrounded by matrix, the opposite of an epithelium. Blood surprises students as a connective tissue; use it to make the point that the category is defined by cells-in-matrix, not by being solid. Blood is also the transport medium of solution 3, so the tissue types are already mapping onto the exchange problem. Epithelia themselves have no blood vessels and depend on the connective tissue beneath them.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
Muscle and nervous tissue






Skeletal
Cardiac
Smooth




Striated
yes
yes
no


Cells
long fibres
branched
spindle


Nuclei
many
one
one


Control
voluntary
involuntary
involuntary




Muscle provides the pumps of bulk flow: the heart, the breathing muscles, the gut wall.
Neurons receive, integrate and transmit signals; glia support them.





The muscle table is exam material and appears in the exercises (3.2). Link function to the story: bulk flow needs a pump, and all animal pumps are muscle. Nervous tissue appears briefly here and returns in A5; for today its role is to sense and control, which is exactly what the feedback slides need.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
section: Three muscle types in the microscope
text:
Three muscle types in the microscope


Skeletal: long, parallel fibres with cross-striations

Photo: Alexander G. Cheroske, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Cardiac: branched cells, one central nucleus each

Photo: Alexander G. Cheroske, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Smooth: spindle cells, no striations

Photo: Alexander G. Cheroske, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons


All three images are at the same magnification (400×), so the sizes are comparable. Ask students to use the table on the previous slide to name each one before revealing the labels: striations or not, branching or not, one nucleus or many. In the skeletal image the fibres are so long that no ends are visible and the striations are very regular; the cardiac cells branch and join, and the dark lines across them in good preparations are intercalated discs; smooth muscle cells taper at both ends and pack together like a bundle of spindles. These are the pumps for bulk flow: heart, breathing muscles and gut wall.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
Reading a tissue section


A section is a thin 2-D slice through a 3-D structure.

A tube cut across gives a ring.
A tube cut lengthwise gives two parallel walls.
A tube cut obliquely gives an oval.

So identify a structure from its tissue layers, cell shapes and scale, not from the outline alone.




This prepares students for the histology practical. The classic error is to see a ring and call it a blood vessel; a duct, gland or gut can look the same. The procedure: check the scale, look at the lining (which epithelium?), the layers outside it (connective tissue, muscle) and then name the organ.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
section: Putting the tissues together: the intestinal wall
text:
Putting the tissues together: the intestinal wall





Layer
Tissue → role




Mucosa
columnar epithelium → large, thin absorbing surface


Submucosa
connective tissue, vessels → carries nutrients away


Muscularis
smooth muscle → mixes and moves contents


Throughout
nervous tissue → coordinates



One organ, four tissues, all three exchange solutions.


Photo: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons


This slide closes the first half of the lecture by returning to the intestine from the levels slide. In the micrograph the lumen is off to the left: purple mucosa with its glands, then the pale, loose submucosa where the blood vessels run, then the thick pink band of smooth muscle. Each tissue maps onto one of the three solutions. But an organ like this only works if its surroundings stay within narrow limits. Transition: building the machinery is not enough; temperature, pH, ion concentrations and glucose around the cells have to be held within limits while the animal eats, runs and the environment changes. That is homeostasis.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
Homeostasis: stability by continual work

Homeostasis: maintaining internal conditions within a range compatible with life, despite disturbances.
Regulated variables include body temperature, blood glucose, blood pH, plasma osmolarity, and blood O₂ and CO₂.
Stable does not mean static. Blood glucose stays near 5 mM while glucose is continuously absorbed and consumed. Input = output is a dynamic balance.
Maintaining it costs energy: ion pumps alone use a large share of resting metabolism.

How does the body detect and correct a deviation?

Emphasise the dynamic nature: a constant concentration is a balance of fluxes, like a bath with the tap running and the plug out. This idea returns in A2 (energy budget), A4 (water and salt balance) and P2 (plant water balance). The bridge to the next slide is the mechanism: negative feedback.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
Negative feedback



Regulated variable: body temperature.
Disturbance: exercise raises it.
Sensor: thermoreceptors.
Control centre: hypothalamus, which compares with the set point.
Effectors: sweat glands and skin blood vessels.
Response: more heat loss, so temperature falls back.

The response opposes the deviation. This is negative feedback.




Go round the loop component by component; the exercises (4.2) ask students to assign these roles. Point out that the effector (skin blood flow) is not the regulated variable: blood flow changes widely in order to keep temperature constant. Other examples to mention briefly: blood glucose and insulin (A2), blood pressure and the baroreceptor reflex (A3), plasma osmolarity and ADH (A4).

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
section: Positive feedback and two common errors
text:
Positive feedback and two common errors
Positive feedback amplifies the change. It needs an end point.

Oxytocin and uterine contractions during birth (ends at delivery).
Blood clotting cascade (ends when the wound is sealed).
Na⁺ channel opening during an action potential (ends with channel inactivation, A5).

Common errors:

“Negative” and “positive” describe the direction of the loop, not whether it is good or bad.
The effector (e.g. sweating) is not the regulated variable (temperature).


Positive feedback is not a failure of regulation: it is used for fast, all-or-none events that must run to completion. Each example has a clear terminating step. The two errors are the ones students make most often in exams, so state them explicitly. Transition: feedback acts within minutes; animals also change over weeks and over generations.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
section: Try it: a temperature control loop
text:
Try it: a temperature control loop




The negative-feedback loop from two slides back, run as a simulation. Exercise adds heat from minute 10 to minute 40 (shaded); the blue trace below shows what the effector (sweating, skin blood flow) is doing. Start at Reset: temperature rises a little and levels off about 0.5 °C above the set point, then returns when exercise stops. Ask: why does it not come all the way back during exercise? Because the response is driven by the deviation itself, so some deviation must remain to keep the sweat glands working. Raise the gain: the remaining error shrinks (“Strong, fast”). Press “None”: nothing opposes the heat load and temperature drifts several degrees. Press “Positive feedback”: the response amplifies the change and runs away, which is why positive feedback needs an end point. Finally “Strong, slow”: the same strong gain with a 1.5 min delay overshoots, and each swing is larger than the last until temperature leaves the survivable range, a reminder that sensing and responding take time. “Cold” shows the same loop working the other way: the effector switches to heat production.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
Three time scales of change









Time scale
Name
Example
Heritable?




Seconds–minutes
Acute response
Ventilation rises when running starts
No


Days–weeks
Acclimation (lab) / acclimatisation (field)
Fish adjusts its enzymes after weeks in warmer water
No


Generations
Evolutionary adaptation
A population in hypoxic water evolves larger gills
Yes




Acute responses and acclimation are changes within an individual.
Adaptation is a change in a population, by natural selection.
That a trait is useful does not by itself show how it evolved.


Students confuse acclimation and adaptation constantly. The test is heritability and the unit: an individual acclimates, a population adapts. Exercise 5.1 practises the classification. The last bullet guards against “just-so stories”. Transition: evolution has produced several different answers to the oxygen problem we started with.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
section: Back to the opening problem: insect versus mammal
text:
Back to the opening problem: insect versus mammal


Both breathe air, and both need O₂ within diffusion range of every mitochondrion.

Insect: air-filled tracheae branch directly to the tissues. The blood plays little part in O₂ transport.
Mammal: lungs exchange O₂ into the blood; the heart pumps it to capillaries near every cell.

Different solutions to the same physics. Neither is more advanced than the other.




Close the loop to the first slide. The insect uses bulk flow and diffusion of air all the way to the cells; diffusion in air is about 10 000 times faster than in water, which is what makes this work. The mammal uses a thin, enlarged surface plus a blood pump. Each has trade-offs: tracheal diffusion limits insect body size; the mammalian system needs a heart and haemoglobin. A3 compares gas exchange across animals in detail.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Levels of organisation
cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism


Internal environment
cells live in interstitial fluid; the gut lumen is outside the body


Surface area : volume
A/V = 6/L for a cube; falls as size increases


Diffusion time
t \approx x^2/2D; 10× distance → 100× time


Three solutions
enlarged surface, thin barrier, bulk flow


Four tissues
epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous


Homeostasis
dynamic maintenance of internal conditions


Negative feedback
response opposes the deviation (sensor → control → effector)


Positive feedback
response amplifies the change; needs an end point


Time scales
acute response, acclimation (individual), adaptation (population)



Next (A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature): the cells now receive O₂ and food. What do they do with them, how much energy does an animal use, and how does temperature change that?
Tutorial · Exercises · Quiz

Read the table as the story in order: where cells live, why size makes supply hard, how bodies solve it with tissues, how feedback keeps it stable, and how animals differ. The preview of A2 follows the oxygen and food into the cell: metabolism, energy budgets and temperature.

title: A1 exercises — Structure, scale and feedback
text: The questions follow the tutorial and slides. Answer each question before opening its answer.

title: A1 exercises — Structure, scale and feedback
text:
Levels of organisation

1.1
Arrange from the smallest to the largest level: organ, organism, cell, organ system, tissue.






Answer





Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.





1.2
In a multicellular animal, most cells exchange materials directly with:

the external environment
interstitial fluid
blood plasma
the gut lumen







Answer






Interstitial (extracellular) fluid surrounds the cells; blood, where present, transports material between exchange organs and the tissues.






1.3
The intestinal wall contains all four primary tissue types. For each tissue type, give its main function in the intestine.






Answer












Tissue
Function in the intestine




Epithelium
Lines the lumen; secretion and absorption


Connective tissue
Supports the epithelium and carries blood vessels


Smooth muscle
Mixes and moves the contents


Nervous tissue
Coordinates secretion and muscle activity








1.4
Put the steps in order for a glucose molecule moving from the gut lumen into a skeletal-muscle cell:

crosses the muscle-cell membrane
crosses the apical membrane of the intestinal epithelial cell
is carried in the blood
crosses the basolateral membrane of the intestinal epithelial cell
enters the interstitial fluid around the muscle fibre







Answer





b → d → c → e → a. Glucose in the lumen has not yet been absorbed, because the lumen is continuous with the outside of the body.

2.2
The time needed for diffusion is proportional to the square of the distance. By what factor does the diffusion time change when the distance increases from:

1 µm to 3 µm
0.1 mm to 1 mm
20 µm to 10 µm







Answer






3² = 9 times longer.
10² = 100 times longer.
(1/2)² = 1/4, i.e. four times shorter.






2.3
Name three ways in which large animals overcome the low surface-area-to-volume ratio of a large body.






Answer






Folding, branching or subdivision of exchange surfaces increases the area (e.g. alveoli, gill lamellae, intestinal villi).
Thin exchange barriers shorten the diffusion distance.
Bulk flow (ventilation and circulation) moves material over long distances.

title: A1 exercises — Structure, scale and feedback
text:
Tissues

3.1
Name the primary tissue type that matches each description.








Description




A
One layer of closely packed cells lining a lumen, with little material between the cells


B
Widely spaced cells among abundant parallel extracellular fibres


C
Long, cylindrical, striated fibres with many nuclei per fibre


D
Cells with long processes, surrounded by many smaller supporting cells









Answer





A: epithelial tissue (simple epithelium). B: connective tissue (dense regular connective tissue, e.g. tendon). C: muscle tissue (skeletal muscle). D: nervous tissue (neurons and glial cells).





3.2
Complete the table.

Cardiac muscle

Striated?

Answer

3.3
Which type of epithelium best suits each function: simple squamous or stratified squamous?

gas exchange
protection against abrasion







Answer






Simple squamous: a single thin layer gives a short diffusion distance.
Stratified squamous: several cell layers protect the tissue beneath.






3.4
Define the terms lumen, apical surface and basal surface.






Answer






Lumen: the inner space of a tube or cavity, such as the gut or a blood vessel.
Apical surface: the side of an epithelial cell that faces the lumen or the outside.
Basal surface: the side of an epithelial cell that faces the basement membrane and underlying tissue.






3.5
A section shows a circular profile with an empty centre. Why is this not enough to identify it as a blood vessel?






Answer





Any tube (such as a duct, gland, gut or vessel) cut in cross-section gives a ring. An oblique cut through the same tube gives an oval. Identification also needs the wall structure, its tissue layers and the scale.

title: A1 exercises — Structure, scale and feedback
text:
Homeostasis and feedback

4.1
Define homeostasis.






Answer





Homeostasis is the active maintenance of internal conditions (such as temperature or the composition of extracellular fluid) within a range compatible with life, despite external and internal disturbances.





4.2
Body temperature in a mammal rises during exercise. Match each item to its role in the feedback loop: regulated variable, sensor, control centre, effector.

sweat glands
hypothalamus
body temperature
thermoreceptors







Answer






effector; b. control centre; c. regulated variable; d. sensor.






4.3
State whether each example is negative or positive feedback.

A rise in blood glucose increases insulin secretion, which lowers blood glucose.
Uterine contractions increase oxytocin release, which strengthens the contractions.
A rise in body temperature increases sweating.
Activated clotting factors activate more clotting factors.
A fall in blood pressure increases heart rate through the baroreceptor reflex.







Answer






Negative. b. Positive. c. Negative. d. Positive. e. Negative.






4.4
True or false? Correct any false statements.

Positive feedback means that the response is good for the animal.
In negative feedback, the response reduces the deviation that triggered it.
Positive feedback must have a way to stop.
A stable internal concentration means that no transport is taking place.







Answer






False. “Positive” refers to the direction of the loop: the response amplifies the original change. It says nothing about benefit.
True.
True. Otherwise the change keeps growing, as in an action potential or during birth.
False. Inputs and outputs can balance while transport continues.

title: A1 exercises — Structure, scale and feedback
text:
Responses, acclimation and adaptation

5.1
Classify each example as an acute response, acclimation or evolutionary adaptation.

Ventilation increases within seconds when an animal starts running.
A fish kept at a higher temperature for four weeks changes its enzyme levels.
A population of fish living in hypoxic water has inherited larger gill surfaces.







Answer






Acute response. b. Acclimation. c. Evolutionary adaptation.






5.2
What is the difference between acclimation and acclimatisation?






Answer





Both are reversible changes within one individual. Acclimation describes the response to a change in one condition, usually in the laboratory. Acclimatisation describes the response to changes in the natural environment.

Complete the table comparing oxygen delivery to the tissues.
