title: A1 exercises — Structure, scale and feedback
text:
Explore: Diffusion limits body size
The demo shows a ball (or flat sheet) of tissue in air-saturated water that gets O₂ only by diffusion from its surface. Colour shows the O₂ level and the readouts give A/V, the diffusion time to the centre, the largest size that diffusion can supply and the O₂ at the centre. Use the radius and O₂-use sliders, or the preset buttons.




E1
Press Reset (sphere, radius 0.50 mm, O₂ use 0.20 mL g⁻¹ h⁻¹). Read off:

A/V
the diffusion time to the centre
the O₂ at the centre, as % of the surface value







Answer






6.00 mm⁻¹ (= 3/r for a sphere).
About 62 s (\(t \approx x^2/2D\) with \(x\) = 0.5 mm and \(D\) = 2 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹).
81 %. Every cell gets O₂.






E2
From Reset, drag the radius up to 1.0 mm.

By what factor has A/V changed?
By what factor has the diffusion time to the centre changed?
What does the readout give as the largest radius that diffusion alone can supply?







Answer






It halves, from 6.00 to 3.00 mm⁻¹ (A/V ∝ 1/r).
It increases four times, from about 62 s to 250 s (shown as 4 min), because diffusion time ∝ r².
1.14 mm. Above this radius an anoxic core appears; at 1.0 mm the centre still has about 23 % O₂.






E3
Press 5 mm ball. What percentage of the tissue gets no O₂?






Answer





About 64 %. The radius is more than four times the largest radius (1.14 mm) that diffusion can supply, so most of the volume is anoxic.





E4
Press Mouse tissue (radius 0.50 mm, O₂ use 2.5 mL g⁻¹ h⁻¹, about 12 times the Reset value).

What is now the largest radius that diffusion can supply?
Which statement explains the change? (i) the largest radius falls in proportion to the O₂ use; (ii) the largest radius falls in proportion to the square root of the O₂ use; (iii) the largest radius does not depend on the O₂ use.







Answer






323 µm (0.32 mm), so the 0.50 mm ball now has an anoxic core (17 % of the tissue).
(ii). The largest radius is \(\sqrt{6DC_0/M}\); 12.5 times the O₂ use gives \(\sqrt{12.5} \approx 3.5\) times smaller radius (1.14 mm → 0.32 mm). A tissue with a mammalian metabolic rate must therefore be supplied over much shorter distances, by capillaries.






E5
Press Flatworm (flat sheet, 0.15 mm half-thickness).

What is the largest half-thickness that diffusion can supply?
Does this limit depend on the length and width of the sheet?







Answer






660 µm (0.66 mm), i.e. a sheet up to about 1.3 mm thick. For a flat sheet the limit is \(\sqrt{2DC_0/M}\), which is \(1/\sqrt{3}\) of the sphere’s limit.
No. Only the thickness sets the diffusion distance, so a flatworm can be several centimetres long and wide as long as it stays thin.

title: A1 exercises — Structure, scale and feedback
section: Explore: Feedback control of body temperature
text:
Explore: Feedback control of body temperature
The demo simulates body temperature under a heat load from exercise (or cold) between minute 10 and minute 40. The effector response is proportional to the deviation from the 37 °C set point. Choose the type of loop with the buttons, set the gain, response delay and disturbance with the sliders, and read the deviations in the readout.




E6
Press Reset (negative feedback, gain 0.5, no delay, disturbance +0.30 °C min⁻¹).

What is the deviation from the set point at minute 40?
Is the temperature back at 37 ± 0.1 °C at 60 min?







Answer






+0.55 °C. Some deviation remains during the whole exercise period, because the effector response is driven by the deviation itself.
Yes.






E7
Keep negative feedback and set the gain to 1.0, then to 2.0 (Strong, fast). Read the deviation at minute 40 each time. What happens to the remaining error when the gain is doubled?






Answer





Gain 1.0: +0.29 °C. Gain 2.0: +0.15 °C. Doubling the gain roughly halves the remaining error; a stronger response holds the regulated variable closer to the set point, but never exactly on it.





E8
Return to Reset and press None, then Positive feedback. For each, read the deviation at minute 40 and say whether the temperature is back at 37 °C by 60 min.






Answer








Loop
Deviation at minute 40
Back at 37 °C at 60 min?




None
+4.66 °C
No


Positive feedback
+13.00 °C (runs off the top of the plot)
No



Without feedback the heat load drives a drift of several degrees. With positive feedback the response amplifies the deviation, so temperature runs away out of the survivable range and does not return when exercise stops.





E9
Press Strong, slow (gain 2.0, delay 1.5 min). Then lower the gain to 0.5 while keeping the 1.5 min delay.

What happens with gain 2.0 and the delay?
What is the largest deviation with gain 0.5 and the delay?







Answer






The temperature overshoots the set point and oscillates with growing amplitude until it leaves the survivable range: a strong response that acts on old information over-corrects.
+0.69 °C (compared with +0.55 °C without delay). With a weaker response the delay causes only a small overshoot, and temperature returns to 37 °C.






E10
Press Cold (disturbance −0.30 °C min⁻¹). What is the deviation at minute 40, and is the effector cooling or heating the body?






Answer





−0.55 °C, the mirror image of Reset. The effector trace lies below the line: it is heating (for example shivering), opposing the fall in temperature.



Continue with the self-check quiz.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
text:
About this lecture
A doctor taps the tendon below your knee and your leg kicks about 30 ms later, before you have decided anything. In A1 every feedback loop had a sensor, a control centre and an effector, and in A4 the messenger of the water loop was a hormone, ADH. Who are the sensors, controllers and messengers, and how does a signal turn into movement? Nerves carry fast, targeted messages; hormones carry slower messages through the blood.

The electrical signal: ion gradients, the resting potential and the action potential.
Passing it on: conduction, synapses and the knee-jerk reflex.
The effector: how a nerve impulse makes a muscle contract, and how force is graded.
The other messenger: nervous systems across animals, hormones and the endocrine glands.
Reproduction: the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis, where feedback changes sign.


The running example for the first two thirds of the lecture is the knee-jerk reflex: a stretch receptor, a sensory neuron, one synapse in the spinal cord, a motor neuron and a muscle. Every slide up to the muscle section explains one link of that chain. Then we turn to the slower messenger system, hormones, using examples students already know (insulin from A2, ADH from A4), and finish with reproduction, which shows both negative and positive feedback in one system. This is the last animal unit, so the summary also pulls A1 to A5 together.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
text:
Ion gradients and equilibrium potentials
The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP) keeps the gradients:



Ion
Outside (mmol L⁻¹)
Inside (mmol L⁻¹)
Equilibrium potential




K⁺
5
140
−89 mV


Na⁺
145
15
+61 mV


Cl⁻
110
10
−64 mV



Nernst equation (37 °C): the voltage at which an ion’s electrical force exactly balances its concentration gradient.
E_\text{ion} = \frac{61.5\ \text{mV}}{z}\,\log_{10}\frac{[\text{ion}]_\text{out}}{[\text{ion}]_\text{in}}
Worked example: E_\text{K} = 61.5 \times \log_{10}(5/140) = 61.5 \times (-1.45) \approx -89 mV. For Cl⁻, z = -1, so the sign flips.
The membrane potential at rest is −70 mV. Why that value?

Start with the gradients, because every electrical signal in the body uses them. The pump builds them; channels let ions run down them. The Nernst equation tells us, for one ion, the voltage at which there is no net movement. K⁺ is high inside, so the inside must be negative to hold it in: E_K is negative. Na⁺ is high outside, so E_Na is positive. Work the K⁺ case on the board and let students check Na⁺; exercise 1.1 asks for all three. Remind them that log10 of a ratio below 1 is negative.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: The resting potential and driving forces
text:
The resting potential and driving forces



At rest the membrane is ~25× more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺ (K⁺ leak channels), so V_m = −70 mV lies close to E_\text{K}.
Driving force = V_m - E_\text{ion}: Na⁺ −131 mV, large, inward; K⁺ +19 mV, small, outward.
The small leaks are balanced by the pump. Only a thin layer of charge lines the membrane; the cytoplasm is neutral.
Outside K⁺ 20 mmol L⁻¹: E_\text{K} ≈ −52 mV and the cell depolarises: why high plasma K⁺ disturbs the heart.




So what happens when Na⁺ channels suddenly open?

The resting potential is a weighted compromise between the equilibrium potentials, weighted by permeability; because K⁺ permeability dominates, the result is near E_K. The driving-force convention: a negative value for a cation means inward movement. Na⁺ is the ion “waiting to get in”, with both concentration and voltage pushing it inward; that stored driving force is what the action potential uses. The high-K⁺ example shows that the resting potential depends on extracellular K⁺; exercise 1.3 uses the same idea with a smaller change.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: Try it: ions, permeability and the membrane potential
text:
Try it: ions, permeability and the membrane potential




The left panel shows the ions (one dot per 5 mmol/L; K+ green, Na+ red), with the width of the two channels in the membrane showing the relative permeability. The right panel places E_K, E_Na (Nernst) and the membrane potential (Goldman equation) on one voltage scale. Start at Rest: -69 mV, close to E_K, because the K+ channel is wide. Click “K+ channels only”: Vm drops onto E_K exactly, which is the Nernst case. Click “K+ out = 20” and ask the class to predict first: E_K rises to about -52 and the cell depolarises (the hyperkalaemia example). Then “Na+ channels open” (P_Na/P_K = 20): Vm jumps to about +50, towards E_Na, which is what happens at the peak of an action potential. Drag P_Na/P_K slowly from 0.04 to 20 to show that Vm is a weighted compromise between the two equilibrium potentials. Point out that the dots hardly change: the potential flips without any change in concentration, which sets up “very few ions move” on the next slide.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
text:
The action potential



A stimulus depolarises the membrane to threshold (~−55 mV).
Rising phase: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open; Na⁺ enters and opens more channels (positive feedback, A1), up to ~+30 mV.
Peak: Na⁺ channels inactivate.
Repolarisation: voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ leaves.
Undershoot (~−80 mV) while K⁺ channels stay open; then rest.

The spike lasts 1–2 ms. Very few ions move (squid axon: Na⁺ inside rises < 0.001 %); the pump is not needed for any single spike.



If every spike looks the same, how does a neuron signal “stronger”?

The trace is computed from the Hodgkin–Huxley model (rest set to −70 mV); the lower panel shows the two conductances. Go through the numbered list as a sequence of channel events; exercise 2.1 asks for this order. The positive-feedback loop (depolarisation opens Na⁺ channels, which depolarises further) is the example promised in A1; inactivation is its built-in end point. The peak does not reach E_Na because Na⁺ channels inactivate and K⁺ channels open. Correct two common errors: the pump does not produce the rising phase (channels do), and concentrations hardly change during one spike.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
text:
All-or-none: refractory periods and coding



Absolute refractory period (~1–2 ms): no stimulus fires a second spike; Na⁺ channels are inactivated.
Relative refractory period (a few ms): a stronger stimulus is needed; some Na⁺ channels still inactivated, K⁺ channels still open.
So the spike travels one way, and firing rate has a ceiling of a few hundred per second.
Spikes are all-or-none. A stronger stimulus raises the frequency of spikes and the number of neurons recruited.




How fast does the spike travel to the end of the axon?

The figure uses the same model as the previous slide: a second stimulus 1.5 ms after a spike fails whatever its strength; at 3 ms it needs to be about twice as strong. The refractory period follows directly from the channel events on the previous slide; exercise 2.2 asks for both definitions and their causes. Coding: a light touch might give 10 spikes per second in one sensory fibre, a firm press 100 per second in that fibre plus activity in its neighbours. The sensory receptor itself produces a graded receptor potential; it is converted to spike frequency at the first point where voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are found.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: Try it: threshold and refractory period
text:
Try it: threshold and refractory period




A Hodgkin–Huxley axon (the same model as the two figures) receives two brief current pulses, S1 and S2. The lower panel shows the fraction of Na+ channels that are not inactivated (green) and the K+ channels that are open (gold). First threshold: click “Too weak”, then drag S1 strength up from 12; between about 15 and 20 the response jumps from a small bump to a full spike, and above that the spike does not get any bigger (all-or-none). Then refractory periods: “2nd at 1.5 ms, 8×” fails even at the largest S2, and the readout says absolute refractory; point at the green trace, almost no Na+ channels are available. “2nd at 3 ms” fails at the same strength, and the readout gives the strength needed (about 60): relative refractory. “3 ms, 2× stronger” fires a second, slightly smaller spike. Then drag the S1 → S2 interval from 2 to 10 ms with S2 = 40 and ask the class to call out when the second spike returns. The model is the squid axon with its rates sped up threefold, so the time course is close to that of a mammalian axon.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
text:
Conduction velocity: diameter and myelin



Larger diameter → lower internal resistance → current spreads further ahead → faster.
Myelin (Schwann cells; oligodendrocytes in the CNS) insulates the axon. Spikes regenerate only at nodes of Ranvier ~1 mm apart and jump between them: saltatory conduction.




Axon
Diameter
Velocity




Unmyelinated pain fibre
~1 µm
~1 m s⁻¹


Squid giant axon
~500 µm
~25 m s⁻¹


Myelinated motor axon
~15 µm
60–120 m s⁻¹



1.0 m in 15 ms: 1.0 ÷ 0.015 ≈ 67 m s⁻¹.


Micrograph: Roadnottaken, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

At the end of the axon the electrical signal reaches a gap. How does it cross?

The micrograph shows a myelinated axon in cross-section: each dark line in the ring is a layer of glial membrane wrapped around the axon (scale bar 500 nm). Two ways to go fast: get bigger or get insulated. The table makes the comparison concrete: a human myelinated axon 15 µm wide outruns a squid axon 30 times wider. In multiple sclerosis, loss of CNS myelin slows or blocks conduction. Exercise 2.4 asks for the two properties and a velocity calculation. Transition: the knee-jerk signal now reaches the spinal cord, where it must pass a synapse.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
text:
The chemical synapse



A spike reaches the terminal.
Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open.
Ca²⁺ enters (outside ~2, inside ~0.0001 mmol L⁻¹).
Vesicles fuse: exocytosis.
Transmitter crosses the 20–40 nm cleft and binds receptors.
Ion channels open: the postsynaptic potential changes.
Removal: acetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh; serotonin and noradrenaline are taken back up (reuptake).




Ca²⁺ is the trigger. Delay ~0.5 ms. One-way: vesicles only before, receptors only after the cleft. Does the transmitter excite or inhibit the next cell?

Walk through the seven steps; exercise 3.1 asks for this order. The essential idea is conversion: electrical signal → chemical signal → electrical signal. Ca²⁺ has an enormous inward gradient (about 20,000-fold), so opening a few channels raises local Ca²⁺ sharply. Drugs and toxins act at nearly every step: botulinum toxin blocks vesicle release; nerve agents block acetylcholinesterase; antidepressants such as SSRIs block serotonin reuptake.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: Excitatory or inhibitory: the receptor decides
text:
Excitatory or inhibitory: the receptor decides


EPSP moves V_m towards threshold; IPSP moves it away, or holds it below.








Transmitter
Receptor and channel
Effect




Acetylcholine
Nicotinic: cation channel (Na⁺ in), skeletal muscle
Excitatory


Acetylcholine
Muscarinic: opens K⁺ channels, cardiac pacemaker
Inhibitory


Glutamate
Channels for Na⁺ and K⁺
Excitatory


GABA
Cl⁻ channels: V_m → E_\text{Cl} (≈ −70), below threshold
Inhibitory




The same transmitter can excite or inhibit: the receptor decides.
EPSPs and IPSPs summate; the neuron fires only if the axon hillock reaches threshold.



Drawing: Santiago Ramón y Cajal, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

Now we can trace a complete pathway: the knee-jerk reflex.

Exercise 3.2 asks for these four cases. The GABA case needs the driving-force idea: the effect of opening a channel depends on where the membrane potential will move, which is towards that ion’s equilibrium potential. If E_Cl is below threshold, opening Cl⁻ channels holds the cell below threshold. Summation at the axon hillock is the neuron’s “control centre” in miniature: it weighs excitatory against inhibitory input. Cajal’s drawing of cerebellar Purkinje cells shows the scale of the problem: each dendritic tree receives synapses from roughly 100,000 or more inputs, and one axon carries the verdict.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: The knee-jerk reflex: a complete loop
text:
The knee-jerk reflex: a complete loop



Receptor: muscle spindle in the quadriceps.
Afferent: sensory neuron into the dorsal spinal cord.
Integrating centre: spinal cord, one synapse.
Efferent: motor neuron.
Effector: quadriceps contracts; the leg kicks.

The contraction opposes the stretch: negative feedback for muscle length (A1). An inhibitory interneuron relaxes the hamstrings. No brain needed: ~30 ms.



The motor neuron has fired. How does its spike make the muscle contract?

This brings the first half of the lecture together in one real loop: receptor potential, action potential, conduction along a fast myelinated axon, a single excitatory synapse, and an effector. Map the components onto the A1 feedback vocabulary. Exercise 3.3 asks for the five components, which are listed on the left and numbered on the figure. Signals also travel up the cord, which is why you feel the tap. The reciprocal inhibition shows an IPSP doing useful work. Transition: the remaining link, from motor neuron to force, is the subject of the next four slides.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
text:
The neuromuscular junction



An action potential arrives at the motor-neuron terminal.
Acetylcholine is released: a chemical synapse, as before.
ACh opens nicotinic channels: an end-plate potential depolarises the muscle fibre to threshold, every time.


Each fibre has one junction; one motor neuron branches to many fibres.
The large safety margin means one motor-neuron spike = one muscle spike.



Micrograph: Hlj55567516, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

How does a spike on the surface reach myofibrils deep inside the fibre?

The neuromuscular junction is the synapse students already know from two slides back, with the muscle fibre as the postsynaptic cell. In the light micrograph, a bundle of motor axons fans out over the striated muscle fibres, and each axon branch ends in a dark motor end plate on a fibre: one motor neuron, many fibres, and one junction per fibre. At electron-microscope scale (not shown), the nerve terminal is full of synaptic vesicles containing acetylcholine, and the muscle membrane opposite is folded, which increases the area for ACh receptors. Unlike a synapse between neurons, where one EPSP is small and must summate, the end-plate potential is large enough to fire the muscle fibre every time: a large safety margin. Curare blocks the nicotinic receptors here; nerve agents block acetylcholinesterase, so ACh accumulates and the muscles cannot relax.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
text:
Excitation–contraction coupling



A muscle action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and down the T tubules.
Voltage-sensing (dihydropyridine) receptors in the T-tubule membrane open the ryanodine receptors of the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).
Ca²⁺ is released from the SR.
Ca²⁺ binds troponin.
Tropomyosin moves and exposes the myosin-binding sites on actin.
Myosin heads bind actin and perform power strokes.


Relaxation

Acetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh.
An ATP-driven Ca²⁺ pump (SERCA) returns Ca²⁺ to the SR.
Troponin releases Ca²⁺; tropomyosin covers the binding sites again.

Ca²⁺ is the switch that couples the electrical event (excitation) to the mechanical event (contraction).

What exactly do the myosin heads pull on, and where does ATP come in?

This continues the numbering from the junction slide; exercise 4.1 asks for all nine steps in order. Split it into three stages: at the junction (steps 1–3, previous slide), in the membrane system (4–6) and in the filaments (7–9). The T tubules carry the signal deep into a fibre up to 100 µm wide, so Ca²⁺ is released close to every myofibril at once.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
text:
The sarcomere



A myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres, Z disc to Z disc (~2.5 µm at rest).
Thick filaments: myosin (~1.6 µm long).
Thin filaments: actin with troponin and tropomyosin, anchored at the Z discs.
Dark A bands (thick filaments) and light I bands (thin only) alternate: the striations of skeletal and cardiac muscle.



Micrograph: Louisa Howard, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

When a muscle shortens, which of these bands change?

Read the electron micrograph with the class before introducing the model: find a Z line (thin and dark), then the dark A band between two Z lines and the light I band either side of each Z line. One sarcomere runs from one Z line to the next (scale bar 1 µm); the myofibrils run diagonally across the image, and a capillary and nucleus are at the top right. The bands are the visible result of the filament arrangement on the next slide, and they are why skeletal and cardiac muscle are called striated.

Sliding-filament model: myosin pulls the thin filaments towards the centre. No filament changes length.



What makes the myosin heads pull, and let go?

The test of understanding is the right-hand column (exercise 4.3): a band shortens only if it is defined by the gap or overlap between filaments. The A band equals the length of the myosin filament, so it cannot change; the I band and H zone are the non-overlapping regions, so they shrink as overlap increases. Striations visible in skeletal and cardiac muscle are these bands.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: The cross-bridge cycle: what ATP does
text:
The cross-bridge cycle: what ATP does



ATP binding makes myosin detach from actin (step 1).
ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the head (step 2).
Pᵢ release drives the power stroke (step 4): ~10 nm per cycle.
ATP also powers relaxation: the SR Ca²⁺ pump.
Rigor mortis: after death ATP runs out, myosin cannot detach, and muscles lock rigid.




One cycle moves a filament 10 nm. How does a whole muscle produce a weak or a strong pull?

The surprising point for students is that ATP binding causes release, not contraction; the power stroke is triggered by phosphate release. Rigor mortis is the proof: without ATP, heads stay attached. Exercise 4.2 asks for the role of each ATP step. Repeated cycles by many asynchronous heads give smooth sliding, like a team pulling a rope hand over hand.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: Grading force: motor units and summation
text:
Grading force: motor units and summation



A motor unit = one motor neuron + all its muscle fibres: ~10 fibres in eye muscles (fine control), ~2,000 in the calf (large force).
Recruitment: activate more motor units, small ones first.
Summation: a twitch lasts ~100 ms, a spike ~2 ms. Spikes at high frequency add twitches up to a smooth tetanus, 3–4× the twitch force.
Force is never graded by larger action potentials: they are all-or-none.




More force costs more ATP. Does it always produce more work?

The same two rules as in sensory coding (number of neurons, frequency of spikes) apply on the output side. Recruiting small units first gives fine control at low force and large increments at high force (the size principle). Summation works because Ca²⁺ is released again before the previous release has been pumped away. Exercise 4.5 tests exactly these four statements. The traces come from the same simple model as the demo on the next slide.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: Try it: summation, tetanus and recruitment
text:
Try it: summation, tetanus and recruitment




The plot shows the force of a muscle of four motor units (sizes 1 to 4, stacked colours) during 500 ms of motor-neuron firing; red ticks below are the spikes. It opens on a single twitch. Click 5 Hz: separate twitches, each relaxing before the next. 15 Hz: the twitches ride on each other (summation, unfused tetanus); ask why, and get the answer that Ca2+ is released again before the previous release has been pumped back. 30 Hz and 80 Hz: a smooth fused tetanus at about 3.5 times the twitch force (readout). Then the second rule: drag Motor units from 4 down to 1 at 80 Hz to show recruitment, smallest first, giving small steps at low force and large steps at high force. Finish with the point from the slide: at no time did any spike get bigger. The model is schematic (each spike adds a fixed twitch-shaped activation that saturates), but the twitch and tetanus ratio match real fast muscle.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: Work, power and the cost of holding still
text:
Work, power and the cost of holding still

Work W = F \times d (force in the direction of movement × displacement).
Power P = W / t.

Example: a muscle lifts a load with 30 N through 0.20 m in 0.50 s.




Calculation
Result




Work while lifting
30 N × 0.20 m
6.0 J


Mean power while lifting
6.0 J ÷ 0.50 s
12 W


Work while holding the load still
30 N × 0 m
0 J




Holding still is an isometric contraction: force without shortening. Cross-bridges keep cycling and Ca²⁺ is continuously pumped, so ATP is used and turned into heat.
Muscle converts at most ~25 % of the chemical energy into work. Lifting 6 J costs about 24 J of metabolic energy.

Skeletal muscle is switched by troponin. Do the heart and the gut wall use the same switch?

The calculation is simple; the conceptual trap is the holding phase. External mechanical work is zero, but metabolic cost is not: this is why holding a heavy bag is tiring. The efficiency figure connects back to A2: most of the energy of muscle work appears as heat, which is why exercise warms the body. Exercise 4.4 has the same calculation with different numbers.

All three use actin and myosin and the cross-bridge cycle.
Smooth muscle relaxes when myosin light-chain phosphatase removes the phosphate.

All of these are controlled by nervous systems. How are nervous systems organised across animals?

In A1 we compared the three types by appearance; here we compare them by control. The key difference for exercise 4.6 is that smooth muscle regulates the thick filament (myosin phosphorylation), whereas striated muscle regulates the thin filament (troponin–tropomyosin). The cardiac long refractory period prevents tetanus, which would stop the heart from refilling between beats.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
text:
Nervous systems across animals



Hydra (cnidarian): diffuse nerve net, no brain, radial body.
Earthworm: cerebral ganglia plus a ventral nerve cord with a ganglion in each segment. Insects: same plan, ganglia fused.
Mammal: brain + dorsal, hollow spinal cord (CNS) and a peripheral nervous system (somatic, autonomic).
Cephalisation: animals that move forwards concentrate sense organs and neurons at the front.




Nerves are fast and point-to-point. What about messages that must reach the whole body for hours?

Exercise 5.1 asks students to match these three types. The ventral versus dorsal nerve cord is a classic difference between annelids and arthropods on one side and vertebrates on the other. Emphasise that there is no single ladder of complexity: each organisation fits the animal’s symmetry and way of moving. Transition to hormones: the second messenger system of the body.

ADH in A4 is the peptide route: V2 receptor → cAMP → aquaporin-2 inserted within minutes.

Which glands make these hormones, and who controls the glands?

Exercise 5.2 asks for this table. The chemistry explains everything else: a water-soluble peptide cannot cross the membrane, so it needs a surface receptor and a second messenger; a lipid-soluble steroid crosses the membrane and acts on genes, which takes longer. Compared with nerves: nerves give milliseconds and one target; hormones give seconds to days and every cell carrying the receptor. The same hormone concentration can therefore affect one tissue and not another.

Reproduction shows how this hierarchy is controlled by feedback.

Exercise 5.3 asks for the source of eight hormones; all are in this table. Point out the hierarchy: hypothalamus → anterior pituitary → peripheral gland. The posterior pituitary is a special case: it is an extension of the brain, and ADH and oxytocin are made in hypothalamic neurons and released from their terminals into the blood. The cross-references to A2 and A4 show that earlier units already used this system.

In the male the axis runs on negative feedback: testosterone inhibits GnRH and LH; inhibin inhibits FSH.
In the female the same axis produces a monthly cycle. How?

Use the male axis as the clean negative-feedback example: three levels, two feedback signals, a stable output. Exercise 6.1 asks for the target-cell table and exercise 6.2 for the sign of each feedback. GnRH reaches the pituitary through a short portal blood system, so very little is needed. The same three-level structure with feedback controls the thyroid and the adrenal cortex.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: The ovary: follicles and the corpus luteum
text:
The ovary: follicles and the corpus luteum



FSH makes several follicles grow; one becomes dominant (the Graafian follicle). Its granulosa cells secrete oestradiol.
The LH surge triggers ovulation: the oocyte leaves the follicle.
The empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone and oestradiol.
No pregnancy: it regresses after ~12 days. Pregnancy: hCG from the embryo keeps it alive.



Micrograph: Ed Uthman, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

How do the hormones time these events?

Start with the structure, because the hormone curves on the next slide only make sense once students can picture a follicle. In the micrograph, the large cavity (antrum) is filled with follicular fluid; the granulosa cells lining it make oestradiol under FSH stimulation; the oocyte sits on a mound of granulosa cells (cumulus) at one side. After ovulation the same granulosa and theca cells become the corpus luteum. hCG, the hormone detected by pregnancy tests, acts like LH on the corpus luteum.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: The ovarian cycle: feedback changes sign
text:
The ovarian cycle: feedback changes sign



Days 1–12: oestradiol rises: negative feedback on FSH and LH.
Days 12–13: oestradiol high for ~2 days: positive feedback, the LH surge.
Day ~14: ovulation; the surge ends.
Days 15–26: corpus luteum: progesterone and oestradiol, negative feedback.
Days 27–28: it regresses; FSH rises; next cycle.

The positive feedback has a clear end point: ovulation (as in A1).



The cycle combines everything in this lecture: sensing, hormonal messengers, target receptors and feedback.

Exercise 6.3 asks for this order. The curves are schematic shapes, not measured values. The key idea is that the sign of the feedback depends on the level and duration of the oestradiol signal: low or moderate oestradiol inhibits, sustained high oestradiol stimulates. It is not a failure of regulation but a timer that ends in one event. Link back to A1, where positive feedback was introduced with oxytocin and birth; here is a second example with a clear stopping point.

text:

The animal half: a body too large for diffusion (A1) fuels its cells (A2), supplies O₂ by bulk flow (A3), keeps their fluid stable (A4) and coordinates it all by feedback through nerves, muscles and hormones (A5).
Next (P1 — Building a functioning plant): a plant faces the same problems of exchange, transport and control, but cannot run, pump blood or send nerve impulses.
Tutorial · Exercises · Quiz

Read the table as the path of one signal: from ion gradients to a spike, along an axon, across a synapse, into a muscle, then the slower hormonal route and the reproductive axis. Then step back to the whole animal half: each unit answered one part of the A1 question of how to keep every cell supplied and its surroundings stable. The plant half asks the same questions about an organism with no muscles, no nerves and no heart, which makes the comparison sharper.

title: A5 exercises — Nerve, muscle, hormones and reproduction
text: The questions follow the tutorial and slides. Answer each question before opening its answer.

title: A5 exercises — Nerve, muscle, hormones and reproduction
text:
Membrane potential

1.1
The Nernst equation at 37 °C is
\[E_\text{ion} = \frac{61.5\ \text{mV}}{z}\,\log_{10}\frac{[\text{ion}]_\text{out}}{[\text{ion}]_\text{in}},\]
where \(z\) is the charge of the ion. Calculate the equilibrium potential of each ion in a mammalian neuron.



Ion
Outside (mmol L⁻¹)
Inside (mmol L⁻¹)




K⁺
5
140


Na⁺
145
15


Cl⁻
110
10









Answer






\(E_\text{K} = 61.5 \log_{10}(5/140) = 61.5 \times (-1.45) \approx -89\) mV.
\(E_\text{Na} = 61.5 \log_{10}(145/15) = 61.5 \times 0.985 \approx +61\) mV.
\(E_\text{Cl} = -61.5 \log_{10}(110/10) = -61.5 \times 1.04 \approx -64\) mV (\(z = -1\)).






1.2
The neuron in 1.1 has a resting membrane potential of −70 mV.

Which ion’s equilibrium potential is the resting potential closest to, and what does this tell you about the resting membrane?
In which direction is the net electrochemical driving force on Na⁺?
In which direction is the net electrochemical driving force on K⁺?







Answer






K⁺. At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ (through leak channels) than to Na⁺.
Inward: both the concentration gradient and the negative inside favour Na⁺ entry.
Outward. The membrane potential (−70 mV) is less negative than \(E_\text{K}\) (−89 mV), so the concentration gradient outweighs the electrical attraction.






1.3
Extracellular K⁺ is raised from 5 to 10 mmol L⁻¹ (intracellular K⁺ stays at 140 mmol L⁻¹). Calculate the new \(E_\text{K}\). Does the membrane depolarise or hyperpolarise?






Answer





\(E_\text{K} = 61.5 \log_{10}(10/140) \approx -70.5\) mV. \(E_\text{K}\) becomes less negative, so the resting membrane depolarises.





1.4
True or false? Correct any false statements.

The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ into the cell per ATP.
The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase directly produces the rising phase of the action potential.
The inside of a resting neuron is negative because all the molecules in the cytoplasm are negatively charged.
During a single action potential, the intracellular Na⁺ concentration changes only very slightly.







Answer






True.
False. The rising phase is caused by Na⁺ flowing in through voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, down its electrochemical gradient. The pump maintains the gradients over the longer term.
False. The cytoplasm as a whole is electrically neutral; only a very small excess of negative charge lies next to the membrane.
True. Very few ions need to cross the membrane to change the voltage.

title: A5 exercises — Nerve, muscle, hormones and reproduction
text:
The action potential

2.1
Put the events of an axonal action potential in order.

Voltage-gated K⁺ channels open and K⁺ leaves the cell.
The membrane is depolarised to threshold.
The membrane briefly hyperpolarises below the resting potential.
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ enters the cell.
Na⁺ channels inactivate.
The membrane potential rises rapidly and becomes positive (overshoot).
K⁺ channels close and the resting potential is restored.







Answer





b → d → f → e → a → c → g. Na⁺-channel inactivation and K⁺-channel opening together cause repolarisation.





2.2
Define the absolute and the relative refractory period, and give the cause of each.






Answer






Absolute refractory period: no stimulus, however strong, can trigger a second action potential. Cause: the voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated.
Relative refractory period: a stronger-than-normal stimulus is needed to trigger an action potential. Cause: some Na⁺ channels are still inactivated and K⁺ conductance is still raised (the membrane is hyperpolarised).

The refractory period makes the action potential travel in one direction only.





2.3
A stronger stimulus is applied to a sensory receptor. Which two properties of the sensory signal increase? Which property stays the same?






Answer





The frequency of action potentials in each neuron and the number of neurons recruited both increase. The amplitude of each action potential stays the same, because the action potential is all-or-none.





2.4

Name two properties of an axon that increase its conduction velocity.
An action potential travels 0.60 m from the spinal cord to a foot muscle in 12 ms. Calculate the conduction velocity in m s⁻¹.







Answer






A larger axon diameter, and myelination (saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier).
0.60 m ÷ 0.012 s = 50 m s⁻¹.

3.1

Transmitter binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open in the presynaptic terminal.
An action potential arrives at the presynaptic terminal.
Synaptic vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release transmitter by exocytosis.
Ca²⁺ enters the terminal.
Ion channels open and the postsynaptic membrane potential changes.
Transmitter is removed by enzymatic breakdown or reuptake.







Answer





c → b → e → d → a → f → g.





3.2
State whether each postsynaptic response is excitatory or inhibitory.

Acetylcholine opens cation channels (nicotinic receptors) on a skeletal muscle fibre.
Acetylcholine binds muscarinic receptors on cardiac pacemaker cells and opens K⁺ channels.
GABA opens Cl⁻ channels, and the membrane potential moves towards \(E_\text{Cl}\) (−70 mV) from a threshold of −55 mV.
Glutamate opens channels permeable to Na⁺ and K⁺.







Answer






Excitatory. b. Inhibitory (it slows the heart). c. Inhibitory.
Excitatory.

Examples a and b show that the same transmitter can excite or inhibit: the effect depends on the receptor.

text:
Skeletal muscle

4.1
Put the steps of excitation–contraction coupling in skeletal muscle in order.

Ca²⁺ binds to troponin.
Acetylcholine is released at the neuromuscular junction.
Ca²⁺ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
An action potential arrives at the motor-neuron terminal.
Tropomyosin moves and exposes the myosin-binding sites on actin.
The muscle action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and into the T tubules.
Myosin heads bind actin and perform power strokes.
An end-plate potential depolarises the muscle fibre to threshold.
Voltage-sensing (dihydropyridine) receptors in the T-tubule membrane open the ryanodine receptors of the sarcoplasmic reticulum.







Answer





d → b → h → f → i → c → a → e → g.
Relaxation follows when acetylcholine is broken down by acetylcholinesterase and Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by an ATP-driven Ca²⁺ pump.





4.2
Give the role of each step in the cross-bridge cycle.

ATP binding to myosin
ATP hydrolysis by myosin
Release of phosphate from myosin

Why do muscles become rigid after death (rigor mortis)?






Answer






Detaches the myosin head from actin.
Re-cocks the myosin head into its high-energy position.
Triggers the power stroke, which pulls the thin filament towards the centre of the sarcomere.

After death ATP runs out, so myosin heads stay bound to actin and cannot detach.





4.3
When a sarcomere shortens, which of the following become shorter and which stay the same length?

A band
I band
H zone
Distance between Z discs
Thick (myosin) filaments
Thin (actin) filaments







Answer





Shorter: b, c and d. Unchanged: a, e and f. The filaments slide past each other without changing length (sliding-filament model).





4.4
A muscle lifts a load with a constant force of 20 N through 0.10 m in 0.50 s, with force and displacement in the same direction. It then holds the load still for 5 s.

Calculate the external mechanical work done while lifting.
Calculate the mean external mechanical power while lifting.
Calculate the external work done while holding the load still.
True or false: the muscle uses no ATP while holding the load still.







Answer






\(W = Fd = 20 \times 0.10 = 2.0\) J.
\(P = W/t = 2.0 / 0.50 = 4.0\) W.
0 J, because there is no displacement.
False. Cross-bridges keep cycling to maintain force (isometric contraction), and Ca²⁺ pumping continues, so ATP is consumed.






4.5
True or false? Correct any false statements.

A motor unit is one motor neuron together with all the muscle fibres it innervates.
Whole-muscle force can be increased by recruiting more motor units.
Whole-muscle force can be increased by raising the frequency of action potentials, so that twitches summate into tetanus.
Whole-muscle force is increased by making each motor-neuron action potential larger.







Answer






True. b. True. c. True.
False. Action potentials are all-or-none; force is graded by recruitment and firing frequency.






4.6
In smooth muscle, Ca²⁺ also triggers contraction, but not through troponin. Name the Ca²⁺-binding protein and the enzyme it activates, and state what the enzyme does.






Answer





Ca²⁺ binds calmodulin. Ca²⁺–calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK), which phosphorylates the myosin light chains. This allows myosin to bind actin and cycle.

The left panel shows K⁺ (green) and Na⁺ (red) on both sides of the membrane, with the channel widths showing the relative permeability; the right panel places \(E_\text{K}\), \(E_\text{Na}\) (Nernst) and the membrane potential \(V_m\) (Goldman equation) on one voltage scale. Use the sliders or the preset buttons, and read the values from the readout below the buttons.




E1.1
Click Rest. Read off \(E_\text{K}\), \(E_\text{Na}\) and \(V_m\). Is \(V_m\) closer to \(E_\text{K}\) or to \(E_\text{Na}\)?

\(V_m\) = −88 mV, practically equal to \(E_\text{K}\) (−89 mV); the K⁺ driving force is only +1 mV. A membrane permeable to one ion only sits at that ion’s Nernst potential.

It depolarises the cell (compare 1.3). This is why hyperkalaemia is dangerous: excitable cells, including heart muscle, are pushed towards and past threshold.





E1.4
Click Na⁺ channels open (\(P_\text{Na}/P_\text{K}\) = 20). What is \(V_m\)? Did the number of ion dots on either side change noticeably?

title: A5 exercises — Nerve, muscle, hormones and reproduction
text:
Explore: Threshold and refractory periods
A Hodgkin–Huxley axon receives two brief current pulses, S1 and S2 (each 0.5 ms). Set their strengths and the S1 → S2 interval with the sliders or the preset buttons. The lower panel shows the fraction of Na⁺ channels that are not inactivated (green) and the open K⁺ channels (gold); the verdict and readout below the buttons report the spikes.




E2.1
Click Too weak (S1 = 12, no S2), then raise S1 strength one step at a time. What is the smallest S1 that produces a spike?






Answer






At 15 the membrane depolarises a little and returns to rest; at 16 a full spike follows. This is the threshold.






E2.2
Click One spike (S1 = 40) and read the peak Vm. Then set S1 to 20 and to 80. What happens to the peak?

It roughly doubles from S1 = 20 to S1 = 80.
It stays about the same (+26 to +32 mV).
The spike disappears at S1 = 80.







Answer






Peak Vm is +30 mV at S1 = 40, +26 mV at 20 and +32 mV at 80. Above threshold the spike is all-or-none: a stronger stimulus does not give a bigger spike (stimulus strength is coded by spike frequency instead). The lowest Vm, the undershoot, is −81 mV in every case.






E2.3
Click 2nd at 1.5 ms, 8× (S2 = 320, eight times S1). Is there a second spike? Which refractory period is this, and what does the green trace show?






Answer





No second spike, even at S2 = 320: the absolute refractory period. The green trace shows that almost all Na⁺ channels are still inactivated, so no stimulus can open enough of them.





E2.4
Click 2nd at 3 ms (S2 = 40). Does S2 fire? According to the verdict, what S2 strength is needed at this interval? Then click 3 ms, 2× stronger: how many spikes now?






Answer





S2 = 40 fails; the verdict says S2 needs about 60 (relative refractory period). At S2 = 80 there are 2 spikes. In the relative refractory period a spike is possible, but only with a stronger stimulus, because some Na⁺ channels are still inactivated and K⁺ channels are still open.





E2.5
Keep S1 = S2 = 40 and drag S1 → S2 upwards from 2 ms in 0.5 ms steps. At which interval does the second spike first appear?






Answer





At 4.0 ms (at 3.5 ms S2 would need about 45). Refractoriness limits the maximum spike frequency and makes spikes travel in one direction only.

title: A3 self-check — Gas exchange and flow
text: Explain each answer before opening the callout. See the tutorial for the complete transport path.

title: A3 self-check — Gas exchange and flow
section: 1. Is ventilation the same as diffusion into the blood?
text:
1. Is ventilation the same as diffusion into the blood?






Answer





No. Ventilation moves the environmental medium by bulk flow. Diffusion crosses an exchange barrier down a local driving gradient. Perfusion supplies blood to the other side of that barrier.

title: A3 self-check — Gas exchange and flow
section: 2. If area doubles and thickness doubles, with all else unchanged, what happens to predicted transfer?
text:
2. If area doubles and thickness doubles, with all else unchanged, what happens to predicted transfer?






Answer





It is unchanged in the simple proportional model: \(2A/(2L)=A/L\). Real organs also have heterogeneous flow and gradients, so the comparison is conditional.

title: A3 self-check — Gas exchange and flow
section: 3. Is countercurrent exchange an example of oxygen diffusing uphill?
text:
3. Is countercurrent exchange an example of oxygen diffusing uphill?






Answer





No. Opposite flow directions can maintain a gradient along the exchange path. At each location oxygen still moves down the local partial-pressure gradient. Comparing remote inlet and outlet values confuses position with local exchange.

title: A3 self-check — Gas exchange and flow
section: 4. Does a normal oxygen partial pressure guarantee normal blood oxygen content?
text:
4. Does a normal oxygen partial pressure guarantee normal blood oxygen content?






Answer





No. Oxygen content also depends strongly on haemoglobin amount and binding. The same partial pressure can coexist with different total oxygen amounts per litre of blood. Pressure, saturation and content are distinct quantities.

title: A3 self-check — Gas exchange and flow
section: 5. Are pulmonary arteries named incorrectly because their blood is relatively deoxygenated?
text:
5. Are pulmonary arteries named incorrectly because their blood is relatively deoxygenated?






Answer





No. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and veins return it. The names refer to direction relative to the heart, not oxygenation state.

title: A3 self-check — Gas exchange and flow
section: 6. Flow is 3 L min⁻¹ and arterial–venous content difference 40 mL O₂ L⁻¹. What oxygen-use rate follows?
text:
6. Flow is 3 L min⁻¹ and arterial–venous content difference 40 mL O₂ L⁻¹. What oxygen-use rate follows?






Answer





\(3\times40=120\) mL O₂ min⁻¹ under the stated steady-state assumptions. Litres of blood cancel. Substituting a partial-pressure difference would not give the required amount balance.



Continue to A4, or revisit the A3 exercises.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
text:
During increased activity, muscle ATP demand rises. Breathing faster is only one possible response. Oxygen must reach the respiratory surface, cross a barrier, enter an internal transport system where needed, leave that system near the tissue and reach mitochondria. This unit follows that pathway and connects ventilation, exchange surfaces, blood and the pump.
By the end, explain diffusion and bulk flow as different processes; compare fish, mammalian and insect gas transport; interpret oxygen content separately from partial pressure; trace mammalian circulation; and connect vessel and respiratory histology to function. Work through the slides, exercises and quiz.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
text:

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
section: Diffusion needs a gradient and a suitable barrier
text:
Diffusion needs a gradient and a suitable barrier
A gas diffuses according to differences in its chemical potential, commonly described in physiology using partial pressure. Partial pressure is the pressure contribution of one gas in a mixture. A gas in solution also has an associated partial pressure related to dissolved, unbound gas. Oxygen can have the same partial pressure in two fluids while their total oxygen contents differ greatly because one contains an oxygen-binding pigment.
For a simple barrier, transfer rate increases with area and the partial-pressure difference and decreases with barrier thickness. We can write the proportional relationship as \(\dot M \propto A\Delta P/L\), holding the material’s diffusion properties constant. Doubling area doubles predicted transfer; doubling thickness halves it. This is a simplified comparison, because actual respiratory surfaces also have flow, varying gradients and heterogeneous structure.
Thinness and large area bring costs. A delicate moist surface needs protection, and a surface exposed to air can lose water. A respiratory organ must therefore combine exchange efficiency with support, protection and ventilation. In mammalian lung tissue, thin alveolar walls and nearby capillaries shorten the route between air and blood. Larger airways have a different task: conducting air, with supporting and protective structures rather than gas exchange across their full walls. See the openly accessible overview of exchange systems.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
section: Ventilation and perfusion renew the two sides
text:
Ventilation and perfusion renew the two sides
Ventilation moves environmental medium over a respiratory surface. Perfusion supplies internal fluid, often blood, to that surface. Both can maintain gradients by replacing fluid that has already exchanged gases. Increasing one alone may do little if the other is severely limiting.
A fish gill presents a large thin area to water. Water and blood commonly move in opposite directions across exchange regions. In an ideal countercurrent arrangement, a gradient can persist along the exchange path, allowing more complete extraction than a comparable co-current arrangement. It is not necessary for oxygen to move “uphill”: at every exchange location the net diffusion remains down a local partial-pressure gradient. Maintaining flow and supporting the gill are themselves physiological tasks.
Mammalian lungs use tidal ventilation: air moves in and out along shared conducting pathways. Fresh incoming air mixes with air already present, and not every part of an inspired breath reaches exchange regions. Birds provide a useful contrast: their rigid exchange lungs and air-sac ventilation support a different flow arrangement. Avoid describing air sacs themselves as the main gas-exchanging surface. The details of avian flow exceed this first explanation; the key point is that lungs are not all built as mammalian alveolar sacs.
Insects provide a further contrast. Tracheae and finer tracheoles bring gases close to tissues; ventilation and diffusion contribute to transport. Their circulating haemolymph generally has a smaller role in oxygen transport than vertebrate blood. This is an important counterexample to the claim that every active animal requires a vertebrate-style blood oxygen pathway.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
text:
Oxygen pressure, content and delivery
In many vertebrates, haemoglobin carries most blood oxygen. Dissolved oxygen contributes to partial pressure; haemoglobin-bound oxygen greatly increases content. Saturation is the fraction of available binding sites occupied, whereas oxygen content is an amount per volume of blood. Neither is a synonym for partial pressure. A blood sample can have a normal oxygen partial pressure yet carry less total oxygen if it contains less haemoglobin.
Cooperative oxygen binding produces an S-shaped relationship between haemoglobin saturation and oxygen partial pressure under typical conditions. The relation supports loading at high partial pressure and unloading as partial pressure falls in tissues. Temperature, pH and carbon dioxide influence affinity, helping coordinate delivery with local conditions. A rightward shift means lower affinity at a stated partial pressure; it does not mean oxygen has disappeared from the system.
Carbon dioxide returns from tissues in several forms, including bicarbonate, bound compounds and dissolved gas. Conversion between carbon dioxide and bicarbonate connects gas transport with acid–base balance. Ventilation can change carbon dioxide loss, but oxygen and carbon dioxide regulation should not be collapsed into a single “more breathing is always better” rule. The supporting reading distinguishes gas exchange and transport.
For a simplified steady-state accounting, oxygen use equals blood flow multiplied by the arterial–venous oxygen-content difference. If flow is 5 L min⁻¹, arterial content 200 mL O₂ L⁻¹ and venous content 150 mL O₂ L⁻¹, oxygen use is \(5(200-150)=250\) mL O₂ min⁻¹. The product uses content, not oxygen partial pressure. The calculation is a whole-system balance and requires representative measurements under the assumed conditions.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
section: A circuit needs pressure differences and valves
text:
A circuit needs pressure differences and valves
In mammalian circulation, the right heart sends blood towards the lungs and the left heart sends blood towards systemic tissues. Trace the circuit: systemic veins → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → systemic arteries. An artery carries blood away from the heart; a vein returns it. Oxygenation does not define these vessel names.





flowchart LR
  V[Systemic veins] --> RH[Right heart]
  RH --> PA[Pulmonary arteries]
  PA --> L[Lung exchange]
  L --> PV[Pulmonary veins]
  PV --> LH[Left heart]
  LH --> SA[Systemic arteries]
  SA --> T[Tissue exchange]
  T --> V






This original circuit sketch shows direction, not anatomical position or the relative size of its compartments.
Valves help prevent reverse flow as chamber pressures change. The ventricular wall develops pressure, but pressure is not identical to flow. A simple relation is flow \(Q=\Delta P/R\), where \(R\) is vascular resistance. With a fixed pressure difference, higher resistance gives lower flow. Smooth muscle can alter vessel calibre and distribute flow among tissues. Narrow vessels have high resistance individually, yet many small vessels arranged in parallel can support substantial total flow and a very large exchange area.
Arteries generally have walls suited to pressure and its fluctuations. Capillaries provide short exchange paths. Veins can hold a substantial blood volume at relatively low pressure, and return is influenced by pressure gradients, surrounding muscle and valves in appropriate locations. An empty or collapsed vessel in a section can look different from a blood-filled one; describe wall layers and surrounding tissue before naming it.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
text:
Comparative circuits and coordinated responses
A fish typically sends blood from its heart through gills and then systemic tissues in a single circuit. Mammals separate pulmonary and systemic circuits with a four-chambered heart. Other vertebrates have other arrangements, including variable separation of blood streams. Open circulations move haemolymph through vessels and body spaces; closed circulations keep the main transport fluid within vessels. “Open” does not mean motionless, and “closed” does not automatically identify the animal’s metabolic rate. Compare the actual route, pressure, control and exchange requirements. A useful overview is the reading on circulatory organisation.
At the onset of exercise, ventilation, cardiac activity and local vascular responses can act together. Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume. Increasing heart rate is only one way to change output, and a measured rate alone does not establish how much blood or oxygen reaches a tissue. Local metabolites and neural/endocrine signals help coordinate supply and demand.
Practise with the exercises, then continue to water, ions and excretion.

title: A2 self-check — Energy and temperature
text: Try each explanation before opening the answer. Use the tutorial for definitions and worked examples.

title: A2 self-check — Energy and temperature
section: 1. Are digestion, absorption and cellular ATP production the same process?
text:
1. Are digestion, absorption and cellular ATP production the same process?






Answer





No. Digestion makes smaller molecules available, absorption moves material across an epithelial barrier, and cellular metabolism transforms fuels and supplies ATP. A complete account connects these processes rather than merging them.

title: A2 self-check — Energy and temperature
section: 2. Intake is 100 kJ day⁻¹; losses are 20 faecal, 5 excreted and 80 metabolic. What is retained?
text:
2. Intake is 100 kJ day⁻¹; losses are 20 faecal, 5 excreted and 80 metabolic. What is retained?






Answer





\(100-20-5-80=-5\) kJ day⁻¹. The animal draws down retained stores in this simplified budget. It has not created negative energy, and the calculation does not diagnose which nutrient may be limiting.

title: A2 self-check — Energy and temperature
section: 3. A 0.10 L chamber loses 0.20 mg L⁻¹ oxygen in 5 min. What is its apparent rate before blank correction?
text:
3. A 0.10 L chamber loses 0.20 mg L⁻¹ oxygen in 5 min. What is its apparent rate before blank correction?






Answer





The amount decline is \(0.10\times0.20=0.020\) mg; dividing by 5 min gives 0.0040 mg min⁻¹. Concentration decline alone is not the amount consumed. An appropriate blank and the protocol’s other assumptions still need checking.

title: A2 self-check — Energy and temperature
section: 4. Does dividing oxygen consumption by body mass remove every size effect?
text:
4. Does dividing oxygen consumption by body mass remove every size effect?






Answer





No. It gives a mass-specific rate, but metabolic rate need not scale linearly with mass. Activity, temperature, feeding state and design can also differ. Normalisation is a stated calculation, not a guarantee of comparability.

title: A2 self-check — Energy and temperature
section: 5. Must an ectotherm have no temperature regulation?
text:
5. Must an ectotherm have no temperature regulation?






Answer





No. An ectotherm can select microhabitats, bask or change behaviour. Ectothermy describes major heat sources; it is not identical to uncontrolled body-temperature variation. Endotherms can also allow body temperature to vary.

title: A2 self-check — Energy and temperature
section: 6. A rate doubles from 10 to 20 °C. May we assume it doubles every further 10 °C?
text:
6. A rate doubles from 10 to 20 °C. May we assume it doubles every further 10 °C?






Answer





The measured \(Q_{10}\) is 2 for that interval. Extrapolation can fail as conditions, physiology or thermal limits change. Acclimation, activity and feeding state must be considered before comparisons.



Continue to A3, or revisit the A2 exercises.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Two animals can eat equal masses of food yet differ in growth, activity and heat production. Food mass alone does not tell us how much energy was absorbed, which essential nutrients were obtained, or how that energy was used. This unit connects digestion to cellular metabolism and whole-animal energy balance, then asks how temperature changes the demands and limits of that system.
You should become able to distinguish ingestion, digestion and absorption; explain digestive specialisation; interpret a simple energy budget and oxygen consumption rate; distinguish aerobic and anaerobic ATP supply; and compare thermal strategies without equating ectothermy with inactivity. Use the slides, exercises and quiz.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
section: From food to an absorbed molecule
text:
From food to an absorbed molecule
Ingestion brings food into the digestive system. Mechanical processing changes particle size and mixes contents. Chemical digestion uses reactions, often enzyme-catalysed hydrolysis, to make smaller molecules available for absorption. Enzymes have particular substrates and working conditions; a digestive tract contains regions with different secretions and environments. The gut lumen is continuous with the outside world. A nutrient reaches the internal environment only after crossing an absorptive barrier.
In a mammalian small intestine, folds, villi and microscopic projections on epithelial cells increase the area available for absorption. Capillaries and lymphatic routes remove absorbed materials, helping maintain transport. Carbohydrate-derived monosaccharides and amino acids commonly enter blood, while much absorbed dietary lipid is packaged and enters lymph first. These routes show why “absorption” is not one identical membrane process for every nutrient. The organs supplying secretions also matter: pancreatic enzymes and bile contribute to processing food in the intestine.
Eliminating unabsorbed material in faeces is egestion. Removing metabolic wastes produced within the animal is excretion. The distinction matters when constructing an energy budget or explaining a kidney’s function. OpenStax offers a supporting account of digestive processes.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
section: Digestive form follows the food problem
text:
Digestive form follows the food problem
Animal diets differ in nutrient concentration, physical structure and chemical defences. A predatory animal faces different processing demands from an animal eating fibrous plant tissue. Many animals lack enzymes that directly digest cellulose effectively. Symbiotic microbes can break down plant polymers and produce compounds the host can use. The host must provide conditions and retention time that sustain that fermentation.
In a ruminant, microbial fermentation occurs before the small intestine. Microbes and their products can then contribute to the host’s nutrition. Hindgut fermenters maintain substantial fermentation later in the tract. Where fermentation occurs changes which products are readily absorbed and whether microbial biomass reaches major sites of protein digestion. These strategies involve trade-offs in passage time, food intake and nutrient recovery; one is not universally superior for every food supply or body size.
For histology, relate an absorptive epithelium to its lumen and underlying transport tissues. Smooth muscle layers help propel contents, while glands and specialised epithelial cells contribute secretions. A diagram that labels “villus” without showing the lumen, epithelial barrier and internal removal route misses the functional explanation. The broad comparative anatomy is covered in the reading on digestive systems.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Keep energy accounting explicit
For a simplified animal over a stated interval, ingested energy is divided between material not absorbed and absorbed energy. After accounting for energy leaving in excreted products, the remaining energy can support metabolic expenditure and net storage or production. Exact ecological bookkeeping conventions vary, so define your terms before calculating. Here we use:
\[
E_{\rm ingested}=E_{\rm faeces}+E_{\rm excreted}+E_{\rm metabolic}+E_{\rm retained}.
\]
All quantities refer to the same interval. If intake is 100 kJ day⁻¹, faecal loss 25, excreted chemical energy 5 and metabolic expenditure 60 kJ day⁻¹, retained energy is 10 kJ day⁻¹. Retained energy can contribute to new tissue, reserves or reproductive products. A negative retained balance can mean the animal is drawing down stores. This arithmetic does not identify which nutrient limited growth, because energy and essential nutrient supplies are distinct.
Avoid double counting. Internal mechanical work ultimately dissipates largely as heat, so a budget that already includes it in metabolic expenditure should not add the same energy again as an independent heat cost. Also distinguish energy in joules from power, an energy rate in watts. One watt is one joule per second. A daily intake and an instantaneous metabolic power cannot be subtracted until converted to compatible units and time intervals.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
section: ATP supply, work and oxygen consumption
text:
ATP supply, work and oxygen consumption
ATP links fuel metabolism to processes such as transport and muscle activity. Aerobic metabolism uses oxygen in mitochondrial electron transfer and can support sustained ATP supply when fuels, oxygen delivery and waste removal are adequate. Anaerobic pathways can supply ATP without that immediate oxygen use, but their ATP yield per unit substrate and sustainable rates differ. An animal may use both during a single bout of activity. Oxygen consumption therefore provides useful information about aerobic metabolism without being a complete record of every ATP-producing process at every instant.
Imagine a supplied respirometry observation: a chamber contains 0.10 L of water, and oxygen concentration falls by 0.40 mg L⁻¹ in 10 minutes. The chamber’s oxygen loss is \(0.10\times0.40=0.040\) mg, giving an apparent rate of 0.0040 mg min⁻¹. If a comparable empty chamber loses 0.0010 mg min⁻¹, the blank-corrected animal rate is 0.0030 mg min⁻¹. The example is a calculation with supplied data, not a procedure for keeping animals in sealed containers.
Rate comparisons require the right denominator and context. Dividing by body mass produces a mass-specific rate, but does not automatically remove all effects of body size. Activity, temperature, feeding state, stress and time of day can also matter. Repeated readings from one animal do not create new independent animals. Any actual experiment must use the established approved protocol and conditions; physiological interpretation begins by understanding what the measurement system measures.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
section: Temperature changes both rates and costs
text:
Temperature changes both rates and costs
An ectotherm obtains much of the heat determining its body temperature from external sources. An endotherm generates substantial metabolic heat for temperature regulation. These terms concern heat sources. They are not identical to poikilothermy and homeothermy, which describe variation or relative stability of body temperature. An ectotherm can regulate temperature behaviourally, and an endotherm may allow body temperature to vary.
Temperature affects reaction rates, membranes and protein function. A rise can increase some physiological rates within a suitable range, yet eventually performance declines as other processes become limiting or damaged. A simple \(Q_{10}\) describes the rate ratio over a 10 °C interval:
\[Q_{10}=\left(\frac{R_2}{R_1}\right)^{10/(T_2-T_1)}.\]
If a rate increases from 2 to 4 units between 10 and 20 °C, \(Q_{10}=2\). It is a description over those conditions, not a universal constant or a license to extrapolate into thermal extremes. Use rates measured under comparable feeding, activity and acclimation conditions.
Endotherms face an energy cost when heat loss must be replaced. Insulation, posture, peripheral blood flow and behaviour alter heat exchange. Below a species- and condition-dependent thermoneutral range, resting metabolic heat production often rises as ambient temperature falls. Above a suitable range, cooling can become demanding; evaporation loses water. An ectotherm’s metabolic rate may rise with environmental warming over a moderate range. Thus two rising metabolic rates can reflect different mechanisms: defending body temperature in cold conditions or temperature-dependent processes in a warming body.
Practise with the exercises, then continue to gas exchange and circulation.

title: A2 exercises — Feeding, metabolism and temperature
text: The questions follow the tutorial and slides. Answer each question before opening its answer.

title: A2 exercises — Feeding, metabolism and temperature
text:
Digestion and absorption

1.1
Define each term: ingestion, digestion, absorption, egestion and excretion.






Answer






Ingestion: taking food into the digestive tract.
Digestion: breaking food down, mechanically and chemically (mainly by enzymatic hydrolysis), into molecules small enough to be absorbed.
Absorption: uptake of the products of digestion across the gut epithelium into the internal environment (blood or lymph).
Egestion: elimination of unabsorbed material from the gut as faeces.
Excretion: elimination of metabolic wastes produced inside the body, such as urea.






1.2
True or false? Correct any false statements.

A starch grain in the lumen of the small intestine is inside the body’s internal environment.
Faeces are the main route for the excretion of nitrogenous waste in mammals.
Bile is a digestive enzyme that hydrolyses fats.
Chemical digestion of food is mostly by hydrolysis.







Answer






False. The gut lumen is continuous with the outside world. Material is inside the internal environment only after it has crossed the epithelium.
False. Faeces are mainly egested, unabsorbed material. Nitrogenous waste (urea) is excreted mainly in urine.
False. Bile contains no digestive enzymes. Its bile salts emulsify fats into small droplets, which increases the surface area for lipase.
True.

glucose is taken up across the apical membrane of the enterocyte
pancreatic amylase hydrolyses starch in the small intestine
brush-border enzymes (such as maltase) hydrolyse disaccharides to glucose
blood from the intestine reaches the liver in the hepatic portal vein







Answer





b → d → e → c → a → f.





1.5
Name three structural features of the mammalian small intestine that increase its absorptive surface area, from the largest to the smallest scale.






Answer






Circular folds of the intestinal wall.
Villi: finger-like projections of the mucosa.
Microvilli: projections of the apical membrane of each epithelial cell (the brush border).






1.6
State whether each absorbed product enters the blood capillaries or the lacteals (lymphatic vessels) of a villus.

glucose
amino acids
long-chain fatty acids and monoglycerides, repackaged as chylomicrons







Answer






Blood capillaries. b. Blood capillaries. c. Lacteals. Chylomicrons are too large to enter the blood capillaries, so they enter the lymph and reach the blood later.

title: A2 exercises — Feeding, metabolism and temperature
text:
Microbial fermentation

2.1
Why do most herbivorous vertebrates depend on symbiotic microbes to use plant cell walls, and which main products do the microbes supply to the host?






Answer





Vertebrates do not produce cellulase, so they cannot hydrolyse cellulose themselves. Microbes ferment the cellulose and supply short-chain (volatile) fatty acids, such as acetate, propionate and butyrate, which the host absorbs and uses as fuel. The microbes themselves are also a source of protein.





2.2
Classify each animal as a foregut fermenter or a hindgut fermenter.

cow
horse
sheep
rabbit







Answer






Foregut (ruminant). b. Hindgut (caecum and colon). c. Foregut (ruminant).
Hindgut (caecum).






2.3
In which type of fermenter is microbial protein digested and absorbed in the small intestine, and why? How do rabbits recover microbial protein?






Answer





In a foregut fermenter. The fermentation chamber lies before the stomach and small intestine, so microbes washed out of it are digested in the small intestine like other food protein. In a hindgut fermenter the microbes grow after the small intestine and are mostly lost in the faeces. Rabbits recover them by caecotrophy: they eat the soft faeces produced from the caecum (coprophagy).

title: A2 exercises — Feeding, metabolism and temperature
text:
Energy budgets

3.1
Over one day, an animal has ingested energy 150 kJ, faecal loss 40 kJ, chemical energy excreted (in urine) 10 kJ and metabolic expenditure 85 kJ. Use the budget
\[
E_{\rm ingested}=E_{\rm faeces}+E_{\rm excreted}+E_{\rm metabolic}+E_{\rm retained}.
\]

Calculate the retained energy.
Calculate the absorbed energy as a percentage of ingested energy.
Calculate the retained energy if metabolic expenditure rises to 110 kJ, with the other terms unchanged. What does the sign of the result mean?







Answer






\(150-40-10-85=15\) kJ.
Absorbed energy is \(150-40=110\) kJ, i.e. \(110/150=73\,\%\) of ingested energy.
\(150-40-10-110=-10\) kJ. The animal spends more than it takes up, so it draws on its energy stores (such as fat or glycogen) and loses body energy.






3.2
Express the metabolic expenditure of 85 kJ day⁻¹ from 3.1 as a mean power in watts. (1 day = 86 400 s.)






Answer





\(85\,000\ \text{J} / 86\,400\ \text{s} = 0.98\) J s⁻¹ \(= 0.98\) W.





3.3
Which quantity is energy and which is power? Give the SI unit of each.

2 000 kJ of food eaten in a day
a resting metabolic rate of 80 W
60 J transferred in 10 s







Answer






Energy (J). b. Power (W = J s⁻¹). c. Energy (J); it corresponds to a mean power of \(60/10=6\) W.

Answer





During a sprint, part of the ATP comes from anaerobic sources (phosphocreatine and glycolysis to lactate), which do not consume O₂. Oxygen consumption measures only aerobic ATP production.





4.3

For C1: \((0.25-0.05)\ \text{mg L}^{-1} \times 0.20\ \text{L} = 0.040\) mg in 10 min \(= 0.0040\) mg min⁻¹; divided by 2.0 g gives 0.0020 mg min⁻¹ g⁻¹.

title: A2 exercises — Feeding, metabolism and temperature
text:
Temperature and metabolism

5.1
Use \(Q_{10}=(R_2/R_1)^{10/(T_2-T_1)}\).

A rate rises from 2.0 to 8.0 units between 10 and 30 °C. Calculate \(Q_{10}\).
A process has \(Q_{10}=2.5\) and a rate of 4.0 units at 20 °C. Predict the rate at 30 °C.







Answer






\(Q_{10}=(8.0/2.0)^{10/20}=4^{0.5}=2.0\).
\(4.0\times2.5=10\) units.






5.2
Match each term to its definition: ectotherm, endotherm, poikilotherm, homeotherm.

an animal whose body temperature varies with environmental temperature
an animal whose body temperature is determined mainly by external heat sources
an animal that keeps a relatively constant body temperature
an animal that warms its body mainly with its own metabolic heat







Answer






Poikilotherm. b. Ectotherm. c. Homeotherm. d. Endotherm.

Ectothermy and endothermy refer to the source of body heat; poikilothermy and homeothermy refer to how much body temperature varies.





5.3
True or false? Correct any false statements.

Ectotherms cannot regulate their body temperature.
In a resting ectotherm, metabolic rate usually rises when environmental temperature rises over a moderate range.
In a resting endotherm, metabolic rate is lowest within the thermoneutral zone.
A measured \(Q_{10}\) can be used to predict rates at any temperature.







Answer






False. Many ectotherms regulate body temperature by behaviour, such as basking, seeking shade and changing posture.
True. Body temperature follows environmental temperature, and reaction rates rise with temperature.
True.
False. \(Q_{10}\) describes only the measured temperature range. Outside it, rates level off and fall as proteins and membranes are damaged.






5.4
The graph of resting metabolic rate against ambient temperature for a mammal has three regions. Name the region in which metabolic rate is at its minimum and constant, and the temperature at its lower boundary. What happens to metabolic rate below that boundary, and why?






Answer





The thermoneutral zone; its lower boundary is the lower critical temperature. Below the lower critical temperature, metabolic rate rises as ambient temperature falls, because the animal must produce more heat (by shivering and non-shivering thermogenesis) to replace the faster heat loss and keep body temperature constant.





5.5
Name the route of heat exchange in each example: conduction, convection, radiation or evaporation.

A lizard warms itself in sunlight.
A dog pants on a hot day.
A snake lies on a warm rock.
Wind cools a bird’s body surface.







Answer






Radiation. b. Evaporation. c. Conduction. d. Convection.






5.6
Name four ways in which a mammal reduces heat loss or increases heat production in the cold.






Answer





Any four of: thicker fur or fat (insulation); piloerection (raising the fur); vasoconstriction of skin blood vessels; countercurrent heat exchange in the limbs; curling up (posture) and huddling; shivering thermogenesis; non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue.
