title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
About this lecture
In A1 we saw how a body brings O₂ and food within reach of every cell. Today we ask what the cells do with them. A 25 g mouse eats about 4 g of food (roughly 55 kJ) every day. A lizard of the same mass, at the same body temperature, lives on about a tenth of that. Where does the mouse’s food energy go, and why does it need so much more?

From food to fuel: ingestion, digestion and absorption, and the enzymes and surfaces that do the work.
Plant food: why herbivores need microbes, and where they keep them.
Energy accounting: the energy budget, and energy versus power.
Turning fuel into ATP: aerobic and anaerobic supply, and how we measure metabolic rate from O₂ consumption.
Temperature: Q_{10}, ectotherms and endotherms, heat exchange and the cost of keeping warm.


Open with the mouse and the lizard, and come back to them on the last content slide. The lecture follows the food: into the gut, across the epithelium, into the energy budget, into ATP, and finally out as heat. The temperature part explains the tenfold difference in the opening question: the mouse is an endotherm and pays for its heat with food. Link to A1 explicitly: there we built the supply lines (exchange surfaces, bulk flow); here we look at what is delivered and what it is used for. A3 then takes the oxygen side in detail.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
section: From food to fuel: five processes
text:
From food to fuel: five processes



Ingestion: taking food into the gut.
Digestion: breaking it into absorbable molecules, mechanically and chemically.
Absorption: uptake across the gut epithelium into blood or lymph.
Egestion: eliminating unabsorbed material as faeces.
Excretion: eliminating metabolic wastes made inside the body, such as urea in urine.

Food in the gut lumen is still outside the body (A1).




These five words are used precisely for the rest of the course, and exercise 1.1 asks for them. The two that students confuse are egestion and excretion: faeces are mostly material that was never absorbed, so they were never inside the body; urea was made by the body’s own metabolism and leaves via the kidney (A4). This distinction matters again in the energy budget, where faecal loss and excretory loss are separate terms. The link to A1 is the gut lumen: a starch grain in the intestine has not yet entered the internal environment.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Chemical digestion is hydrolysis









Enzyme

Substrate

Starch

Small-intestine epithelium

Glucose, amino acids




Each reaction splits a bond by adding water: hydrolysis.
Bile (from the liver) contains no enzymes. Bile salts emulsify fat into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase.

So what route does one meal take through these enzymes?

This is the table students complete in exercise 1.3. Group it by food class: carbohydrate (amylase, then brush-border disaccharidases), protein (pepsin in the acid stomach, then trypsin, then peptidases at the brush border) and fat (bile plus lipase). Stress that most digestion happens in the small intestine, because the pancreas delivers most of the enzymes there. The bile point is a classic misconception: bile does not digest anything, it is a detergent that does for fat what chewing does for bread, namely increases surface area. Next slide follows one food, starch, all the way to the liver.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Following a starch meal



Mouth: salivary amylase starts on starch.
Small intestine: pancreatic amylase → maltose.
Brush border: maltase → glucose.
Apical membrane: glucose enters with Na⁺ (SGLT1).
Basolateral membrane: glucose leaves to the blood (GLUT2).
Hepatic portal vein: to the liver first.

Steps 4 and 5: different transporters on the two sides (A1 polarity).


Photo: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Absorption needs a large surface. How large is it?

Exercise 1.4 asks for this order. The micrograph shows where steps 3 to 5 happen: each finger is a villus, covered by one layer of columnar enterocytes whose brush border faces the lumen. Walk it in space: lumen, brush border, apical membrane, cell, basolateral membrane, capillary, portal vein. The two transporters show why epithelial polarity (A1) matters: the Na⁺-glucose co-transporter on the apical side uses the Na⁺ gradient made by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase on the basolateral side, so absorption itself costs ATP. The hepatic portal vein means the liver sees absorbed nutrients first and can store glucose as glycogen before it reaches the rest of the body.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
The absorptive surface


The small intestine multiplies its area at three scales:

Circular folds of the wall (×3).
Villi, finger-like projections of the mucosa (×10).
Microvilli on each epithelial cell, the brush border (×20).

Two exit routes from a villus:

Blood capillaries: glucose, amino acids.
Lacteal (lymph): fats, repackaged as chylomicrons, too large for capillaries.





This is A1’s solution 1, enlarging the surface, applied three times over: roughly 3 × 10 × 20, about 600-fold relative to a smooth tube. Exercise 1.5 asks for the three features from largest to smallest. The exit routes (exercise 1.6): water-soluble products enter the capillaries and go via the portal vein to the liver; fatty acids and monoglycerides are reassembled into triglycerides inside the enterocyte, packed with protein into chylomicrons, and leave into the lacteal. They reach the blood later where the thoracic duct joins a vein. Transition: all of this assumes the animal has the enzymes for its food. A herbivore does not.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Plant food: the cellulose problem



Plant cell walls are mostly cellulose; vertebrates make no cellulase.
Symbiotic microbes ferment it in a gut chamber.
The host absorbs their end products, short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate): ~70 % of a cow’s energy.
The microbes are also a protein source if the host can digest them.
Fermentation is slow: food is retained for hours to days.



Photo: Ajznponar, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

So where along the gut should the fermentation chamber be?

Exercise 2.1. The key idea is that the herbivore does not digest grass; its microbes do, and the herbivore lives largely on their waste products (short-chain fatty acids) and on the microbes themselves. Fermentation also produces methane and heat, which are losses for the host. The final bullet sets up the trade-off on the next slide: a fermentation chamber needs retention time, and its position relative to the small intestine decides whether microbial protein can be digested.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Foregut and hindgut fermenters


Foregut (before the small intestine): cow, sheep, deer (ruminants), kangaroo.

Ruminant stomach: rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum (the true stomach).
Microbes washed out are digested in the small intestine.

Hindgut (after the small intestine): horse, rabbit, many rodents.

Fermentation in the caecum and colon.
Microbial protein is mostly lost in faeces.
Rabbits recover it by caecotrophy: eating soft faeces from the caecum.





Exercises 2.2 and 2.3. The figure makes the logic visible: order matters. In a ruminant, food and microbes flow from the rumen into the abomasum and small intestine, so the host digests microbial protein like any other protein. In a horse or rabbit, the microbes grow downstream of the small intestine, so their protein passes out in the faeces unless the animal eats the caecotrophs. The trade-off: a ruminant extracts more from each mouthful but must hold food for a long time; a horse passes food faster and compensates by eating more. Transition: whatever the gut, we can now ask how much of the eaten energy the animal actually keeps.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
The energy budget


Over one stated interval:
E_{\rm ingested}=E_{\rm faeces}+E_{\rm excreted}+E_{\rm metabolic}+E_{\rm retained}

Faeces: energy never absorbed (egestion).
Excreted: chemical energy in urine, mainly urea.
Metabolic: energy used and released as heat.
Retained: new tissue, fat stores, offspring.
Absorbed =E_{\rm ingested}-E_{\rm faeces}.





This is energy conservation applied to an animal. Every term must be for the same interval (here one day). The egestion/excretion distinction from the first slide appears here as two separate terms. Metabolic expenditure includes all work done inside the body; that work ends up as heat, so heat is not added as an extra term. In the figure, 150 kJ in, 40 kJ in faeces, so 110 kJ absorbed, which is 73 % of intake. Next slide: what retained energy means, and what happens when it is negative.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Retained energy can be negative


Intake 150 kJ, faeces 40 kJ, excreted 10 kJ: 100 kJ available for metabolism and retention.



Metabolic
Retained




85 kJ
+15 kJ


110 kJ
−10 kJ




Positive: the animal grows or stores fat.
Negative: it draws on stores (fat, glycogen) and loses body energy.




Budgets are in joules per day; metabolic rates are usually in watts. How do they compare?

Work both lines on the board. A negative retained term is normal for short periods: overnight, during migration, in a lactating mother, in a hibernating mammal. It does not mean negative food; it means stored energy is converted to heat and work. Point out that this budget counts only energy: an animal can have a positive energy balance and still fail to grow if, for example, it lacks an essential amino acid. Transition to units.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Energy is not power



Energy is an amount: joules (J).
Power is a rate: J s⁻¹ = watts (W).
To compare, convert to the same time unit. 1 day = 86 400 s.

Example: a human uses about 8 400 kJ day⁻¹.
\frac{8\,400\,000\ \text{J}}{86\,400\ \text{s}} \approx 97\ \text{W}
A person is a ~100 W heater, all day.




Exercises 3.2 and 3.3 test this. The figure shows the same 60 J delivered over different times: same energy, different power. The human example makes the watt tangible: a room of 30 students adds about 3 kW of heat. Emphasise that “2 000 kJ eaten” is an energy and “80 W resting” is a power; they cannot be added or subtracted until one is converted. Transition: the metabolic term is spent inside cells, as ATP. How do cells make it?

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Turning fuel into ATP











Anaerobic glycolysis
Aerobic metabolism




Where
Cytosol
Cytosol, then mitochondria (citric acid cycle, electron transport chain)


Needs O₂?
No
Yes: final electron acceptor

Lactate
CO₂ + H₂O


ATP per glucose
2

Rate
Fast, short-lived
Slower, sustainable




Aerobic metabolism gets ~15× more ATP from each glucose.
Anaerobic glycolysis makes ATP fast, but lactate accumulates.




So which does a running animal use?

This is the table of exercise 4.1. Glycolysis happens in the cytosol either way; the difference is what happens to pyruvate. With O₂, pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is oxidised fully to CO₂, and the electron transport chain uses O₂ as the final electron acceptor, giving about 30 ATP per glucose in total. Without enough O₂, pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺, and the cell gets only the 2 ATP of glycolysis. Fats and proteins also feed the aerobic pathway, which is why fat can be burned only aerobically.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
section: A sprint uses three ATP sources
text:
A sprint uses three ATP sources





Source
O₂?
Sustains hard work




Phosphocreatine (PCr + ADP → Cr + ATP)
No
~10 s


Anaerobic glycolysis → lactate
No
~1–2 min


Aerobic metabolism
Yes
Hours




A sprint runs mostly on the first two.
O₂ uptake measures only aerobic ATP, so in a sprint it underestimates ATP use.
Afterwards O₂ uptake stays high while PCr is rebuilt and lactate cleared (excess post-exercise O₂ consumption).



Photo: Clément Bucco-Lechat, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Even so, O₂ consumption is the standard measure of metabolic rate. How is it measured?

Exercise 4.2. The three systems overlap rather than switch on in sequence, but their capacities differ greatly. A 100 m sprinter runs mostly on phosphocreatine and glycolysis; a marathon runner almost entirely aerobically. Because the anaerobic sources are later repaid aerobically, O₂ consumption averaged over a longer period still tracks total energy use. At rest and during steady activity, nearly all ATP is aerobic, which is why O₂ consumption is used as the measure of metabolic rate: each litre of O₂ consumed corresponds to about 20 kJ of energy released.

Concentration × volume = amount.
The blank removes O₂ use that is not the animal’s (microbes, drift).





The figure shows the raw data behind the table: the steeper fall with the animal, the shallow fall in the blank. Go through the units at every row; students’ usual error is to forget the volume and report mg L⁻¹ as if it were an amount. The blank corrects for microbial respiration and sensor drift; if the blank is given per interval as a concentration change, subtract it before multiplying by volume. Dividing by mass lets animals of different size be compared; mass-specific rate is a fair comparison between similar-sized animals; across large size ranges metabolic rate does not scale in direct proportion to mass, so mass-specific rate falls with size. Transition: one animal gives one number. To compare two temperatures, we need several animals.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature

Comparing temperatures: what is a replicate?

The independent replicate is the animal: n = 3 per temperature, not 15. Repeated readings from one animal are not new animals.
Keep other conditions equal: activity, feeding state, time of day, acclimation.

The rate rose 2.5-fold over 10 °C. How do we describe that?

Exercise 4.4 asks the same question for its own data. Pseudoreplication (treating the 15 readings as 15 samples) inflates confidence. Other variables that change metabolic rate must be held constant: a recently fed animal has a higher rate (the cost of digesting), an active one far higher. Acclimation (A1) also matters: animals kept at 25 °C for weeks may differ from animals moved there an hour ago. Transition to Q10.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Temperature and rate: Q_{10}


Q_{10} is the factor by which a rate changes over 10 °C:
Q_{10}=\left(\frac{R_2}{R_1}\right)^{10/(T_2-T_1)}

Previous slide: 0.0020 → 0.0050 over 15 → 25 °C, so Q_{10}=2.5.
Each further 10 °C multiplies the rate again: the curve is exponential.
Most biological rates: Q_{10} of 2–3.





The figure shows what a constant Q10 means: the same factor for every 10 °C step, so the curve bends upwards. Three curves through the same measured point at 15 °C show how much the prediction depends on the Q10 value at higher temperatures. The gold step is the 15 → 25 °C comparison from the respirometry data.

Q_{10} describes only the measured range. At higher temperatures rates level off and then fall as proteins and membranes are damaged.

So does every animal’s metabolic rate simply follow the temperature around it?

Exercise 5.1 uses both forms of the calculation. The exponent 10/(T₂ − T₁) converts any interval to a 10 °C interval: over 20 °C the ratio is Q10 squared, so the square root gives Q10. Q10 of 2–3 reflects the temperature dependence of enzyme-catalysed reactions. The limitation in the last bullet is exercise 5.3d: never extrapolate a Q10 beyond the measured range. The transition question: this is true of our resting ectotherm, but not of a mouse.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Heat source and temperature stability











Temp. varies (poikilotherm)
Temp. stable (homeotherm)




External heat (ectotherm)
Frog, most insects
Deep-sea fish


Metabolic heat (endotherm)
Hibernating ground squirrel
Mouse, human, birds




Ecto/endotherm: the source of body heat.
Poikilo/homeotherm: how much body temperature varies.
An endotherm’s resting rate is 5–10× an ectotherm’s at the same mass and body temperature.



Photo: Bouke ten Cate, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

How does heat enter and leave an animal?

Exercise 5.2. The two pairs of terms answer different questions, so the 2×2 table has an example in every cell. The off-diagonal cells are the ones that break the old “cold-blooded / warm-blooded” labels: a deep-sea fish has a very constant temperature without making heat; a hibernating squirrel is an endotherm that lets its body cool to a few degrees. The 5–10× figure is the answer to the opening question: endothermy is expensive. Exercise 5.3a: ectotherms are not unable to regulate; they regulate by behaviour. The photo shows it: a basking lizard flattens its body and orients it towards the sun to gain heat by radiation and from the warm stone, and moves into shade when it is warm enough, holding about 35 °C during the day.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Four routes of heat exchange



Radiation: infrared and sunlight; no contact.
Conduction: direct contact, e.g. a warm rock.
Convection: carried by moving air or water.
Evaporation: water to vapour, ~2.4 kJ per g; panting, sweating.

The first three can add or remove heat; evaporation only removes it. Body temperature is stable when heat gained equals heat lost.



For an endotherm, how much heat must metabolism supply?

Exercise 5.5. Radiation and conduction are the ones students mix up: radiation needs no contact, conduction does. Convection is conduction plus a moving fluid, which is why wind chills. Evaporation is the only route that works when the surroundings are hotter than the body, and it costs water (a link to A4). The heat balance sentence is A1’s “input equals output” again, now for heat. Transition: the endotherm must make up whatever it loses, so its metabolic rate depends on the ambient temperature.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
The thermoneutral zone



Thermoneutral zone (TNZ): metabolism minimal and constant; blood flow and posture adjust heat loss.
Below the lower critical temperature (LCT): heat loss ∝ (body − ambient), so metabolism rises.
Above the upper critical temperature: active cooling costs energy and water.
Unclothed human: TNZ ~28–32 °C. Arctic fox: LCT ~−40 °C.




So what can a mammal do to save heat or make more of it?

Exercise 5.4. The figure is the classic U-shaped curve: flat in the middle, rising on both sides. The two lines below the zone show the effect of insulation: with thick fur the same basal heat production balances losses down to a much lower ambient temperature. Within the zone, the animal controls heat loss cheaply by adjusting skin blood flow, posture and fur; below it, those adjustments are exhausted and only extra heat production remains. The Arctic fox comparison (Scholander’s classic data) shows that insulation moves the lower critical temperature: a well-insulated animal pays nothing extra until it is very cold. Exercise 5.3c: metabolic rate is lowest in the thermoneutral zone.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
section: Try it: mouse versus lizard across temperatures
text:
Try it: mouse versus lizard across temperatures




The thermoneutral-zone curve for a 25 g mouse (red) next to a 25 g lizard (blue) whose body follows the air. Drag the gold handle along the temperature axis, or use the presets. At 20 °C the mouse is below its lower critical temperature and spends about 40 kJ a day, roughly 90 times the lizard. Move to 32 °C: the mouse is in its thermoneutral zone and the ratio drops to about 13, close to the 5–10× of the previous slides. Go to 0 °C: the mouse’s cost climbs steeply while the lizard’s falls. Now add fur (“Thick winter fur”): the lower critical temperature moves down and the cost at 0 °C falls by a factor of four, which is why insulation is the first line of defence (next slide). Tick “Log scale” to see the lizard properly: its Q₁₀ curve becomes a straight line, and the Q₁₀ slider changes its slope. Model: basal rate 0.20 W, heat loss = conductance × (37 − Ta), conductance divided by the insulation factor; lizard rate = basal/8 at 37 °C scaled by Q₁₀.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Staying warm in the cold


Reduce heat loss

Insulation: fur, feathers, fat; piloerection traps more air.
Vasoconstriction of skin vessels.
Countercurrent heat exchange in limbs: feet run cold.
Posture and huddling: less exposed surface (A1’s A/V).

Increase heat production

Shivering: contraction without movement; ATP use becomes heat.
Brown adipose tissue: UCP1 lets protons leak back into mitochondria, so fuel is oxidised without making ATP: all heat.



Micrograph: unknown author (US government), Public domain, Wikimedia Commons


Exercise 5.6 asks for four of these. Each one can be mapped to the previous slides: insulation and posture reduce conduction and convection; countercurrent exchange is the same principle we will see for O₂ in fish gills in A3; brown fat reuses the ATP slide, because it short-circuits the electron transport chain. Brown fat is prominent in newborn mammals, small mammals and hibernators arousing from torpor. The micrograph shows brown adipose tissue: each brown adipocyte holds many small fat droplets (multilocular) rather than one large one, with a central nucleus, and its granular cytoplasm is packed with mitochondria, which give the tissue its colour. Compare white fat, where one large droplet pushes the nucleus to the edge. Huddling also uses surface-to-volume: a group of mice behaves like one larger animal.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
section: Back to the opening problem: mouse versus lizard
text:
Back to the opening problem: mouse versus lizard



Photo: Ahunt, CC0, Wikimedia Commons
Mouse (endotherm): ~37 °C in any weather, active at night and in winter; pays with ~55 kJ of food a day.


Photo: Michael Jagger, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons
Lizard (ectotherm): temperature set by basking and shelter, active only when warm; needs about a tenth of the food.

Rising O₂ use with temperature change means different things: the cold mouse defends 37 °C; the warming lizard speeds up its reactions.
Both still need O₂ delivered to their mitochondria. That is A3.

Close the loop to the first slide. Neither strategy is better: the mouse buys independence from the weather at a high food cost; the lizard saves food but loses activity time. The final contrast is exercise 5.3b and the last paragraph of the tutorial: an increase in O₂ consumption when temperature changes can mean defence of body temperature (endotherm below its lower critical temperature) or faster reactions in a warming body (ectotherm). Bridge to A3: the respirometer measured O₂ consumption; next we follow that O₂ from the air to the mitochondrion.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Five processes
ingestion, digestion, absorption, egestion (faeces), excretion (metabolic waste)


Digestion
enzymatic hydrolysis; amylase, pepsin, trypsin, lipase; bile emulsifies


Absorptive surface
folds, villi, microvilli; sugars and amino acids → blood, fats → lacteals


Fermentation
microbes digest cellulose → short-chain fatty acids; foregut (cow) vs hindgut (horse)


Energy budget
ingested = faeces + excreted + metabolic + retained, over one interval


Energy vs power
J vs W = J s⁻¹; 1 day = 86 400 s


ATP supply
anaerobic: 2 ATP/glucose, lactate; aerobic: ~30 ATP/glucose, needs O₂


Respirometry
O₂ use = Δconcentration × volume / time − blank; replicate = animal


Q_{10}
(R_2/R_1)^{10/(T_2-T_1)}; typically 2–3; valid only in the measured range


Thermal terms
ecto/endotherm = heat source; poikilo/homeotherm = temperature variation


Thermoneutral zone
minimal metabolism; below lower critical temperature, metabolism rises



Next (A3 — Gas exchange and circulation): follow the O₂ that the respirometer measured, from the air or water to the mitochondrion: exchange surfaces, haemoglobin and the heart.
Tutorial · Exercises · Quiz

Read the table in story order: food enters, is digested and absorbed, possibly with microbial help; its energy is partitioned in the budget; the metabolic part is turned into ATP, measured as O₂ consumption; and temperature changes that rate, very differently in ectotherms and endotherms. The A3 preview follows the oxygen side of metabolism.

title: A3 exercises — Exchange, blood and flow
text: The questions follow the tutorial and slides. Answer each question before opening its answer.

title: A3 exercises — Exchange, blood and flow
text:
Diffusion and exchange surfaces

1.1
For each step in the path of oxygen from air to a mammalian muscle mitochondrion, state whether the main process is bulk flow or diffusion.

air moving through the trachea and bronchi to the alveoli
O₂ crossing the alveolar wall and capillary endothelium into the plasma
blood carrying O₂ from the lungs to the muscle
O₂ moving from the muscle capillary to the mitochondria







Answer






Bulk flow (ventilation). b. Diffusion. c. Bulk flow (circulation).
Diffusion.






1.2
Dry air at sea level has a total pressure of 101.3 kPa and contains 20.9 % O₂. Calculate the partial pressure of O₂.






Answer





\(P_{\rm O_2}=0.209\times101.3\ \text{kPa}=21.2\) kPa (about 159 mmHg).





1.3
Use Fick’s relationship \(\dot M\propto A\,\Delta P/L\), with the diffusion properties of the barrier held constant. Surface 1 has area 10 units, thickness 2 units and partial-pressure difference 4 units. Surface 2 has twice the area, twice the thickness and half the partial-pressure difference. Calculate the transfer rate across surface 2 relative to surface 1.






Answer





Surface 1: \(10\times4/2=20\). Surface 2: \(20\times2/4=10\). Transfer across surface 2 is half that across surface 1 (\(2\times\tfrac12/2=0.5\)).





1.4
Define ventilation and perfusion, and state how each helps to maintain the partial-pressure gradient across a respiratory surface.






Answer






Ventilation: bulk flow of the respiratory medium (air or water) over the respiratory surface. It replaces medium from which O₂ has been taken, keeping external \(P_{\rm O_2}\) high.
Perfusion: bulk flow of blood (or other internal fluid) through the respiratory surface. It removes O₂-loaded blood and brings O₂-poor blood, keeping internal \(P_{\rm O_2}\) low.

title: A3 exercises — Exchange, blood and flow
text:
Gills, lungs and tracheae

2.1
Name the main gas-exchange structure in each animal.

bony fish
mammal
bird
insect







Answer






Gill lamellae (secondary lamellae of the gill filaments). b. Alveoli of the lungs. c. Air capillaries of the parabronchi in the lungs. d. Tracheoles, the fine endings of the tracheal system.






2.2
The values below are O₂ partial pressures (kPa) along a fish gill lamella. Water flows from position 1 to position 4; blood flows from position 4 to position 1.



Position
1
2
3
4




Water \(P_{\rm O_2}\)
20
16
12
8


Blood \(P_{\rm O_2}\)
18
14

6




Give the \(P_{\rm O_2}\) of the water entering and leaving, and of the blood entering and leaving the lamella.
In which direction does O₂ diffuse at each position, and what is the local partial-pressure difference?
What is this flow arrangement called?
If blood and water flowed in the same direction, could the blood leave with a higher \(P_{\rm O_2}\) than the water leaving? Explain.







Answer






Water enters at 20 kPa and leaves at 8 kPa. Blood enters at 6 kPa and leaves at 18 kPa.
From water to blood at every position; the difference is 2 kPa everywhere.
Countercurrent exchange.
No. In co-current flow the two streams approach the same \(P_{\rm O_2}\), so blood can at most equal the \(P_{\rm O_2}\) of the water leaving. In countercurrent flow, blood leaves at 18 kPa, higher than the water leaving (8 kPa), although O₂ always diffuses down the local gradient.






2.3
True or false? Correct any false statements.

In mammals, air flows in one direction through the lungs.
In birds, the air sacs are the main gas-exchange surface.
In insects, the haemolymph carries most of the O₂ to the tissues.
Part of each breath in a mammal stays in the conducting airways and does not reach the alveoli.







Answer






False. Mammalian ventilation is tidal: air moves in and out through the same airways.
False. Exchange occurs in the parabronchi of the rigid lungs; the air sacs act as bellows that ventilate the lungs, giving one-way flow through the parabronchi.
False. The tracheal system carries O₂ in gas phase directly to the tissues; haemolymph has a small role in O₂ transport.
True. This volume is the anatomical dead space.

title: A3 exercises — Exchange, blood and flow
section: Oxygen and carbon dioxide in blood
text:
Oxygen and carbon dioxide in blood

3.1
Define partial pressure of O₂, haemoglobin saturation and O₂ content of blood, and give a unit for each.






Answer






\(P_{\rm O_2}\): the pressure exerted by O₂ (in blood, by the dissolved, unbound O₂); kPa or mmHg.
Saturation: the percentage of haemoglobin O₂-binding sites that are occupied; %.
O₂ content: the total amount of O₂ (bound plus dissolved) per volume of blood; mL O₂ L⁻¹.






3.2
Each gram of haemoglobin binds at most 1.34 mL O₂. Blood contains 150 g haemoglobin per litre. Ignore dissolved O₂.

Calculate the O₂ content at 100 % saturation.
Calculate the O₂ content at 75 % saturation.
An anaemic person has 75 g haemoglobin per litre and the same arterial \(P_{\rm O_2}\) and saturation (98 %) as a healthy person. Calculate their arterial O₂ content and state which of \(P_{\rm O_2}\), saturation and content differ from the healthy person.







Answer






\(150\times1.34=201\) mL O₂ L⁻¹.
\(0.75\times201=151\) mL O₂ L⁻¹.
\(75\times1.34\times0.98=98\) mL O₂ L⁻¹. Only the content differs (it is halved); \(P_{\rm O_2}\) and saturation are unchanged.






3.3
Why is the haemoglobin–O₂ dissociation curve sigmoid (S-shaped)?






Answer





Haemoglobin has four subunits that bind O₂ cooperatively: binding of O₂ to one subunit increases the O₂ affinity of the others. Affinity is therefore low at low \(P_{\rm O_2}\) and high at intermediate \(P_{\rm O_2}\), giving a steep middle part to the curve.





3.4
State whether each change shifts the haemoglobin–O₂ dissociation curve to the right or to the left, and whether it favours O₂ unloading in the tissues.

increased \(P_{\rm CO_2}\)
decreased pH
decreased temperature
increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) in red blood cells







Answer






Right; favours unloading. b. Right; favours unloading (Bohr effect).
Left; reduces unloading. d. Right; favours unloading.

A right shift means lower affinity: less O₂ is bound at a given \(P_{\rm O_2}\).





3.5

Name the three forms in which CO₂ is carried in mammalian blood, from the largest to the smallest fraction.
Write the reaction catalysed by carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells, including the dissociation of the product.







Answer






Bicarbonate ions (about 70 %), bound to haemoglobin as carbamino compounds (about 20 %), dissolved CO₂ (about 10 %).
\(\mathrm{CO_2 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_2CO_3 \rightleftharpoons H^+ + HCO_3^-}\). Carbonic anhydrase catalyses the first step.

title: A3 exercises — Exchange, blood and flow
text:
Circulation

4.1
Put the structures in order, starting from the systemic veins, for blood flowing through a mammal: left atrium, pulmonary veins, right ventricle, systemic arteries, lung capillaries, left ventricle, right atrium, pulmonary arteries.






Answer





Systemic veins → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary arteries → lung capillaries → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → systemic arteries.





4.2
True or false? Correct any false statements.

Arteries always carry oxygenated blood.
Heart valves prevent the backflow of blood.
In a fish, blood passes through the heart once for each complete circuit of the body.
In an open circulatory system, the circulating fluid does not move.







Answer






False. Arteries carry blood away from the heart. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood.
True.
True. Fish have a single circulation: heart → gills → systemic tissues → heart.
False. Haemolymph is pumped by the heart and flows through vessels and body spaces (sinuses) before returning to the heart.






4.3
Classify the circulatory system of each animal as open or closed.

earthworm
grasshopper
octopus
mussel
frog







Answer






Closed. b. Open. c. Closed. d. Open. e. Closed.






4.4
Complete the table.




Artery
Capillary
Vein




Direction of flow relative to the heart





Wall





Blood pressure





Main function












Answer















Artery
Capillary

Direction of flow relative to the heart

Wall

Endothelium only, one cell thick

Blood pressure
High, pulsatile

Main function

Return blood to the heart; hold most of the blood volume








4.5
Use \(Q=\Delta P/R\).

The pressure difference across a vascular bed stays constant while its resistance doubles. By what factor does flow change?
Resistance of a tube is proportional to \(1/r^4\), where \(r\) is the radius. By what factor does resistance change when an arteriole constricts to half its radius?







Answer






Flow halves.
\(2^4=16\): resistance increases sixteen-fold, so at constant \(\Delta P\) flow falls to 1/16.






4.6
At rest, heart rate is 80 beats min⁻¹, stroke volume 0.050 L beat⁻¹, arterial O₂ content 190 mL O₂ L⁻¹ and mixed venous O₂ content 140 mL O₂ L⁻¹. During exercise, heart rate is 120 beats min⁻¹, stroke volume 0.080 L beat⁻¹ and the arterial–venous O₂ content difference 100 mL O₂ L⁻¹.

Calculate cardiac output at rest and during exercise.
Calculate whole-body O₂ consumption at rest and during exercise (Fick principle).
By what factor does O₂ consumption increase?







Answer






Rest: \(80\times0.050=4.0\) L min⁻¹. Exercise: \(120\times0.080=9.6\) L min⁻¹.
Rest: \(4.0\times(190-140)=200\) mL O₂ min⁻¹. Exercise: \(9.6\times100=960\) mL O₂ min⁻¹.
\(960/200=4.8\). Both cardiac output and the O₂ extraction from each litre of blood increased.

title: A3 exercises — Exchange, blood and flow
text:
Explore: Haemoglobin loading and unloading
The blue curve is haemoglobin under lung conditions, where blood loads at the arterial PO₂; the red curve is the same haemoglobin under the tissue’s pH and temperature, where it unloads at the tissue PO₂. Use the sliders or presets, or drag the red point; read the results from the readout below the sliders.




E1
Press Rest. Read off (a) the tissue P₅₀, (b) the percentage of haemoglobin that is unloaded (gold bar) and (c) the O₂ delivered per litre of blood. Compare (c) with the arterial–venous O₂ difference at rest in question 4.6.






Answer






3.6 kPa (tissue pH 7.37 shifts the curve very slightly right of 3.5 kPa).
24 % (arterial 97 %, venous 74 %).
48 mL O₂ L⁻¹ (196 − 148). This is close to the 50 mL O₂ L⁻¹ a–v difference in question 4.6: at rest only about a quarter of the O₂ is used.






E2
Press Exercise, no shift and read the O₂ delivered per litre. Then press Exercise and read it again. Starting from the rest value in E1, which contributes more to the extra O₂ delivered during exercise?

the fall in tissue PO₂ from 5.3 to 2.7 kPa
the right shift of the curve (pH 7.2, 39 °C)







Answer





Exercise, no shift: 129 mL O₂ L⁻¹. Exercise: 162 mL O₂ L⁻¹.

The fall in tissue PO₂ adds 129 − 48 = 81 mL O₂ L⁻¹; the right shift adds a further 162 − 129 = 33 mL O₂ L⁻¹. The low PO₂ lies on the steep part of the curve, where a small drop in PO₂ releases a lot of O₂.






E3
Press Exercise. Set Tissue temp. back to 37 °C (pH stays at 7.2) and read the O₂ delivered. Then press Exercise again and set Tissue pH back to 7.40 (temperature stays at 39 °C) and read it again. Which part of the exercise right shift, acidity (Bohr effect) or warming, contributes more in this model?






Answer





pH 7.2 at 37 °C: 153 mL O₂ L⁻¹ (P₅₀ 4.4 kPa). pH 7.4 at 39 °C: 142 mL O₂ L⁻¹ (P₅₀ 3.9 kPa). Acidity contributes more: it alone gives most of the 33 mL O₂ L⁻¹ gain of the full exercise shift.





E4
Press Altitude (arterial PO₂ 6.5 kPa, about half the sea-level value). Read off the arterial saturation and arterial O₂ content, and compare them with the Rest values (97 %, 196 mL O₂ L⁻¹). Which statement is correct?

Saturation falls in proportion to PO₂, to about half.
Saturation falls much less than PO₂, because sea-level loading takes place on the flat top of the curve.
Saturation does not change, because the curve is flat everywhere above 5 kPa.







Answer





Arterial saturation 84 %, content 169 mL O₂ L⁻¹. b: halving PO₂ lowers saturation by only 13 percentage points, because the arterial point moves from the plateau down onto the shoulder of the sigmoid curve.





E5
Press Anaemia ([Hb] 100 instead of 150 g L⁻¹) and compare with Rest. Which of the readouts change? Give the O₂ delivered per litre.

the percentage unloaded only
the O₂ contents and the O₂ delivered only
both







Answer






The saturations (97 % and 74 %) and the 24 % unloaded are the same as at rest, because the curve depends on PO₂, pH and temperature, not on how much haemoglobin there is. The O₂ delivered falls from 48 to 32 mL O₂ L⁻¹, by one third, in proportion to [Hb] (capacity 1.34 mL O₂ per g Hb).

text:

In co-current flow the two streams approach the same PO₂ and the exchange stops; in countercurrent flow a gradient is kept along the whole lamella.





E7
Set the exchanger size to 10 (flow ratio 1.00) and read the blood PO₂ out in each arrangement. In which arrangement can the blood leave with a higher PO₂ than the water leaving the gill?






Answer





Countercurrent: 18.4 kPa (water leaves at 3.6 kPa). Co-current: 11.0 kPa, the same as at size 5. Only countercurrent: in co-current flow the blood can at best equilibrate with the outflowing water, the mixed value of 11 kPa, however large the exchanger.

In countercurrent mode with exchanger size 5, set Blood ÷ water flow to 0.50 and then to 2.00. For each, read the blood PO₂ out and the O₂ taken from the water. Which statement is correct?

High blood flow gives both the highest blood PO₂ and the highest extraction.
The flow ratio does not matter in countercurrent exchange.







Answer

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
text:
About this lecture
In A2 we measured metabolic rate as O₂ consumption, and saw that sustained work needs aerobic ATP. A person at rest uses about 250 mL of O₂ per minute. Start running, and within a minute that rises more than tenfold, to about 3 L min⁻¹. How does the body move ten times more oxygen from the air into working muscle mitochondria? We follow one O₂ molecule along the whole route.

Physics of exchange: partial pressure, Fick’s law, ventilation and perfusion.
Exchange organs: fish gills, mammalian lungs, bird lungs, insect tracheae.
Oxygen in blood: haemoglobin, the dissociation curve and its shifts; CO₂ transport.
The pump and the pipes: the double circulation, vessels, pressure, resistance and flow.
Back to the runner: cardiac output and the Fick principle.


The running example is a person starting to run; we return to them on the last content slide with real numbers. Link to A1: the three solutions (large surface, thin barrier, bulk flow) are exactly what we now examine organ by organ. Link to A2: the respirometer measured O₂ disappearing; now we ask how it got to the mitochondria. Mention that A4 will show the cost of this design: a thin, wet, permeable surface exchanges water and ions as well as gases.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
section: The path of oxygen: bulk flow and diffusion alternate
text:
The path of oxygen: bulk flow and diffusion alternate



Bulk flow moves the whole fluid, driven by a pressure difference. Fast over any distance, but needs a pump.
Diffusion moves molecules down a partial-pressure difference. Fast only over µm (A1: t \approx x^2/2D).
So diffusion steps cross thin barriers; bulk flow covers the long distances.




What exactly drives the diffusion steps?

Exercise 1.1 asks students to classify these four steps. This is A1’s “three solutions” turned into a route. Ventilation and circulation are the two pumps; the alveolar wall and the muscle capillary wall are the two diffusion steps, each less than a few micrometres. Emphasise the different drivers: total pressure for bulk flow, partial pressure for diffusion. The next slide defines partial pressure.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
text:
Partial pressure drives diffusion
Partial pressure = the share of the total pressure due to one gas (Dalton’s law): P_{\rm O_2} = F_{\rm O_2} \times P_{\rm total}


Dry air at sea level: 0.209 \times 101.3 = 21.2 kPa (159 mmHg).

O₂ moves down this cascade at every diffusion step.
In a liquid, P_{\rm O_2} refers to the dissolved O₂ only.
1 kPa = 7.5 mmHg.




How fast does it cross each barrier?

Exercise 1.2 is the Dalton calculation. Alveolar P_O2 is lower than in air because inspired air is humidified and mixes with air already in the lungs, and O₂ is constantly removed. The mitochondria act as the sink that keeps the whole cascade going. Point out that diffusion follows partial pressure, not concentration: this matters later when blood with haemoglobin holds far more O₂ than water at the same P_O2.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
text:
Fick’s law of diffusion
\dot M \propto \frac{A\,\Delta P}{L}



Change
Effect on transfer rate




Double the area A
×2


Double the partial-pressure difference \Delta P
×2


Double the barrier thickness L
×½




Human lung: about 100 m² of alveolar surface, an air–blood barrier about 0.5 µm thick.
Lung disease shows the law at work: emphysema destroys alveolar walls (smaller A); pulmonary oedema thickens the barrier (larger L).
The cost: a large, thin, moist surface is fragile and loses water.

Diffusion uses up the gradient. What keeps \Delta P high?

Exercise 1.3 combines several changes: multiply the factors (for example, twice the area, twice the thickness and half the ΔP give 2 × ½ / 2 = ½). The diffusion coefficient and solubility of the gas are held constant in the proportionality. The last bullet links forward to A4: a surface built to let O₂ through also lets water and ions through. Transition: as O₂ diffuses into the blood, the gas side would lose O₂ and the blood side would fill up, and the gradient would vanish without bulk flow on both sides.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
section: Ventilation and perfusion keep the gradient
text:
Ventilation and perfusion keep the gradient









Ventilation

Both are bulk flow, both need a pump (breathing muscles, heart).
Exchange is limited by whichever is lower: ventilating an unperfused alveolus achieves nothing.

Air and water are very different media to ventilate. How different?

Exercise 1.4. A respiratory surface has two sides and each needs renewing. Without ventilation, alveolar P_O2 would fall towards venous P_O2 within seconds; without perfusion, the blood in the capillary would equilibrate with alveolar air and no further uptake would occur. The matching of ventilation and perfusion is regulated locally in the lung. Transition to the comparison of media, which explains why fish and mammals have such different organs.

Breathing water versus breathing air

A fish must pump a dense, viscous medium that holds little O₂.
So it moves water in one direction over the gills, rather than in and out, and extracts as much O₂ as possible from each litre.
Air breathers can afford tidal ventilation: the medium is light and rich in O₂.

How does a gill extract so much from so little?

This slide explains the design differences on the next four slides from first principles. Water at the same P_O2 as air carries about thirty times less O₂ because O₂ is poorly soluble. Ventilating water costs a fish a substantial share of its resting metabolism; for a resting mammal, breathing costs only a few per cent. Unidirectional flow avoids having to stop and reverse a heavy column of water. A1’s diffusion numbers also return: diffusion in water is slow, so gill lamellae are extremely thin.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
section: Fish gills: a one-way flow over thin lamellae
text:
Fish gills: a one-way flow over thin lamellae



Gill arches → filaments → secondary lamellae, the exchange surface.
Water flows one way: mouth → gills → operculum.
Blood in the lamellae flows opposite to the water.
Fish extract up to 80 % of the O₂ in the water; a mammal removes ~25 % of the O₂ in each breath.



Photo: Krishna satya 333, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons


Exercise 2.1a: the exchange structure is the secondary lamella. In the photo the red, feathery structures are the filaments on each gill arch; their colour comes from the blood running just below a very thin surface. Each filament carries hundreds of tiny plate-like secondary lamellae, too small to see here, and it is in those that blood flows against the water. Ask why fish gills collapse and stop working in air: without water to hold them apart the filaments stick together and the surface area is lost.

In co-current flow, the two streams approach a common P_O2 and exchange stops; the blood can at most reach the P_O2 of the water leaving (exercise 2.2d). title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
text:
Try it: countercurrent versus co-current




A model gill lamella. The two bands at the top are the water and blood streams coloured by PO₂ (red = rich, slate = poor); the plot shows the same along the lamella, with the other arrangement dashed. Start with countercurrent at the defaults: blood leaves at 17 kPa, the table from two slides back. Click Co-current: blood can now only reach 11 kPa, the same as the water leaving, and the gold gap closes early on, so the second half of the lamella is wasted. Then drag “Exchanger size” up in both modes: co-current never gets past the mixed value, countercurrent keeps improving towards 20 kPa. Finally move “Blood ÷ water flow”: in countercurrent, when blood flow is low the blood comes close to the inlet water; when it is high the water is stripped of O₂ instead. Fish adjust both ventilation and perfusion of the lamellae. Teaching simplification: blood O₂ content is treated as proportional to PO₂ (no haemoglobin curve).

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
text:
Mammalian lungs: tidal ventilation



Trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli: 300–500 million, ~100 m².
Tidal: air flows in and out through the same airways.
Conducting airways are dead space, ~150 mL.
Breaths of 500 mL, 12 min⁻¹: (500-150) \times 12 = 4.2 L min⁻¹ reaches the alveoli.
Fresh air mixes with stale air, so alveolar P_{\rm O_2} (13.3 kPa) stays below air (21.2 kPa).



Photo: Yale Rosen from USA, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

Is tidal flow the only way to ventilate a lung?

Exercise 2.3a and 2.3d. In the micrograph, the bronchiole is a conducting airway (dead space); the lace-like air spaces around it are alveoli, whose walls are so thin that they are barely visible at this magnification: that is Fick’s large A and small L made visible. Each breath, the last 150 mL inhaled stays in the airways and is breathed out unchanged. That is why slow deep breathing ventilates the alveoli more effectively than fast shallow breathing at the same total ventilation: 250 mL breaths at 24 per minute give only (250 − 150) × 24 = 2.4 L min⁻¹. Exercise 2.1b: exchange occurs in the alveoli. Tidal ventilation is the weakness the bird lung avoids.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
text:
Bird lungs: one-way flow



Small, rigid lungs with parabronchi; exchange in air capillaries (3–10 µm).
Air sacs are bellows: they ventilate but do not exchange gas.
Air passes the parabronchi in one direction during both inspiration and expiration.
No dead space in the exchange region; blood crosses the air stream (cross-current).



Figure: Cruithne9, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons


Exercise 2.1c and 2.3b. The diagram shows the plumbing: the trachea leads through the primary and intrapulmonary bronchus to the posterior air sacs, and the lung between the anterior and posterior sacs is a stack of parallel parabronchi, open at both ends, where the air capillaries branch off. The air sacs are large balloons; the lung itself is small and does not change volume. Air takes two breath cycles to pass through: inspiration 1 fills the posterior sacs, expiration 1 pushes that air through the lung, inspiration 2 moves it into the anterior sacs and expiration 2 sends it out. The result is that the lung always receives fresh air flowing one way, which is part of why birds can fly at altitudes where mammals struggle.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
section: Insects: air piped to the cells
text:
Insects: air piped to the cells



Spiracles → tracheae → tracheoles (< 1 µm), within a few µm of mitochondria.
O₂ travels in air almost to the cell: ~10 000× faster diffusion than in water.
Active insects pump the abdomen.
Haemolymph carries little O₂.
Spiracles close to limit water loss.



Photo: Tgru001, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

In vertebrates, blood carries the O₂. But O₂ dissolves poorly in water. How does blood hold enough?

Exercise 2.1d and 2.3c. The micrograph shows a trachea teased out of an insect: the fine spiral rings (taenidia) of cuticle keep the tube open, like the cartilage rings of our own trachea. The insect is A1’s other solution: skip the blood and bring air to the tissue. The limit is the diffusion distance along the tracheae, which is one reason insects stay small. Transition back to vertebrates and the problem of carrying O₂ in a watery fluid.

text:
Haemoglobin: pressure, saturation and content


Plasma dissolves only ~3 mL O₂ L⁻¹; haemoglobin raises this ~65-fold.

P_{\rm O_2}: pressure of the dissolved, unbound O₂ (kPa).
Saturation: % of Hb binding sites occupied.
O₂ content: total O₂ per litre of blood (mL O₂ L⁻¹).

Content = [Hb] × 1.34 mL O₂ g⁻¹ × saturation:

Anaemia: same P_{\rm O_2} and saturation, less content.


Photo: Bruce Wetzel (photographer). Harry Schaefer (photographer), Public domain, Wikimedia Commons


Exercises 3.1 and 3.2. The three quantities are the most common source of confusion in this unit. P_O2 is set by the gas the blood equilibrated with; saturation is set by P_O2 through the dissociation curve; content then depends on how much haemoglobin there is. The anaemic patient has normal arterial P_O2 and saturation, because their lungs work, but each litre of blood carries a third less O₂. The 1.34 mL per gram is the maximum binding capacity. The micrograph shows where the haemoglobin is: packed inside biconcave red cells, about 7 µm across, whose shape gives a large surface and a short diffusion distance to every haemoglobin molecule. Transition: how does saturation depend on P_O2?

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
text:
The dissociation curve is sigmoid



Why S-shaped? Four subunits bind O₂ cooperatively: each bound O₂ raises the affinity of the others.
Flat top: still ~90 % saturated at 8 kPa, e.g. at moderate altitude.
Steep middle: a small fall in tissue P_{\rm O_2} releases much O₂.
At rest only ~25 % is unloaded: a reserve for exercise.




Can the curve itself move to help the working muscle?

The curve is the Hill equation with n = 2.7 and P50 = 3.5 kPa, drawn through the standard reference points: 98 % at 13.3 kPa (arterial), 75 % at 5.3 kPa (mixed venous at rest), 50 % at 3.5 kPa and about 35 % at 2.7 kPa (exercising muscle). Exercise 3.3 asks why it is sigmoid: cooperative binding among four subunits. Myoglobin, with one subunit, gives a hyperbolic curve that lies to the left, so it takes O₂ from haemoglobin in muscle. The reserve is important for the runner: from 75 % saturation at rest, venous blood from hard-working muscle falls to about 35 %, so each litre of blood delivers more than twice as much O₂.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
text:
Shifting the curve


Right shift (lower affinity, more unloading): ↑ P_{\rm CO_2}, ↓ pH (Bohr effect), ↑ temperature, ↑ 2,3-BPG. The opposite shifts left.

Working muscle is warm, acidic and high in CO₂: three of the four push right exactly where O₂ is needed.
Loading in the lung, on the flat top, hardly changes.
Left-shifted: fetal Hb, myoglobin.




Working muscle makes CO₂. How does the blood carry it away?

Exercise 3.4. In the figure, the working-muscle curve uses pH 7.2 and 39 °C (P50 rises from 3.5 to about 4.9 kPa). At the same muscle PO2 of 2.7 kPa, an extra 16 % of the haemoglobin gives up its O2, yet at the lung’s 13.3 kPa both curves are near the top: the O2 goes to the tissue, it is not lost. Teach the rule as “the conditions in an active tissue shift the curve to the right”, which removes the need to memorise four separate facts. P50 rises with a right shift. Fetal haemoglobin binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so it sits to the left of maternal haemoglobin and O₂ moves from mother to fetus across the placenta. 2,3-BPG in red cells rises over days at high altitude, an example of A1’s acclimatisation. Transition: the CO₂ that shifts the curve has to be removed.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
section: Try it: loading in the lung, unloading in the muscle
text:
Try it: loading in the lung, unloading in the muscle




Blue is the curve under lung conditions, where the blood loads at the arterial PO₂ (blue point). Red is the curve under the tissue’s own pH and temperature, where it unloads at the tissue PO₂ (red point, draggable). The gold bar is the share of haemoglobin that gives up its O₂, and the bottom line converts it to mL O₂ per litre of blood. Start at Rest: about 25 % unloaded, about 50 mL per litre, matching the a–v difference on the Fick slide. Press “Exercise, no shift”: muscle PO₂ falls to 2.7 kPa on the normal curve. Then “Exercise”: now the muscle is at pH 7.2 and 39 °C, the red curve moves right and each litre of blood delivers about 30 mL more. Ask the room which of the three changes did the most. “Altitude” lowers arterial PO₂ to 6.5 kPa: loading falls off the flat top. “Anaemia”: the percentages are unchanged but the mL delivered fall by a third, the content point from the haemoglobin slide. Model: Hill equation, n = 2.7, P50 = 3.5 kPa at pH 7.4 and 37 °C; log P50 changes by −0.48 per pH unit and +0.024 per °C.

Carbonic anhydrase in red cells: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻.
HCO₃⁻ out, Cl⁻ in (chloride shift); H⁺ on Hb helps release O₂.
Reversed in the lung, so ventilation sets blood pH.




Gases are loaded and unloaded. Now: what moves the blood?

Exercise 3.5. The full reaction is CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; carbonic anhydrase speeds the first step. Breathing faster lowers P_CO2 and raises pH. Carbonic anhydrase is one of the fastest enzymes known; without it the hydration of CO₂ would be far too slow for the short time blood spends in a capillary. The reaction links gas transport to acid–base balance: CO₂ is an acid that the lungs can remove within minutes, while the kidney adjusts bicarbonate over hours to days (A4). Transition from the gases to the pump and the circuit.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
text:
The mammalian double circulation



Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins towards it. The pulmonary arteries carry O₂-poor blood.
Valves prevent backflow: tricuspid, mitral; pulmonary, aortic.
Systemic ~120/80 mmHg, pulmonary ~25/8 mmHg: the left ventricle makes ~5× the pressure of the right.




Is this the only way to build a circulation?

Exercise 4.1 is the order of this loop, and 4.2a and 4.2b are the artery definition and valves. Each side of the heart pumps the same volume per minute, but the left side generates about five times the pressure, because the systemic circuit is long and has high resistance while the lung circuit is short and must keep pressure low to avoid fluid leaking into the alveoli. Transition: compare with fish and with invertebrates.

“Open” does not mean motionless: the heart pumps haemolymph, which returns through openings (ostia).

In a closed circulation, how do the vessels differ along the circuit?

Exercises 4.2c, 4.2d and 4.3. In a fish, blood passes through the heart once per circuit, and much of the pressure is lost in the gill capillaries, so blood reaches the body at low pressure. The double circulation solves the fish’s problem: blood returns to the heart after the lungs and is re-pressurised before going to the body. Cephalopods are the instructive exception among molluscs: active predators with a closed system and extra hearts for the gills. The open system works for insects partly because their O₂ does not depend on the blood (previous slides). Transition to vessel structure.

Exercise 4.4 is this table. Relate each wall to its job and its tissue types from A1: elastic connective tissue and smooth muscle in the artery, a single squamous endothelium in the capillary (A1’s thin barrier), thin walls and large lumens in veins, which act as a reservoir. The capillary is where the diffusion step of the O₂ route happens. Transition to the flow equation.

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
section: An artery and a vein in section
text:
An artery and a vein in section





Micrograph: OpenStax College (Regents of the University of Michigan Medical School), CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons


Artery: thick muscular wall, round, small lumen. Vein: thin wall, wide or collapsed lumen; it can look like a slit.
Identify vessels by wall layers, not outline (A1).

Pressure drops along the circuit. What sets how much flows where?

This is the comparison students make in the histology practical, where artery and vein usually lie side by side in the same bundle: the micrograph on the right is exactly that, a muscular artery and its companion vein in fatty connective tissue. The artery has the thick wall of smooth muscle and elastic tissue and a round lumen. The vein beside it carries the same flow back at a much lower pressure, so it needs only a thin wall; its lumen is wider and often collapsed or irregular in a fixed section. The capillary, shown as a small inset, is a single endothelial cell around a lumen barely wide enough for one red cell. Transition: in this circuit, pressure falls from the aorta to the veins; what decides how much blood each organ receives?

title: A3 — Gas exchange and circulation
text:
Pressure, resistance and flow
Q = \frac{\Delta P}{R} \qquad\qquad R \propto \frac{1}{r^4}



Flow Q is driven by \Delta P and opposed by resistance R, like current in Ohm’s law.
Poiseuille: halve r → 16R, Q/16; widen by 19 % → R/2, 2Q.
Arterioles have smooth muscle, so they decide which tissues get the blood.
Exercise: muscle arterioles dilate, gut arterioles constrict.




So how much blood does the heart deliver, and how much O₂ does it bring?

Exercise 4.5. Doubling resistance at constant pressure halves flow. Because resistance goes as 1/r⁴, a small change in arteriole radius has a large effect: a 19 % dilation doubles flow. This is why arterioles, not the heart, distribute blood among organs. Capillaries are individually narrow, but there are billions in parallel, so their combined resistance is lower than that of the arterioles. Transition to cardiac output.

Photo: Lucyin, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

How does the body produce that elevenfold increase?

Exercise 4.6 is the same calculation with other numbers. The photo is a sheep heart cut across the ventricles: the left ventricle (left in the photo) has the thick, round wall, the right ventricle is a thin crescent wrapped around it. Both eject the same stroke volume, so cardiac output is the same for the two circulations, but the left ventricle works against about five times the pressure. The product is a mass balance: every litre of blood passing through the tissues gives up the difference between arterial and venous content, so total uptake is flow times that difference. At rest this matches the 250 mL min⁻¹ from the opening slide. Ask students which factors increased: cardiac output nearly fourfold and extraction threefold. The next slide puts all the mechanisms from today together.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
text:
An animal detecting food, escaping a threat or reproducing must connect information to action. Neural activity, endocrine signals and muscle do not operate as isolated topics. They link sensory input and internal state to effectors while using the transport and metabolic support developed in earlier units. This unit builds those links from membrane properties to whole-organism behaviour and reproductive regulation.
You should explain membrane potential and action potentials without confusing voltage with ion concentration; trace a chemical synapse and a reflex pathway; connect calcium, ATP and muscle force; distinguish hormone concentration from target-cell response; and explain a reproductive feedback loop. Use the slides, exercises and quiz.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: Ion gradients create possibilities for electrical signals
text:
Ion gradients create possibilities for electrical signals
A membrane potential is a voltage difference across a cell membrane. Ion concentrations differ inside and outside cells, and membranes are selectively permeable. The combined electrical and chemical tendencies determine each ion’s electrochemical driving force. Resting membranes are often more permeable to some ions than others. ATP-dependent transport, including the sodium–potassium pump in many animal cells, maintains gradients that leak pathways would otherwise dissipate.
The inside of a resting neuron is commonly negative relative to the outside. This does not mean that all intracellular material is negatively charged: only a small charge separation near the membrane is needed for a voltage. Opening a channel changes permeability; the direction of ion movement depends on that ion’s electrochemical gradient. A sodium channel is not itself an ATP-driven sodium pump.
A small local electrical change may decay with distance. An action potential is regenerated when voltage-dependent channels activate in adjacent membrane. In a typical vertebrate axon, rapid sodium entry drives depolarisation and subsequent channel changes, including potassium conductance, contribute to repolarisation. Refractory properties limit immediate re-excitation and help organise propagation. Exact waveforms and ion contributions differ among cell types, so treat this as a representative mechanism, not a universal recipe for every excitable cell. The supporting reading explains neuronal communication.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: A signal can be coded without becoming a larger spike
text:
A signal can be coded without becoming a larger spike
Once threshold is reached under comparable conditions, an individual action potential is approximately stereotyped. Stronger stimulation can change firing frequency, timing and the number of recruited neurons rather than making each spike proportionately taller. A sensory neuron is also selective: receptor properties and neural pathways determine what kind of change it can encode. An electrical recording alone does not reveal the animal’s conscious experience.
At a chemical synapse, arrival of an action potential can open presynaptic calcium channels. Calcium entry promotes neurotransmitter release. Transmitter acts on postsynaptic receptors, changing the receiving cell’s activity. Effects depend on receptor type and the target cell’s conditions; the same transmitter name is not a complete explanation of excitation or inhibition.





flowchart LR
  S[Stimulus] --> R[Sensory receptor and afferent neuron]
  R --> I[Integration in neural circuit]
  I --> M[Motor neuron]
  M --> E[Muscle or other effector]
  E --> O[Response changes conditions]






This original reflex sketch shows a functional route rather than a detailed anatomical circuit. A simple reflex can operate without waiting for conscious decision, while information may also reach other brain regions. The existence of a fast local pathway does not imply that the entire nervous system has one linear input and one output. Integrating excitatory, inhibitory and modulatory signals helps make context-dependent responses possible.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: Muscle converts chemical energy into force
text:
Muscle converts chemical energy into force
Skeletal muscle contains fibres with organised contractile machinery. Within sarcomeres, interactions between actin and myosin generate force through cycles requiring ATP. In skeletal muscle, calcium binds troponin, which moves tropomyosin and exposes the myosin-binding sites on actin. ATP binding permits myosin to detach; ATP hydrolysis prepares subsequent interactions. Therefore ATP is necessary for controlled cycling and relaxation as well as work.
At a vertebrate neuromuscular junction, motor-neuron signalling triggers a muscle electrical response. That response reaches internal membrane systems and promotes calcium release from intracellular stores. Calcium recovery helps end activation. The sequence connects a neural signal to a mechanical effect: it is more informative than saying “the nerve contracts the muscle”. OpenStax provides a supporting account of muscle contraction.
An isometric contraction develops force without an overall change in muscle length. Mechanical work on a load requires displacement; for a constant force aligned with movement, \(W=Fd\). A muscle can consume ATP while holding a load stationary even though the external mechanical work in that simple calculation is zero. Efficiency calculations must define which energy input and output are being compared.
Force varies with recruitment, activation timing, muscle length and loading conditions. A motor unit consists of a motor neuron and the muscle fibres it innervates. Recruiting more units can increase whole-muscle force without changing the amplitude of each axon’s action potentials. Smooth and cardiac muscle share actin–myosin interactions but differ in organisation and control. Smooth muscle is not simply skeletal muscle without visible stripes; its calcium regulation and activation patterns differ.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
text:
Nervous systems are diverse
Cnidarian nerve nets, ganglia and longitudinal nerve cords in many invertebrates, and vertebrate central/peripheral systems illustrate different organisations. Cephalisation concentrates sensory and integrating structures near a leading end in many bilaterally organised animals. These arrangements reflect body plans and behaviour, rather than a single scale of intelligence.
Sensory systems detect mechanical, chemical, light and other changes through specialised receptor processes. A receptor converts a stimulus into a cellular signal; subsequent neural pathways carry and interpret information. Adaptation of a sensory response to a continuing stimulus differs from evolutionary adaptation. Biological clocks add an internal timing component: daily rhythms can persist under constant conditions while environmental cues entrain their phase. State whether “adaptation” refers to receptor response, an individual’s adjustment or a heritable population feature.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: Hormones work through responsive target cells
text:
Hormones work through responsive target cells
An endocrine hormone enters internal transport fluid and can reach distant cells. Only cells with suitable receptors and downstream machinery respond in the relevant way. Peptide hormones often signal through surface receptors; many steroid hormones act through intracellular receptors. The eventual response can involve enzyme activity, transport, gene expression or several of these together. “Hormones are always slow” is an unreliable rule: some effects appear rapidly, while others require longer changes in cellular state.
The response depends on secretion, transport, breakdown, receptor abundance and interactions with other signals. A high measured hormone concentration does not guarantee a large effect at every target. Neuroendocrine cells connect neural input to hormone release. Negative feedback can occur at several levels of a regulatory axis, allowing the state of a target process to influence upstream secretion. The reading on hormone action expands this distinction between signal and response.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: Reproduction integrates timing, resources and feedback
text:
Reproduction integrates timing, resources and feedback
Reproduction includes gamete production, fertilisation, development and the allocation of parental resources. Species vary in internal/external fertilisation, sex organisation, reproductive cycles and parental investment. A mammalian endocrine example provides a concrete feedback model without representing all animals.
Hypothalamic GnRH stimulates pituitary release of gonadotropins, including LH and FSH. These act on gonadal cells involved in steroid production and gametogenesis. Gonadal signals feed back on hypothalamic/pituitary activity. The sign and timing of feedback can change: sustained high oestrogen under appropriate conditions can contribute to positive feedback leading to an LH surge and ovulation. It would be incorrect to describe the entire reproductive cycle as one unchanging negative-feedback loop. In male mammals, gonadal and other signals also provide feedback governing endocrine activity and sperm production. Consult the supporting account of hormonal reproductive control.
Energy availability, environmental timing and stress can influence reproduction. These links explain why studying reproductive organs alone is insufficient. The circulation carries signals, tissues need fuel, and neural pathways provide information about surroundings. In a seasonal breeder, a prediction about reproductive timing should therefore consider environmental cues and physiological state rather than one hormone measurement alone.
