Xylem as a tissue still contains living parenchyma cells; only the conducting cells are dead.





3.5
Give the order in which CO₂ passes these leaf structures on its way from the atmosphere to the site of fixation: mesophyll cell, stomatal pore, chloroplast stroma, intercellular air space, plasma membrane.






Answer





Stomatal pore → intercellular air space → plasma membrane → mesophyll cell (cytosol) → chloroplast stroma. CO₂ dissolves in the water of the wet cell wall before crossing the plasma membrane.





3.6
Why does opening the stomata increase both CO₂ uptake and water loss?






Answer





CO₂ diffuses in and water vapour diffuses out through the same pore. The cuticle is nearly impermeable to both, so opening the pore raises the conductance for both gases at once.

title: P1 exercises — Building a functioning plant
text:
Meristems and growth

4.1
Name the meristem responsible for each of the following.

Increase in length of a root
Production of secondary xylem and secondary phloem
Production of the protective outer bark tissue (periderm)
Regrowth of a grass leaf after its tip has been cut







Answer






Root apical meristem. b. Vascular cambium (secondary xylem inward, secondary phloem outward). c. Cork cambium (phellogen). d. Intercalary (basal) meristem.






4.2
A root segment contains 100 cells arranged end to end. Ignore spaces between cells.

Calculate the segment length in mm when the mean cell length is 40 µm.
With no cell division, the mean cell length becomes 70 µm. Calculate the new segment length and the increase.
How many 40 µm cells would give the same final length as in (b)?







Answer






100 × 40 µm = 4000 µm = 4 mm.
100 × 70 µm = 7000 µm = 7 mm; increase = 3 mm.
7000 µm / 40 µm = 175 cells. The same length can result from cell expansion or from cell division, so length alone does not identify the process.






4.3
True or false? Correct any false statements.

Cell differentiation requires a change in the DNA sequence.
Primary growth increases the length of roots and shoots.
Every mature plant cell can regenerate a whole plant under any conditions.







Answer






False. Differentiation results from differences in gene expression; the DNA sequence is unchanged.
True.
False. Some cells can resume division and regenerate, but this depends on genotype, developmental state and culture conditions.

title: P1 exercises — Building a functioning plant
text:
Three genomes

5.1
Name the three genomes of a plant cell and state which one encodes most of the proteins that function inside chloroplasts.






Answer





Nuclear, plastid (chloroplast) and mitochondrial genomes. Most chloroplast proteins are encoded in the nucleus, synthesised in the cytosol and imported into the chloroplast.





5.2
A mutation in a nuclear gene encoding a chloroplast-imported protein reduces photosynthesis, while the chloroplast DNA is unchanged. Is this possible? Explain in one sentence.






Answer





Yes. The protein functions in the chloroplast but its gene is in the nucleus, so a nuclear mutation can impair chloroplast function.





5.3
Leaf and root cells of one plant have the same nuclear genome but different functions. What is the reason?






Answer





They express different sets of genes (tissue-specific gene expression).

title: P1 exercises — Building a functioning plant
section: Explore: Growth of a walled cell
text:
Explore: Growth of a walled cell
The demo models one elongating cell with the Lockhart equation, relative growth rate r = φ(P − Y), where P is turgor, Y the wall yield threshold (both in MPa) and φ the wall extensibility (MPa⁻¹ h⁻¹). Set the sliders or click a preset; the readout gives r and the doubling time, and “Grow for 8 h” grows the cell from 20 µm.




E1.1
Use the default settings (P = 0.60, Y = 0.30, φ = 1.0). What is the growth rate r, the doubling time, and the cell length after 8 h (to the nearest µm)?






Answer





r = 1.0 × (0.60 − 0.30) = 0.30 h⁻¹; doubling time ln 2 / 0.30 = 2.3 h; length after 8 h = 20 × e^(0.30 × 8) ≈ 220 µm.





E1.2
Click “Stiff wall: P < Y” (P = 0.60, Y = 0.70). The cell is fully turgid. What is the growth rate, and why?






Answer





r = 0. Turgor (0.60 MPa) does not exceed the yield threshold (0.70 MPa), so the wall only stretches elastically and does not yield. A turgid cell is not necessarily a growing cell.





E1.3
Keep Y = 0.30. Which change gives the larger growth rate: (a) doubling φ to 2.0 with P = 0.60, or (b) raising P to 0.90 with φ = 1.0?






Answer





Neither: both give r = 0.60 h⁻¹ (2.0 × 0.30 and 1.0 × 0.60), with a doubling time of 1.2 h. Doubling the extensibility has the same effect as doubling the excess of turgor over the yield threshold.





E1.4
Click “Acid growth (auxin)” (P = 0.60, Y = 0.20, φ = 1.5). What is r, and by what factor is it higher than in the default? Which wall proteins, activated by low wall pH, does this preset represent?






Answer





r = 1.5 × (0.60 − 0.20) = 0.60 h⁻¹, twice the default 0.30 h⁻¹. Turgor is unchanged; the wall was loosened. Auxin stimulates plasma-membrane H⁺-ATPases, the wall acidifies and expansins loosen the cellulose–hemicellulose network (higher φ, lower Y).





E1.5
Click “Low turgor” (P = 0.35, Y = 0.30, φ = 1.0), as in a mildly water-stressed root. What is r and the doubling time? Roughly how long is the cell after 8 h?






Answer





r = 1.0 × 0.05 = 0.05 h⁻¹, doubling time 13.9 h; after 8 h the cell is only about 30 µm (20 × e^0.4 ≈ 29.8 µm). A small drop in turgor nearly stops growth because only the excess above Y drives expansion.

title: P1 exercises — Building a functioning plant
section: Explore: Root growth, more cells or longer cells?
text:
Explore: Root growth, more cells or longer cells?
Two root tips, A and B, are shown with the tip held still on the right. Each meristem produces new cells at a set rate per cell file; each cell leaves the meristem at 10 µm, elongates to a set final length and then matures. Set the two sliders for each root and press “Grow for 8 h”; the readouts give the number of new cells, the distance the tip moved, and the growth rate.




E2.1
Use the “Slide example” (A: 2.2 cells/h, final length 40 µm; B: 1.25 cells/h, 70 µm) and grow for 8 h. How many new cells does each root make, and how far does each tip move?






Answer





A: 17 new cells, B: 10 new cells. Both tips move 0.70 mm (growth rates 2.2 × 40 = 88 µm/h and 1.25 × 70 = 87.5 µm/h). Root length alone cannot tell the two roots apart.





E2.2
A drug that blocks cell division halves root A’s cell production to 1.1 cells/h without changing the final cell length (40 µm). What is A’s growth rate, and how far does its tip move in 8 h?






Answer





1.1 × 40 = 44 µm/h (0.044 mm/h); the tip moves 0.35 mm in 8 h, half as far as before.





E2.3
Set root B’s cell production to 1.10 cells/h. Which final cell length (slider in steps of 5 µm) makes B grow at exactly the same rate as the default root A?






Answer





80 µm: 1.1 × 80 = 88 µm/h = 2.2 × 40. Both tips then move 0.70 mm in 8 h.





E2.4
Click “Identical roots” (1.5 cells/h, 60 µm). Then set A’s final cell length to 120 µm, as in a mutant with more extensible walls. By what factor does A’s growth rate change, and which zone of the root tip is responsible?






Answer





It doubles (from 1.5 × 60 = 90 µm/h to 1.5 × 120 = 180 µm/h). The change is in the elongation zone, where cells expand; the meristem still produces the same number of cells.



Continue with the self-check quiz.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
About this lecture
A thirsty mouse walks to water, a hungry one finds food, and a frightened one runs. A maize seedling can do none of this. It stays where its seed landed, yet in three months it grows from a 0.3 g seed into a 2 m plant. How does an organism that cannot move get carbon, water and minerals to every cell, and hold itself up? In A1 we asked the same question of an animal; today we start the plant half and see the plant’s answers.

The contrast: what changes when an organism cannot move, makes its own food and has walls around its cells.
The plant cell: wall, vacuole and turgor, plastids and mitochondria.
Growth: how a walled cell enlarges, and how cells stay connected.
Tissues and organs: three tissue systems, xylem and phloem, the leaf and the root.
Meristems: where new cells are made, and more cells versus longer cells.
Three genomes: nucleus, plastid and mitochondrion working together.


Open with the contrast to the animal half, which students have just finished. The plant faces the same physics as the mouse in A1 (surface area, diffusion distance, the need for bulk flow), but under three constraints: it cannot move, it builds its own organic carbon from CO₂ and light, and every cell is enclosed in a wall. Each section of the lecture follows from one of these constraints. P2 and P3 then take the two big supply problems in turn: water and minerals, and carbon.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
section: The problem: a mouse versus a maize plant
text:
The problem: a mouse versus a maize plant









Mouse
Maize plant




Carbon and energy
eats organic food
makes sugar from CO₂, water and light


Water and minerals
drinks and eats them
takes them up from the soil through roots


Escaping danger, finding resources
moves
cannot move; grows towards resources


Body plan
fixed in the embryo; adult form complete
keeps adding leaves, roots and branches all its life


Support
skeleton and muscle
turgor and thickened cell walls


Cell boundary
plasma membrane
plasma membrane plus a cell wall




A plant must collect light and CO₂ above ground and water and minerals below ground, at the same time and in the same place.
It responds to its surroundings by growing, not by moving.

So how do the A1 rules about surfaces and distances apply to a plant?

Each row of the table is a constraint that shapes plant structure. The two that matter most today are the body plan (growth from meristems, later in the lecture) and the wall (which affects support, growth and transport). The point of the bullet about above and below ground: the plant is spread between two environments, so it needs long-distance transport between them, which we meet as xylem and phloem.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
section: The A1 physics, solved by a plant
text:
The A1 physics, solved by a plant








A1 solution
In an animal
In a plant




Enlarge the exchange surface
alveoli, ~100 m² in a human lung
leaves for light and CO₂; roots and root hairs for water


Make the barrier thin
air–blood barrier < 1 µm
leaf ~0.2 mm thick; every mesophyll cell faces an air space


Use bulk flow
blood pumped by the heart
xylem (water, roots → shoot) and phloem (sugar, sources → sinks), with no heart




One rye plant grown for four months had ~600 km of roots and ~10 000 km of root hairs, a root surface of ~640 m².
Diffusion is still used over short distances: CO₂ inside the leaf, ions in the soil next to a root hair.

These surfaces and tubes are built from cells. What does a plant cell have that an animal cell lacks?

This slide reuses the three solutions from A1 so students see the plant as a new answer to a known problem. The rye figures (Dittmer 1937) make the point that the root system is an enormous exchange surface, far larger than the shoot. Stress that the plant has bulk flow without a pump: P2 shows that evaporation drives xylem flow and P3 that osmotic pressure drives phloem flow. Transition into the cell.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
section: The plant cell: compartments and boundaries
text:
The plant cell: compartments and boundaries





Structure
Main function




Plasma membrane
selects what enters and leaves


Primary wall
resists pressure; sets the direction of growth


Tonoplast
membrane around the vacuole


Central vacuole
solutes and turgor; up to ~90 % of cell volume


Chloroplast
photosynthesis


Mitochondrion
aerobic respiration





Photo: Cimice50, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons


The wall is porous: water and small solutes pass freely. Selection happens at the plasma membrane, as in an animal cell. Three boundaries: wall, plasma membrane, tonoplast.

Why does a plant cell need a huge vacuole and a strong wall?

In the Elodea leaf the walls outline each cell; the chloroplasts sit in a thin layer of cytoplasm pressed against the wall, because the clear central vacuole fills most of the cell (in live cells you can watch them stream around it). Exercise 1.1 asks students to match these structures and functions. The common error, tested in 1.4c, is to think the wall is selectively permeable. It is not: the wall resists pressure, the membrane selects. Keep the three boundaries distinct, because P2 asks which boundary water or an ion crosses at each step of uptake. The vacuole and wall work together, which is the next slide.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
section: Vacuole and turgor: a hydraulic skeleton
text:
Vacuole and turgor: a hydraulic skeleton



The vacuole accumulates solutes (K⁺, sugars, organic acids); water follows by osmosis.
The protoplast presses on the wall and the wall pushes back: turgor pressure, typically 0.3–1 MPa (a car tyre is ~0.2 MPa).
Turgid cells pressing on each other make a stem or leaf rigid.
The vacuole also stores pigments and defence compounds, buffers cytoplasmic pH, breaks down cell material, and makes a large cell from little cytoplasm.




When turgor falls, a non-woody shoot wilts. Its cells are still alive and recover when water returns.

Turgor is the plant’s hydraulic skeleton: it replaces the muscle-and-bone support of an animal in non-woody tissues. The numbers make it concrete: several times the pressure in a car tyre, held by a wall a fraction of a micrometre thick. Exercise 1.2 asks for the definition and the effect of falling turgor; 1.3 asks for three vacuole functions. In P2 we quantify turgor as the pressure potential Ψp. The last vacuole function links to growth: a cell can become large mostly by filling its vacuole with water.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
Plastids and mitochondria





Plastid
Role; where




Proplastid
precursor; meristems


Chloroplast
photosynthesis; green tissue


Amyloplast
starch; tubers, seeds, root cap


Chromoplast
pigments; petals, fruits



All develop from proplastids: a chloroplast is one type of plastid.


Photo: Aleromjar1403, CC0, Wikimedia Commons


Most root cells have no functioning chloroplasts.
Every living plant cell respires, in light and dark: a leaf both fixes CO₂ (chloroplast) and releases it (mitochondrion).

So the cell has the parts. How does a cell enclosed in a wall manage to grow?

The photo is a potato tuber, an organ with no chloroplasts at all: iodine stains the starch in its amyloplasts blue-black. Exercise 1.4 tests three misconceptions: all plastids are chloroplasts; leaves respire only at night; roots photosynthesise. The point that a green leaf both fixes and releases CO₂ returns in P3, where the light-response curve has a negative value in darkness and the compensation point is where the two balance. Transition to the wall and growth.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
The cell wall


Primary wall (growing cells, ~0.1–1 µm)

Cellulose microfibrils, a few nm wide, carry the load, in a matrix of hemicelluloses, pectins and proteins.
Microfibrils wound transversely, like hoops around a barrel, let the cell lengthen but not widen.

Secondary wall (after growth stops)

Laid down inside the primary wall; thicker, often with lignin.
Rigid support; stops xylem conduits collapsing under tension. Wood is mostly secondary wall.




But a wall strong enough to hold 0.5 MPa of turgor should also stop the cell from growing. How does it grow?

Exercise 2.1 asks for cellulose as the load-bearing component and lignin as the reinforcing polymer of xylem secondary walls. The hoop analogy explains why cells in a root or stem elongate in one direction: the orientation of microfibrils sets the direction in which the wall can yield. The secondary wall is for cells that have stopped growing, such as fibres and xylem conduits; P2 explains why xylem walls must resist collapse (the water inside is under tension).

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
How a walled cell grows



Turgor supplies the force: water uptake pushes on the wall.
The wall is loosened: H⁺ pumped into the wall lowers its pH and activates expansins; tethers slip and the wall yields irreversibly.
New material is added: cellulose made at the plasma membrane, matrix from the Golgi, and new plasma membrane.

Turgor without loosening gives a turgid cell that does not grow. Most of the volume gained is vacuole.



Cells are now walled boxes. How do neighbouring cells exchange material?

This is the answer to the previous slide and to exercise 2.2: the wall property that must change is extensibility (loosening), and the materials to supply are new wall and new membrane. The figure is acid growth: a plasma-membrane H⁺-ATPase acidifies the wall, expansins become active at the lower pH and let the load-bearing microfibrils slide apart, and turgor then does the stretching. Auxin works this way in P4. Stress that growth is mostly water uptake into the vacuole: a root cell can lengthen more than 10-fold with little increase in cytoplasm, which is why expansion is fast and cheap compared with making new cytoplasm. The next slide lets students play with the two ingredients.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
section: Try it: turgor and wall loosening
text:
Try it: turgor and wall loosening




A single elongating cell, using the Lockhart growth equation: the relative growth rate is r = φ(P − Y), where P is turgor, Y the yield threshold of the wall and φ its extensibility. Below the threshold the wall behaves elastically and the cell does not grow at all. Press “Grow for 8 h” on the default: P = 0.6, Y = 0.3, φ = 1, so the cell grows at 0.3 per hour and doubles every 2.3 h, from 20 µm to about 220 µm. Then “Stiff wall: P < Y”: the same turgor, but no growth, which is the turgid-but-not-growing cell from the slide. “Low turgor”: P only just above Y, so growth crawls, which is what happens in a mildly water-stressed root. “Acid growth (auxin)” lowers Y and raises φ: the same turgor now gives twice the rate. Best trick: start a run on “Growing” and halfway through drag φ up; the curve bends upwards at that moment, as when auxin is added to a coleoptile segment and growth speeds up within minutes. Ask: which two things must the cell control to grow? (Turgor via solutes and water uptake, and wall extensibility via H⁺ pumping and expansins.) The model holds turgor constant, i.e. it assumes water uptake keeps pace with expansion.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
section: Apoplast and symplast: two routes between cells
text:
Apoplast and symplast: two routes between cells



Apoplast: the continuous system of cell walls, intercellular spaces and dead xylem conduits, outside the plasma membranes.
Symplast: the cytoplasm of all cells connected by plasmodesmata.
Plasmodesma: a membrane-lined channel through the wall, ~50 nm wide, joining the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells. Thousands per cell.




To move from the apoplast into the symplast, a substance must cross a plasma membrane. This is where the plant selects what it takes up (P2).

Exercise 2.3 asks for the three definitions and 2.4 for the boundary crossed. Plasmodesmata are the plant’s equivalent of gap junctions, but larger and lined by the plasma membrane, so the symplast is one continuous cytoplasm across many cells. These are routes, not tissues. In P2 the root endodermis blocks the apoplastic route and forces water and ions through a membrane. Transition: from cells to tissues.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
Three tissue systems



Dermal: protection and exchange; epidermis with cuticle, guard cells, root hairs.
Ground: photosynthesis, storage, support; mesophyll, cortex, pith.
Vascular: long-distance transport and support; xylem, phloem.
Every organ contains all three, continuous through the whole plant.
Compare A1: epithelium ↔︎ dermal; connective ↔︎ ground; vascular ↔︎ blood vessels.



Photo: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

The ground tissue is built from three cell types with very different walls.

Find the three systems in the section: the epidermis is the outermost single layer, the vascular bundles form a ring (xylem towards the centre, phloem towards the outside), and everything else is ground tissue (cortex outside the ring, pith inside). This is the plant counterpart of the four animal tissue types in A1, and it is the map for the next slides. The analogy to animal tissues is useful but loose: the vascular tissue transports and also supports. Exercise 3.1 asks for this table with one example per system.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
Ground tissue: three cell types










Parenchyma
Collenchyma
Sclerenchyma




Living at maturity?
yes
yes
usually no


Wall
thin primary wall
unevenly thickened primary wall, thick at the corners
thick, lignified secondary wall


Main function
metabolism, photosynthesis, storage
flexible support of growing organs
rigid support


Example
leaf mesophyll, potato tuber
celery “strings”
fibres (flax, hemp), sclereids (grit in pears)




The wall predicts the function: thin wall → metabolism; thick but stretchable wall → support while growing; lignified wall → support after growth stops.

The vascular tissue also contains dead cells with lignified walls: the xylem conduits.

Exercise 3.2 is this table. Teach recognition from the wall: students should be able to identify a cell type in a section from wall thickness, the presence of contents, and position. Collenchyma is living and can still stretch, so it supports young stems and petioles; sclerenchyma is dead and rigid. The bridge: xylem conduits are like sclerenchyma (dead, lignified), while phloem conducting cells must stay alive.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
Xylem and phloem











Xylem
Phloem




Transports
water and mineral ions
sugars (mainly sucrose), amino acids, signals


Conducting cells
tracheids and vessel elements
sieve-tube elements


Living at maturity?
no: hollow tubes of lignified wall
yes, but without a nucleus


Helper cells
xylem parenchyma (living)
companion cells (nucleated, linked by plasmodesmata)


End walls
vessel elements have perforation plates
sieve elements are joined by sieve plates


Direction
roots → shoot
sources → sinks, up or down





Photo: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library, CC0, Wikimedia Commons


Only the xylem’s conducting cells are dead: an empty conduit offers little resistance, while a living sieve element can load and unload sugar.

Where does the leaf use these supplies?

Exercises 3.3 and 3.4 use this table. The micrograph is a longitudinal section through pumpkin phloem at 400x: the sieve-tube elements run vertically, and the dark crosswise bands are sieve plates, the perforated end walls through which sap passes from one element to the next. The narrow cells beside them are companion cells and phloem parenchyma. Students should be able to name cells A–C in 3.3 from the descriptions: vessel element, sieve-tube element, companion cell. The functional logic: water moving under tension needs a rigid, empty pipe; sugar transport needs living membranes to load and unload, so the sieve element stays alive and depends on its companion cell, which carries the nucleus. Direction in phloem depends on where sugar is made and used, which is the topic of P3.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
section: The leaf: gas exchange and its cost
text:
The leaf: gas exchange and its cost



A waxy cuticle makes the epidermis nearly impermeable to water and gases.
Gas exchange goes through stomata: pores between two guard cells, ~100–300 per mm², ~1–2 % of the leaf area when open.
Mesophyll cells face a large internal air space: their surface is 10–40× the leaf area.

CO₂ route: pore → air space → water film of the wall → plasma membrane → cytosol → chloroplast stroma.


Photo: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

CO₂ diffuses in and water vapour diffuses out through the same pore. Opening a stoma raises both.

Exercise 3.5 asks for this route and 3.6 for the reason opening increases both fluxes. The leaf is the plant’s lung: a large internal surface behind a small, regulated opening. Because the cuticle blocks both gases, the plant cannot take up CO₂ without losing water; this trade-off runs through P2 (stomatal regulation, transpiration) and P3 (C4 and CAM). The water film step matters: CO₂ dissolves before crossing the membrane.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
section: The root: surface and a selective barrier
text:
The root: surface and a selective barrier


From the outside in:

Epidermis with root hairs: extensions of single epidermal cells that multiply the absorbing surface.
Cortex: parenchyma with air spaces; often colonised by mycorrhizal fungi.
Endodermis: one cell layer with the Casparian strip, a band of suberin in its walls that blocks the apoplast.
Stele: xylem and phloem.



Photo: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

The endodermis is to the root what the plasma membrane is to a cell: the point of selection.
Leaves and roots have to keep extending into new space. Where do the new cells come from?

In the buttercup section most of the root is cortex, a storage tissue; the stele is the small cylinder in the centre, ringed by the endodermis. Exercise 3.3 asks students to name root hairs and the endodermis from descriptions. This slide sets up P2, where we follow water from the soil across these layers into the xylem. The key idea is that the apoplast is open up to the endodermis and closed there, so the plant controls entry at one cell layer. Transition to growth: a plant that cannot move finds new soil and light by growing.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
Meristems: growth throughout life








Meristem
Location
Produces




Shoot apical
shoot tip
stem, leaves, flowers (primary growth in length)


Root apical
root tip, under the root cap
root length (primary growth)


Vascular cambium
cylinder in stem and root
secondary xylem inward, secondary phloem outward


Cork cambium
outer stem and root
periderm (cork, bark)


Intercalary
base of grass leaves and internodes
regrowth after the tip is cut or grazed




Primary growth (length) comes from apical meristems; secondary growth (girth) from the lateral meristems: vascular and cork cambium.
An animal’s body plan is complete early; a plant keeps making new organs.


Exercise 4.1 asks for the meristem in each case. This is the plant answer to “it cannot move”: it keeps building new roots into new soil and new leaves into new light. Intercalary meristems explain why a lawn survives mowing and grasses survive grazing: the growing region is at the base, below the cut. Transition: how a root tip actually gets longer.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
The root tip: three zones


Behind the protective root cap, three overlapping zones:

Division zone: small cells dividing (within ~1 mm of the tip).
Elongation zone: cells stop dividing and lengthen many-fold.
Maturation zone: cells differentiate; root hairs appear.

A root gets longer by division, expansion, or both.


Photo: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

Which of the two processes made a root longer?

Point out the zones on the section: the cap at the very tip (pale blue-green, loosely arranged cells), and the meristem as files of small, densely stained cells just behind it. The elongation zone starts beyond the top edge of the photo, about 1 mm from the tip. The zones grade into each other. The root cap protects the meristem as the root pushes through soil and senses gravity (P4). Cells are displaced backwards from the meristem: a cell never moves relative to its neighbours, but its distance from the tip increases as cells in front of it divide and lengthen.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
More cells or longer cells?


A file of 100 cells, end to end:



Cells
Mean cell length
Segment length




100
40 µm
4 mm


100
70 µm
7 mm (expansion only)


175
40 µm
7 mm (division only)





Photo: G Lens Microscopist, Megan Gerber, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons


Same final length, two different mechanisms.
Length alone does not identify the process. Count cells and measure their length.
At steady state, root growth rate = cell production rate × final cell length.


The micrograph is an Arabidopsis root with its cell walls stained: the smooth stretch behind the tip holds the division and elongation zones, and root hairs appear where cells have stopped elongating, in the maturation zone. Hairs that formed in the elongation zone would be torn as the cells lengthen. Exercise 4.2 is this calculation. Work it on the board: 100 × 40 µm = 4000 µm = 4 mm; 100 × 70 µm = 7 mm; 7000 / 40 = 175 cells. The general point is experimental: a mutant or treatment with a shorter root might divide less, expand less, or both, and only measuring cell number and cell length distinguishes them. The last bullet is the kinematic rule used in root biology: each cell leaving the meristem eventually adds its final length to the root.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
Try it: two root tips



Cells leaving the meristem become epidermis, xylem or cortex, yet all carry the same DNA. How?

Two root tips with the tip held still on the right, as if we were riding on it. The dark green block is the meristem; each new cell leaves it at 10 µm, elongates (light green) to its final length and then matures (pale, with root hairs); grey is older root. The red bracket shows how far the tip has moved through the soil. Press “Grow for 8 h” on the slide example: root A makes 2.2 cells per hour that end at 40 µm, root B only 1.25 cells per hour but they end at 70 µm. Both tips move 0.70 mm in 8 hours: A has 17 new cells, B 10. Ask: if you only had a ruler, could you tell these roots apart? No; you have to count cells and measure them. Then drag one slider: halve A’s production, as a treatment that blocks division would, and A falls behind; or raise B’s final length, as an auxin-insensitive or wall mutant might change it. “Identical roots” gives two equal roots to start from. The rule shown in the readout: growth rate = production rate × final cell length.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
Differentiation: same genome, different genes



A leaf mesophyll cell and a root cortex cell have the same nuclear genome; they express different sets of genes.
Differentiation changes gene expression and cell structure, not the DNA sequence.
Some mature cells can resume division: wound healing, rooting cuttings, regeneration from tissue culture.
Regeneration is not guaranteed: it depends on genotype, cell type, developmental state and hormones.



Photo: Iripseudocorus, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

A plant cell has not one genome but three.

The photo is callus: a mass of dividing, undifferentiated cells grown from pieces of a differentiated plant on a medium with auxin and cytokinin; changing the hormone balance can make it form shoots or roots. Exercises 4.3 and 5.3 test these statements. Contrast with animals: many plant cells keep the ability to dedifferentiate and divide, which is the basis of propagation by cuttings and of plant biotechnology (P5). But “every cell can make a plant” is false as a general rule. Hormonal control of regeneration returns in P4.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
Three genomes in one cell





Genome
Arabidopsis




Nuclear
~135 Mb, ~27 000 genes


Plastid
~154 kb, ~130 genes


Mitochondrial
~370 kb, ~60 genes




A chloroplast contains ~3000 different proteins; its own genome encodes about 100. The rest are encoded in the nucleus, made in the cytosol and imported.




Rubisco, the CO₂-fixing enzyme, needs both genomes: a nuclear mutation can block photosynthesis while chloroplast DNA is unchanged.

Exercises 5.1 and 5.2 use these facts. Rubisco is the ideal example because it is assembled from products of two genomes, and it is the enzyme at the centre of P3. Point out that the location of a protein does not tell you where its gene is. Plastid and mitochondrial genomes are inherited mostly from the mother in many species, but not all.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
Back to the seedling


The maize seedling solved the A1 problem without moving:



Need
Plant solution




Surface for light, CO₂
thin leaves, air spaces, stomata


Surface for water, minerals
roots, root hairs


Long-distance transport
xylem and phloem


Support
turgor; lignified walls


New resources
growth from meristems





Photo: Tangopaso, public domain, Wikimedia Commons

Two open questions: how does water get from the soil to the top of the plant (P2), and how is light turned into sugar for the whole plant (P3)?

Close the loop to the opening slide. Each row is a structure from today matched to the need it serves. The two transport questions are the next two lectures: P2 follows water and minerals from soil to air, P3 follows carbon from the air into sugar and out to the roots.

title: P1 — Building a functioning plant
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Plant versus animal
cannot move, makes its own food, cells have walls, grows all its life


Boundaries
wall (mechanical, porous), plasma membrane (selective), tonoplast (vacuole)


Turgor
pressure of protoplast against wall, ~0.3–1 MPa; loss → wilting


Plastids
chloroplast, amyloplast, chromoplast, all from proplastids


Cell growth
turgor + wall loosening + new wall and membrane


Apoplast / symplast
walls and spaces / cytoplasm linked by plasmodesmata


Tissue systems
dermal, ground (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma), vascular


Xylem / phloem
dead tracheids and vessels / living sieve tubes with companion cells


Meristems
apical (length), vascular and cork cambium (girth), intercalary


Three genomes
nuclear, plastid, mitochondrial; most organelle proteins are nuclear-encoded



Next (P2 — Water, minerals and transport): water moves from soil to air through a plant with no pump. What drives it, why can salty wet soil still dry a plant out, and how do stomata and roots control the flow?
Tutorial · Exercises · Quiz

Read the table as the story: the plant’s constraints, the cell that meets them, how cells grow and connect, the tissues they form, where growth happens, and the genomes behind it. P2 takes the water half of the supply problem, using turgor (as pressure potential), the apoplast and symplast, the endodermis, xylem and stomata from today.

title: P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text: The questions follow the tutorial and slides. Answer each question before opening its answer.

title: P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Abiotic stress

1.1
For each stress, name the main physiological problem it causes.



Stress
Main problem




Drought



Salinity



Heat



Freezing










Answer












Stress
Main problem




Drought
Low soil water potential; reduced water uptake and loss of turgor


Salinity
Osmotic effect (low soil water potential) plus ion toxicity, mainly from Na⁺ and Cl⁻


Heat
Protein denaturation and increased membrane fluidity


Freezing
Ice formation in extracellular spaces dehydrates cells; ice crystals can damage membranes








1.2
Which hormone accumulates in leaves during drought, and what is its main immediate effect?






Answer





Abscisic acid (ABA). It causes stomatal closure, which reduces transpiration.





1.3
What is the cost to the plant of the response in 1.2?






Answer





Closed stomata also reduce CO₂ uptake, so photosynthesis falls. Less transpiration also means less evaporative cooling, so leaf temperature rises.





1.4
Name two kinds of compatible solutes, and explain how accumulating them helps a plant under drought or salinity.






Answer





Examples are proline, glycine betaine and sugars or sugar alcohols such as sucrose and mannitol. They lower the cell’s solute potential, so the cell can keep taking up water from a soil with low water potential. They do so without inhibiting enzymes.





1.5
Name two classes of proteins induced by heat or drought stress that help protect cells.






Answer





Heat shock proteins (chaperones that refold or stabilise proteins) and dehydrins/LEA (late embryogenesis abundant) proteins. Antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase and catalase are also accepted.





1.6
Reactive oxygen species (ROS) can damage cells. Name one other role they play in plants.






Answer





Signalling. For example, ROS act in stress signalling, stomatal closure and defence against pathogens.





1.7
Classify each as acclimation or evolutionary adaptation.

Plants of a species become more freezing-tolerant after two weeks at 4 °C.
A population on saline coastal soil has heritably higher salt tolerance than inland populations grown under the same conditions.







Answer






Acclimation (cold acclimation). b. Evolutionary adaptation.

title: P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Biotic stress and defence

2.1
Name two constitutive (pre-existing) defences and two induced defences of plants.






Answer





Constitutive: the cuticle, cell walls, thorns or trichomes, and stored specialised metabolites. Induced: callose deposition, phytoalexin production, proteinase inhibitors, and the hypersensitive response.





2.2
Match each attacker to the main defence hormone pathway: salicylic acid (SA) or jasmonic acid (JA).

A biotrophic pathogen that feeds on living tissue
A chewing caterpillar
A necrotrophic fungus that kills tissue before feeding on it







Answer






SA. b. JA. c. JA, together with ethylene. The SA and JA pathways often act antagonistically.






2.3
What is the hypersensitive response, and why is it effective against biotrophic pathogens?






Answer





It is rapid, localised death of the plant cells at the infection site. A biotrophic pathogen needs living host cells, so killing the infected cells deprives it of nutrients and limits its spread.





2.4
What is systemic acquired resistance (SAR), and which hormone is required for it?






Answer





SAR is long-lasting, broad-spectrum resistance in uninfected parts of the plant after a local infection. It requires salicylic acid.





2.5
Name the three major classes of plant specialised (secondary) metabolites, and give one example of each.






Answer






Terpenoids, e.g. pyrethrins, essential oils such as menthol, or carotenoids.
Phenolics, e.g. flavonoids, tannins or lignin.
Nitrogen-containing compounds, e.g. alkaloids such as nicotine, caffeine or morphine, and cyanogenic glycosides.






2.6
Why are many defence compounds stored as inactive precursors, such as glucosinolates or cyanogenic glycosides?






Answer





The active compound is toxic to the plant itself. The precursor is stored separately from the activating enzyme, and they meet only when tissue is damaged by a herbivore. The toxin is therefore released only at the site of attack.





2.7
True or false? Correct any false statements.

Defence compounds use carbon and nitrogen that could otherwise be used for growth.
A plant with constitutively activated jasmonate signalling grows larger than a wild-type plant.
Natural plant compounds are harmless to humans.







Answer






True. This is the basis of the growth–defence trade-off.
False. Constitutive defence activation usually reduces growth.
False. Many, such as nicotine, ricin or cyanogenic glycosides, are toxic.

title: P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Model systems

3.1
Give three properties that make Arabidopsis thaliana a useful model plant.






Answer





Any three of: a short life cycle (about 6–8 weeks); small size; a small, fully sequenced genome; self-pollination; many seeds; easy transformation with Agrobacterium (floral dip); large collections of mutants.

title: P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Transformation and tissue culture

4.1
Put the steps of Agrobacterium-mediated transformation in order.

Regenerate whole plants from the transformed cells
Insert the gene of interest into the T-DNA of a binary vector
Select transformed cells on medium containing an antibiotic or herbicide
Co-cultivate plant explants with Agrobacterium
Confirm the insertion and expression of the transgene







Answer





b → d → c → a → e.





4.2
What is a selectable marker gene? Give an example.






Answer





It is a gene, transferred together with the gene of interest, that allows only transformed cells to survive on a selective medium. Examples are nptII (kanamycin resistance), hpt (hygromycin resistance) and bar (resistance to the herbicide glufosinate).





4.3
What is the difference between stable transformation and transient expression?






Answer





In stable transformation, the transgene is integrated into the plant genome and inherited by the offspring. In transient expression, the introduced DNA is expressed for a few days without integration and is not inherited.





4.4
Name a method for delivering DNA into plant cells that does not use Agrobacterium.






Answer





Particle bombardment (biolistics). Protoplast transformation, using polyethylene glycol or electroporation, is also accepted.





4.5
What property of plant cells makes it possible to regenerate a whole plant from a single transformed cell?






Answer





Totipotency: many differentiated plant cells can dedifferentiate and regenerate all the organs of a whole plant.





4.6
In tissue culture, what does an explant form at each auxin-to-cytokinin ratio?

High auxin : cytokinin
Intermediate (roughly balanced)
Low auxin : cytokinin (high cytokinin)







Answer






Roots. b. Undifferentiated callus. c. Shoots. The exact concentrations depend on species and tissue.






4.7
Why must several independent transgenic lines be analysed, rather than one?






Answer





The T-DNA inserts at a random position in the genome. It can disrupt or activate a native gene, and tissue culture can itself cause mutations (somaclonal variation). A phenotype seen consistently in independent lines is more likely to be caused by the transgene.

title: P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Promoters and reporters

5.1
Match each promoter type to its expression pattern.







Promoter
Pattern




a. Constitutive (e.g. CaMV 35S)
1. Expressed only after exposure to a signal


b. Tissue-specific
2. Expressed in nearly all tissues at all times


c. Inducible
3. Expressed only in particular cell types, e.g. guard cells









Answer





a–2, b–3, c–1.





5.2
Name two reporter genes used in plants, and how each one is detected.






Answer






GUS (β-glucuronidase): a blue product after staining with X-Gluc.
GFP (green fluorescent protein): fluorescence under blue/UV light.
Luciferase: light emission when luciferin is supplied.

title: P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Genetically modified crops

6.1
Match each GM trait to the gene or mechanism used.







Trait
Gene or mechanism




a. Insect resistance
1. Bacterial EPSP synthase insensitive to glyphosate


b. Herbicide tolerance
2. Carotenoid biosynthesis genes in the endosperm


c. Golden Rice
3. Cry toxin gene from Bacillus thuringiensis









Answer





a–3, b–1, c–2. Golden Rice makes β-carotene (provitamin A) in the grain.





6.2
How does the Bt (Cry) protein kill insect larvae, and why is it harmless to mammals?






Answer





In the alkaline gut of susceptible larvae, the protoxin is activated by proteases. It binds to specific receptors on the gut epithelium and forms pores, so the gut cells lyse. Mammals have an acidic stomach and lack these receptors.





6.3
What is a refuge strategy in Bt crop cultivation, and what problem does it delay?






Answer





Non-Bt plants are grown next to the Bt crop. Susceptible insects survive on the refuge and mate with any resistant insects, which keeps the resistance alleles rare. This delays the evolution of Bt resistance in the pest.





6.4
How does genome editing with CRISPR–Cas9 differ from classical transgenesis?






Answer





Classical transgenesis inserts foreign DNA into the genome. CRISPR–Cas9 makes a targeted cut in an existing gene, which can create a small mutation in that gene. The Cas9 construct can then be removed by crossing, so the final plant may contain no foreign DNA.





6.5
Classify each question as empirical (it can be answered by measurement) or value-based.

Does pollen from a GM crop reach a wild relative 100 m away?
How much uncertainty about environmental effects is acceptable?
Does a Bt crop reduce insecticide use in a region?
Who should decide whether a GM crop is grown?







Answer






Empirical. b. Value-based. c. Empirical. d. Value-based.

The demo shows a stoma closing as ABA rises in the guard cells, and how conductance, water loss, CO₂ uptake, CO₂ gained per water lost and leaf temperature (leaf minus air) change. Use the drought buttons or the ABA slider; “Air dryness” sets the vapour pressure deficit (VPD) of the air. The curves show water loss and CO₂ uptake as % of the fully open value.

Less transpiration means less evaporative cooling, so the leaf warms: with severe drought it is about 8 °C above air temperature.





E1.2
Compare well watered with mild drought.

By what percentage does water loss fall, and by what percentage does CO₂ uptake fall?
Does CO₂ gained per water lost increase or decrease? Give both values.
Why does CO₂ uptake fall less than water loss?







Answer






Water loss falls by 50 % (9.9 → 4.9); CO₂ uptake falls by only about 20 % (28.0 → 22.6).
It increases, from 2.8 to 4.6 µmol CO₂ per mmol H₂O.
Water loss is proportional to stomatal conductance, but CO₂ uptake is limited by two steps in series, the stomata and carboxylation in the chloroplast. Partly closing the stomata therefore costs less carbon than water.






E1.3
Set ABA to 0 and move air dryness from 2 to 4 kPa. Which of these change: conductance, water loss, CO₂ uptake, leaf temperature? Give the new water loss.






Answer





Water loss doubles to 19.7 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹ and the leaf cools (to −10.7 °C relative to the air). Conductance (0.50) and CO₂ uptake (28.0) do not change: in this model dry air drives transpiration through the same open stomata. Real plants also close their stomata partly in dry air.

section: Explore: Auxin and cytokinin in tissue culture
text:
Explore: Auxin and cytokinin in tissue culture
An explant grows on a medium with auxin and cytokinin. Set the two concentrations with the sliders (log scale, mg/L), drag the dot on the map, or use the preset buttons; the dish shows the explant after four weeks and the readout gives the outcome and the auxin : cytokinin ratio. “Infected by wild Agrobacterium” adds the hormones that a crown-gall T-DNA makes inside the plant cells. The model is a rule of thumb, not fitted to data.

Answer

High auxin : cytokinin gives roots, low gives shoots, and a balance gives undifferentiated callus (Skoog and Miller). The No-hormones medium has the same ratio as Callus, but too little of either hormone for growth: the absolute level matters too.





E2.2
Set cytokinin to 0.10 mg/L and auxin to 0.10 mg/L, then raise auxin in steps. At what auxin concentration does the outcome first change from Callus, and to what? What is the ratio then?






Answer





At 0.56 mg/L auxin it changes to “Roots from callus” (ratio 5.6); from 0.71 mg/L it is “Roots”. Up to 0.50 mg/L (ratio 5.0) the explant forms only callus. Swapping the two hormones gives the mirror result: shoots from callus once cytokinin reaches 0.56 mg/L at 0.10 mg/L auxin.





E2.3
Press “No hormones” and tick “Infected by wild Agrobacterium”. What does the explant form? Then press “Rooting” with the box still ticked: what is the outcome and the ratio now?






Answer





With no hormones in the medium it forms a tumour (crown gall), with ratio 1.0. On the rooting medium it is still a tumour, and the ratio falls from 100 to 2.9. The wild T-DNA carries genes for auxin and cytokinin synthesis, so the infected cells make their own hormones and proliferate whatever the medium. Disarmed strains used for transformation lack these genes.

title: P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Explore: Refuges and Bt resistance
The demo follows the frequency of a resistance allele R in a pest over generations. Bt maize kills 99 % of susceptible (SS) larvae; a refuge of non-Bt maize lets all genotypes survive, and adults from both mate at random. Set the refuge size, the dominance of R (h = 0: recessive, h = 1: dominant) and the starting frequency of R. The readout gives the number of generations until R reaches 50 % and the fitness of each genotype.




E3.1
Keep the starting frequency at 0.001 and h = 0. How many generations does it take for R to reach 50 % with no refuge, a 5 % refuge, a 10 % refuge and a 20 % refuge?






Answer








Refuge

Susceptible adults from the refuge mate with the rare resistant survivors, so most R alleles end up in RS offspring, which are killed on Bt maize when R is recessive.





E3.2
Press “20% refuge”, then “20%, dominant R”. Read off the generations to 50 % and the fitness of RS for each. Which is the more important condition for the refuge to work?






Answer









RS fitness

20 % refuge, h = 1

With dominant resistance, RS larvae survive on Bt maize as well as RR, and the refuge no longer slows resistance (6 generations, faster even than no refuge with a recessive allele). The refuge strategy therefore requires a high-dose Bt crop that kills heterozygotes, which makes R effectively recessive.





E3.3
Set a 20 % refuge, h = 0, and the starting frequency of R to 0.01 instead of 0.001. How many generations does R take to reach 50 %?






Answer





31 generations (compared with more than 150 at 0.001). The refuge works best when R is very rare, because almost all R alleles are then in heterozygotes. Refuges must be in place from the first Bt planting, not added after resistance has been detected.
