title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
About this lecture
A maize field in a dry summer: the soil dries out, the irrigation water is slightly salty, the afternoons reach 38 °C, a fungus spreads on the leaves and corn borer caterpillars tunnel into the stems. The plant cannot move away from any of it. How does a plant survive stress and attack, and how can we use that knowledge to build a better crop? In P4 we saw signals regulate development. Today the same signalling, ABA, jasmonic acid and salicylic acid among them, is used to cope with a hostile environment.

Abiotic stress: drought, salinity, heat and freezing, and how cells are protected.
Biotic stress: constitutive and induced defence, the hypersensitive response, SAR, the SA and JA pathways, and defensive chemicals.
From mechanism to crop: Arabidopsis, Agrobacterium, tissue culture, promoters and reporters.
GM crops: Bt maize, herbicide tolerance, Golden Rice, CRISPR, and how to separate evidence from values.


The running example is a maize field, and the lecture follows it in three steps: what the environment does to the plant, what attackers do to it, and how a gene can be put into the plant to help. The final slides return to the field with Bt maize. This is the last lecture of the course, so the summary also draws the plant half together and points to the animal half.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
section: What stress does to a plant
text:
What stress does to a plant


Stress: a condition that pushes a plant’s function outside its normal range.



Stress
Main problem




Drought
Low soil ψ: less uptake, loss of turgor


Salinity
Osmotic effect plus Na⁺ and Cl⁻ toxicity


Heat
Proteins denature; membranes too fluid


Freezing
Ice between cells draws water out



Stress can reduce survival, growth or seed yield: different outcomes.


Photo: CraneStation, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

The commonest stress in our field is drought. What does the plant do first?

Exercise 1.1. Note that drought and salinity share the osmotic problem from P2: water flows to lower water potential, and a salty or dry soil has a low one. Freezing is effectively a drought inside the tissue, because extracellular ice has a lower water potential than the cell sap. Transition: the first response to drought is fast, hormonal and happens in the guard cells.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Drought: ABA closes the stomata



Soil dries; ABA is made in roots and leaves.
ABA binds receptors in the guard cells.
Ion channels open: K⁺ and anions leave.
Water follows, turgor falls, the stoma closes.


Within minutes, transpiration falls.
Cost: less CO₂ uptake, and less evaporative cooling, so the leaf warms.




How large is that cost? Try it.

Exercises 1.2 and 1.3. This is the fast branch of the signal chain from P4: no new genes are needed for the guard cells to close, just ion channels. The trade-off links P2 (transpiration) and P3 (CO₂ uptake): a plant under drought must choose between water and carbon. The heat cost matters on a hot afternoon in our maize field. Transition: the slower, longer-term response is to change the water potential inside the cells.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
section: Try it: water saved versus carbon lost
text:
Try it: water saved versus carbon lost




Start at “well watered” and read out water loss, CO₂ uptake and leaf temperature. Then click “mild drought”: water loss roughly halves but CO₂ uptake falls by only about a fifth, so CO₂ gained per water lost rises. Ask why: CO₂ uptake is limited by both the stomata and the chloroplast, so partial closure costs less carbon than water. Then click “severe drought”: CO₂ uptake collapses and the leaf ends up about 8 °C warmer than the air. Finally raise the air-dryness slider at fixed ABA to show that dry air raises water loss without changing the stomata. This connects P2 (transpiration), P3 (CO₂ uptake) and the heat stress on the previous slide.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Osmotic adjustment and salt


Compatible solutes (proline, glycine betaine, sucrose, mannitol) lower ψs without inhibiting enzymes, so water still flows into the root.
Salinity harms a plant twice:

Osmotic: salty soil water has a low ψ, so uptake is hard, as in drought.
Ionic: Na⁺ that does get in is toxic to enzymes in the cytoplasm.



Photo: Willem van Aken, CSIRO, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

How does a cell keep Na⁺ out of its cytoplasm?

Exercise 1.4. Recall from P2 that water potential = solute potential + pressure potential: accumulating solutes makes the cell’s water potential more negative than the soil’s, so uptake continues. “Compatible” means the solute can reach high concentrations without disrupting protein function, unlike Na⁺. The photo shows the extreme case: land in the Western Australian wheat belt (1981) where clearing of deep-rooted native vegetation let saline groundwater rise; salt has crusted the surface and killed the trees, and no crop can establish. Salt tolerance therefore has two parts: the osmotic part, shared with drought, and the ion part, on the next slide.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
section: Salt: keeping Na⁺ out of the cytoplasm
text:
Salt: keeping Na⁺ out of the cytoplasm



SOS1 pumps Na⁺ back out of root cells.
NHX stores Na⁺ in the vacuole, where it helps lower ψs.
The cytoplasm keeps a high K⁺ : Na⁺ ratio.





Exercise 1.4. The ion part of salt tolerance is solved by exclusion and vacuolar storage: SOS1 is a Na⁺/H⁺ antiporter in the plasma membrane and NHX one in the tonoplast, both driven by the proton gradients from P2. Na⁺ stored in the vacuole is not wasted: it lowers the vacuole’s ψs and so contributes to osmotic adjustment. Transition: whatever the stress, proteins and membranes need protection.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Protecting the cell, and acclimating







Protective molecule
What it does




Heat shock proteins (chaperones)
Refold or stabilise damaged proteins


Dehydrins / LEA proteins
Protect proteins and membranes during dehydration


Antioxidant enzymes (superoxide dismutase, catalase)
Remove reactive oxygen species




Reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as H₂O₂ damage lipids, proteins and DNA. But ROS are also signals: in stomatal closure, stress signalling and defence.
Acclimation: an individual becomes more tolerant over days. Example: plants gain freezing tolerance after two weeks at 4 °C (cold acclimation).
Adaptation: a population differs heritably. Example: a coastal population is more salt-tolerant than an inland one when both are grown in the same conditions.

So far the threats were physical. What if the threat is alive?

Exercises 1.5 to 1.7. LEA stands for late embryogenesis abundant: the same proteins protect the dry seed from P4. The dual role of ROS is important: a plant does not simply minimise them, it uses them as a signal, and we meet them again in the hypersensitive response. The acclimation versus adaptation distinction repeats the time scales from A1; the “same conditions” clause is what separates heritable differences from acclimation. Transition: the fungus and the caterpillar in our field.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
section: Defence: always on, or switched on?
text:
Defence: always on, or switched on?











Constitutive
Induced




Physical
Cuticle, walls, thorns, trichomes
Callose plugs


Chemical
Stored metabolites
Phytoalexins, proteinase inhibitors


Cellular
—
Hypersensitive response



Three kinds of attacker: biotrophs feed on living cells (rusts, mildews); necrotrophs kill cells first (Botrytis); herbivores remove tissue.


Photo: Richard Blood, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

To induce a defence, the plant must first detect the attacker. How?

Exercise 2.1. Constitutive defences cost resources even when there is no attack; induced defences save that cost but take time to switch on. The attacker classes matter because a defence that works against one can help another: killing infected cells starves a biotroph but feeds a necrotroph. Proteinase inhibitors, induced by wounding in tomato, block the caterpillar’s digestive enzymes. Transition: recognition and the hypersensitive response.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
section: Detecting the pathogen: the hypersensitive response
text:
Detecting the pathogen: the hypersensitive response



Receptors recognise conserved microbial molecules (e.g. bacterial flagellin); R proteins recognise specific pathogen effectors.
Recognition triggers a ROS burst and a rise in salicylic acid.
Hypersensitive response (HR): rapid death of the cells at the infection site. A biotroph needs living cells, so it is starved and cannot spread.



Photo: DanieliusKa, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Does the rest of the plant benefit?

Exercise 2.3. The HR is a striking case of cells sacrificed to protect the whole, comparable to programmed cell death in development (P4 senescence). The brown spots in the photo are the dead cells; the pathogen is trapped inside them. Transition: the infection also sends a signal to the rest of the plant.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Systemic acquired resistance



SAR: long-lasting, broad-spectrum resistance in uninfected leaves after a local infection.
A signal moves through the phloem from the infected leaf.
SAR requires salicylic acid and induces pathogenesis-related (PR) proteins.
Plants that cannot accumulate SA (expressing the bacterial enzyme NahG) develop no SAR.





Exercise 2.4. SAR is the plant’s closest analogue to immunological memory, but it is not specific to one pathogen. The NahG experiment is the classic test that SA is required. Transition: SA is one of two main defence hormones; the other is jasmonic acid.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
section: SA versus JA: matching the defence to the attacker
text:
SA versus JA: matching the defence to the attacker





Attacker
Pathway




Biotrophic pathogen
SA: HR, SAR, PR proteins


Necrotrophic pathogen
JA + ethylene


Chewing insect
JA: proteinase inhibitors




SA and JA often act antagonistically.
Tomato: wounding releases the peptide systemin → JA → proteinase inhibitors in unwounded leaves.
JAZ repressors hold JA signalling off; JA causes their degradation.




What are the chemical weapons these pathways produce?

Exercise 2.2. The logic is the HR again: cell death is useful against biotrophs but would feed a necrotroph, so the plant uses a different pathway for each. Antagonism means that some pathogens manipulate the balance; for example, Pseudomonas syringae makes coronatine, a JA mimic, to suppress SA defence. The JAZ repressors return on the growth–defence slide. Transition: the outputs of these pathways are often specialised metabolites.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Chemical defence: specialised metabolites









Class
Examples




Terpenoids
Pyrethrins, menthol


Phenolics
Flavonoids, tannins, lignin


N-containing
Alkaloids (nicotine, caffeine), cyanogenic glycosides




Often stored as inactive precursors, apart from the activating enzyme: glucosinolates + myrosinase; cyanogenic glycosides → HCN.
Damage mixes them, so the toxin forms only at the site of attack.
“Natural” does not mean harmless: nicotine, ricin, cyanide.



Photo: Jebulon, CC0, Wikimedia Commons


Exercises 2.5 to 2.7c. The three classes are defined by biosynthetic origin, and students should give one example of each. Compartmentation is the key idea: the plant keeps its own toxin safe by storing the parts separately, often in different cells or in the vacuole versus the cytoplasm. Pyrethrins from chrysanthemum flowers are the basis of common insecticides. Transition: if defence is so useful, why not keep it switched on all the time?

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
The growth–defence trade-off



Defence uses carbon, nitrogen and energy that could go into growth.
An Arabidopsis mutant lacking ten JAZ repressors has constitutive JA signalling: strong insect resistance, but much smaller plants and fewer seeds (Guo et al., 2018).
A plant with defence always on loses without attack and wins under heavy attack.
So induced defence is common: pay only when attacked.




To test ideas like these we need genes, mutants and a model plant.

Exercise 2.7 a and b. The JAZ decuple mutant is a direct test of the trade-off: removing the brakes on JA signalling buys defence at a growth cost. Stress the table: whether a defence is worth it depends on the environment, which is also why a crop bred for a pest-free greenhouse can fail in the field. Transition: almost everything on the previous slides was discovered in one small plant.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Arabidopsis thaliana: the model plant









Property
Why it helps




Life cycle 6–8 weeks
Many generations per year


Small genome (~135 Mb), sequenced 2000
Every gene has an ID, e.g. FT = AT1G65730


Self-pollinating, many seeds
Mutants breed true


Floral-dip transformation
No tissue culture needed


Large mutant collections
A knockout for almost every gene



Gene records are collected in TAIR. A mechanism found here must be tested again in a crop.


Photo: Quentin Groom, public domain, Wikimedia Commons

How do we put a new gene into a plant?

Exercise 3.1. The stable identifier (AGI code) matters because gene names and aliases change; AT1G65730 means chromosome 1, gene 65730. Floral dip means the inflorescence is dipped in an Agrobacterium suspension and some of the seeds are transformed, so Arabidopsis avoids the tissue culture step that most crops need. The last bullet is the bridge to crops: FT from P4 exists in rice and tomato, but its regulation differs. Transition: Agrobacterium is the natural genetic engineer that made plant transformation possible.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Agrobacterium: nature’s genetic engineer



Agrobacterium tumefaciens causes crown gall tumours.
It transfers part of its Ti plasmid, the T-DNA, into the plant genome.
The T-DNA lies between left and right borders; the bacterium’s vir genes cut it out and transfer it.
Wild T-DNA carries auxin and cytokinin synthesis genes: the infected cells overproduce both hormones and grow into a tumour.



Photo: Scot Nelson, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

Anything between the borders is transferred. Can we swap in our own gene?

The natural system links to P4: the bacterium makes the plant cells overproduce auxin and cytokinin, the same hormones we use in tissue culture later in this lecture. Transition: the binary vector.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
The binary vector



A binary vector carries a T-DNA in which the tumour genes are replaced by our gene plus a selectable marker. A disarmed Ti plasmid supplies the vir genes.
Stable transformation: T-DNA integrated and inherited.
Transient expression: not integrated, lost within days; used for fast tests in leaves.
Without Agrobacterium: particle bombardment, or PEG / electroporation of protoplasts.





Exercises 4.3 and 4.4. Splitting the system into two plasmids makes the small binary vector easy to handle in E. coli. Particle bombardment was important for cereals, which were initially hard to transform with Agrobacterium. Transition: the full workflow.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
From construct to transgenic plant


Only a few cells are transformed. A selectable marker in the same T-DNA lets only those survive:



Marker gene
Resistance to




nptII
Kanamycin


hpt
Hygromycin


bar
Glufosinate (herbicide)



Confirm the insert by PCR and its expression by RT-PCR or a protein assay.




Exercises 4.1 and 4.2. The order is the one students must reproduce: construct, co-cultivation, selection, regeneration, confirmation (by PCR for the insert and RT-PCR or a protein assay for expression). The marker and the gene of interest sit in the same T-DNA, so surviving cells usually carry both. Transition: regeneration relies on a property of plant cells that animal cells mostly lack.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Tissue culture: totipotency



Totipotency: many differentiated plant cells can dedifferentiate and regenerate a whole plant.
A single transformed cell can therefore become a transgenic plant.
Typical sequence: explant → callus → shoots → roots → plantlet in soil.



Photo: Annalisa Giovannini, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

What decides whether the culture makes roots, shoots or callus?

Exercise 4.5. Most animal cells lose this capacity during differentiation; plant cells keep it, which is what makes transformation followed by regeneration possible. Transition: hormone ratios.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
section: Tissue culture: the auxin : cytokinin ratio
text:
Tissue culture: the auxin : cytokinin ratio


Skoog and Miller (1957), tobacco:



Auxin : cytokinin
Explant forms




High
Roots


Intermediate
Callus


Low (high cytokinin)
Shoots



Exact concentrations depend on species, genotype and tissue.




Exercise 4.6. Connect to the hormones from P4: auxin promotes root initiation (rooting powder), cytokinin promotes shoot meristems. The crown gall is a callus caused by the bacterium’s own auxin and cytokinin genes. Transition: try it.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Try it: grow an explant




Start at the balanced medium: the explant forms callus. Drag the point towards high cytokinin and shoots appear; towards high auxin and roots appear. Ask the room to predict before each move. Then tick “wild Agrobacterium” with no hormones in the medium: the explant still forms a tumour, because the T-DNA makes the cells produce their own auxin and cytokinin. This joins the crown-gall slide to the Skoog–Miller map. The model is a rule of thumb, not fitted to data.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
section: Is the phenotype caused by the transgene?
text:
Is the phenotype caused by the transgene?



The T-DNA inserts at a random position: it can disrupt or activate a native gene.
Tissue culture itself causes mutations: somaclonal variation.
So compare several independent lines and an empty-vector control.
A phenotype seen in all independent lines, and absent from the controls, is attributed to the transgene.





Exercise 4.7. Each independent line has the T-DNA in a different place and has been through its own culture, so position effects and somaclonal mutations differ between lines; only the transgene is common to all. The empty-vector control shows the effect of the transformation procedure itself. Expression level also varies between lines because of insertion position, which is another reason to analyse several. Transition: promoters.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Promoters: where and when





Promoter type
Expression




Constitutive (CaMV 35S)
Nearly all tissues, all the time


Tissue-specific
Particular cell types, e.g. guard cells


Inducible
Only after a signal, e.g. drought or wounding




A guard-cell promoter driving a gene that closes stomata saves water. CO₂ uptake, leaf temperature and yield must be measured too.



Image: Alex Costa, CC BY 2.5, Wikimedia Commons

How do we see where a promoter is active?

Exercise 5.1. The image shows GFP expressed only in guard cells, exactly what a guard-cell promoter is for. The guard-cell example returns to the ABA slide and the stomata demo: closing stomata has a carbon and temperature cost. Transition: reporter genes.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Reporters: making expression visible





Reporter
Detected by




GUS (β-glucuronidase)
Blue product after staining with X-Gluc


GFP
Green fluorescence under blue light


Luciferase
Light emission when luciferin is supplied




Fuse a promoter to a reporter to see where and when it is active.
A stress-induced promoter + reporter gives a plant that signals when stressed, but it must be tested for specificity.



Photo: D. S. Rathore, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons


Exercise 5.2. Reporters fused to a promoter show where and when that promoter is active; this was how the senescence promoter in P4 was characterised. Many stress promoters respond to several stresses, so a reporter plant used as a sensor needs controls. Transition: back to the maize field, with crops that are actually grown.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
GM crops in the field









Trait
Gene or mechanism




Insect resistance (maize, cotton)
cry toxin gene from Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt)


Herbicide tolerance (soybean, maize)
Bacterial EPSP synthase insensitive to glyphosate


Golden Rice
Carotenoid synthesis genes in the endosperm → β-carotene



Golden Rice targets vitamin A deficiency: β-carotene is provitamin A, and normal rice endosperm makes none.


Photo: International Rice Research Institute, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

How does the Bt protein kill a caterpillar but not us?

Exercise 6.1. Glyphosate inhibits EPSP synthase in the shikimate pathway, which makes aromatic amino acids; the bacterial enzyme still works in its presence. Transition: the Bt mechanism.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
How Bt toxin works



The caterpillar eats the Cry protoxin.
In the alkaline larval gut, proteases activate it.
It binds specific receptors on gut epithelial cells and forms pores.
Gut cells lyse; the larva stops feeding and dies.

Safe for mammals: an acidic stomach and no receptors for the toxin.



If every plant in the field kills the pest, what does natural selection do?

Exercise 6.2. The mechanism explains the specificity: each Cry protein matches receptors in a particular insect group. Bt sprays have been used in organic farming for decades. Transition: resistance evolution.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
The refuge strategy



Bt maize selects for resistance alleles in the pest, the European corn borer.
A refuge of non-Bt plants is grown next to the Bt crop.
Susceptible insects from the refuge mate with the rare resistant survivors.
Resistance is usually recessive, so the heterozygous offspring still die on Bt maize, and resistance evolves much more slowly.



Photo: Keith Weller, USDA ARS, public domain, Wikimedia Commons

How much refuge is enough? Try it.

Exercise 6.3. The refuge is applied evolution: the same natural selection from A1, now in a pest population. Because resistant insects are rare, they almost always mate with susceptible insects from the refuge. Transition: the demo.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
section: Try it: Bt resistance and the refuge
text:
Try it: Bt resistance and the refuge




Start with no refuge: the resistance allele reaches 50% in about 15 generations. Set a 20% refuge with a recessive allele (h = 0): more than 150 generations. Then make the allele dominant (h = 1) with the same refuge: the refuge helps far less, because heterozygotes now survive on Bt maize. This is why refuges are combined with a high-dose Bt crop that kills heterozygotes. Tick the drift option to show that chance matters when the allele is very rare. Ask: what would farmers gain by planting no refuge, and who pays when resistance appears?

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Genome editing versus transgenesis











Transgenesis
CRISPR–Cas9




Change
Foreign DNA inserted
Targeted cut in a gene


Position
Random
Chosen by guide RNA


Final plant
Carries the transgene
Small mutation; Cas9 crossed out



The final edited plant may carry only a small deletion that could also arise by mutation.



The science says what a crop does. Should it be grown? That is a different kind of question.

Exercise 6.4. Whether edited plants are regulated as GM differs between countries. Transition: empirical versus value questions.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Evidence and values








Question
Type
How it is answered




Does pollen from a GM crop reach a wild relative 100 m away?
Empirical
Measure gene flow in the field


Does a Bt crop reduce insecticide use in a region?
Empirical
Compare spraying records


How much uncertainty about environmental effects is acceptable?
Value
Weigh benefits and risks: a societal choice


Who should decide whether a GM crop is grown?
Value
Governance and law




Empirical questions are settled by data; value questions by argument and decision.
Data inform value questions but do not answer them.
Risks depend on the trait and setting, not on the label “GM”: gene flow matters only where wild relatives grow.


Exercise 6.5. The skill is classification: a question that a measurement could settle is empirical, even if the measurement is hard. Students should not be asked to take a side here; the point is to recognise which kind of question is being asked, so that a debate does not confuse the two. Example of the last bullet: Bt maize in Europe has no wild relatives to cross with, while in Mexico, the centre of maize diversity, gene flow into landraces is a real question. This closes the lecture and the plant half of the course.

title: P5 — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Abiotic stress
drought: low ψ; salt: osmotic + Na⁺/Cl⁻ toxicity; heat: denaturation; freezing: extracellular ice


Drought response
ABA → stomata close; cost: less CO₂, warmer leaf


Tolerance
compatible solutes, Na⁺ exclusion and vacuolar storage, HSPs, LEA proteins, antioxidants


Defence
constitutive vs induced; HR starves biotrophs; SAR needs SA


SA vs JA
SA: biotrophs; JA (+ ethylene): necrotrophs and chewing insects; often antagonistic


Trade-off
constant defence costs growth; induced defence pays only under attack


Transformation
binary vector → Agrobacterium → selection → regeneration → confirmation


Tissue culture
high auxin : cytokinin → roots; low → shoots; intermediate → callus


GM crops
Bt kills via gut receptors; refuges delay resistance; CRISPR edits without inserting DNA



The plant half: P1 built the plant; P2 supplied water and minerals; P3 fixed and moved carbon; P4 used signals to decide what to build and when; P5 used the same signals to survive. The animal half solved the same problems differently: feedback (ABA closing stomata; ADH in the kidney), hormones carried in transport fluids (phloem, blood), and exchange surfaces (leaf and root, lung and gut).
Revision questions · Tutorial · Exercises · Quiz

Read the table in the order of the lecture: the field’s physical stresses, its attackers, and the tools for changing the crop. Then step back to the whole course. Both halves start from the same physical problem set out in A1: getting resources to cells across exchange surfaces and keeping conditions stable. ABA and stomatal closure is a negative feedback loop just like ADH and water reabsorption in A4: a fall in water status triggers a hormone that reduces water loss. The revision page has integration questions that combine units from each half.

title: P2 exercises — Water, minerals and transport
text: The questions follow the tutorial and slides. Answer each question before opening its answer.

title: P2 exercises — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Water potential

1.1
Define water potential (Ψ), state its usual unit in plant physiology, and give the water potential of pure water at atmospheric pressure.






Answer





Water potential is the chemical potential (free energy per unit volume) of water relative to that of pure water at atmospheric pressure and the same temperature. It is expressed in megapascals (MPa). Pure water at atmospheric pressure has Ψ = 0 MPa.





1.2
Arrange from the highest to the lowest water potential: −0.8 MPa, 0 MPa, −1.5 MPa, −0.2 MPa. In which direction does water move passively?






Answer





0 > −0.2 > −0.8 > −1.5 MPa. Water moves passively from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential.





1.3
Use Ψ = Ψs + Ψp (ignore gravity and matric potential). Both cells are placed in the same external solution with Ψ = −0.4 MPa.



Cell
Ψs (MPa)
Ψp (MPa)
Ψ (MPa)
Initial net water movement




A
−0.8
+0.2




B
−0.7
+0.5











Answer








Cell
Ψs (MPa)
Ψp (MPa)
Ψ (MPa)
Initial net water movement




A
−0.8
+0.2
−0.6
Into the cell (−0.4 > −0.6)


B
−0.7
+0.5
−0.2
Out of the cell (−0.2 > −0.4)



Cell B loses water even though its solute potential is more negative than the external solution, because total Ψ determines direction.





1.4
Calculate the solute potential at 25 °C (298 K) of

0.1 mol L⁻¹ sucrose
0.1 mol L⁻¹ NaCl (assume complete dissociation)

Use Ψs = −cRT, where c is the osmolar concentration and R = 0.008314 L MPa mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.






Answer






Ψs = −(0.1 mol L⁻¹)(0.008314 L MPa mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)(298 K) = −0.25 MPa.
NaCl gives two particles, so c = 0.2 osmol L⁻¹ and Ψs = −0.50 MPa.






1.5
A flaccid cell (Ψp = 0) has Ψs = −0.6 MPa. Assume the cell volume, and hence Ψs, does not change.

What is its Ψ?
It is placed in pure water. What are Ψ and Ψp at equilibrium?
It is instead placed in a solution with Ψ = −0.8 MPa. In which direction does water move, and what is Ψp at the end?







Answer






Ψ = −0.6 + 0 = −0.6 MPa.
Water enters until Ψ = 0 MPa; then Ψp = 0 − (−0.6) = +0.6 MPa.
Water leaves the cell (−0.6 > −0.8). Ψp stays at 0 (it cannot become strongly negative in a living cell); the protoplast shrinks away from the wall (plasmolysis).






1.6
A root cell has Ψ = −0.4 MPa. Give the initial direction of net water movement between the cell and the soil solution when the soil solution has

Ψ = −0.1 MPa
Ψ = −0.6 MPa (saline soil)







Answer






From soil into the root cell.
From the root cell into the soil. Saline soil can therefore cause water stress although it is wet.

title: P2 exercises — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Uptake by roots

2.1
Name the three routes by which water crosses the root cortex and state which structure each route passes through.






Answer






Apoplastic: through cell walls and intercellular spaces, without crossing membranes.
Symplastic: from cytoplasm to cytoplasm through plasmodesmata.
Transmembrane (transcellular): across the plasma membrane (and tonoplast) of each successive cell.






2.2

In which cell layer is the Casparian strip found?
Which compounds make it?
What is its function?







Answer






The endodermis, in the radial and transverse walls.
Suberin (with lignin).
It blocks the apoplastic route into the stele, so water and solutes must cross a plasma membrane, which allows selective uptake.






2.3
True or false? Correct any false statements.

Aquaporins pump water into root cells using ATP.
The plasma-membrane H⁺-ATPase uses ATP to build an electrochemical proton gradient.
A proton-coupled carrier can move a nutrient ion against its own concentration gradient.
Inhibiting the H⁺-ATPase directly stops passive water flow through aquaporins.







Answer






False. Aquaporins are channels that increase membrane permeability to water; water moves passively down its potential gradient.
True.
True. Energy comes from protons moving down their electrochemical gradient (secondary active transport).
False. It reduces proton-coupled solute uptake; water flow through aquaporins is passive and not directly driven by ATP.






2.4
Waterlogged soil contains plenty of water, yet mineral uptake by roots falls. Give the chain of causes.






Answer





Water fills the soil pores → little O₂ reaches the roots → aerobic respiration falls → less ATP → H⁺-ATPase activity and the proton gradient decline → less active (proton-coupled) uptake of mineral ions.

title: P2 exercises — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Xylem transport and transpiration

3.1
Arrange the steps of water movement in a transpiring plant in order:

water vapour diffuses out through the stomatal pore
water crosses the root endodermis
water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls into the air spaces
water enters the root from the soil
water moves up the xylem under tension







Answer





d → b → e → c → a.





3.2
Match each term to its definition: cohesion, adhesion, tension, cavitation.

Negative hydrostatic pressure in the xylem water
Attraction between water molecules through hydrogen bonding
Breakage of the water column and formation of a gas bubble in a conduit
Attraction between water molecules and the conduit walls







Answer





Cohesion–2, adhesion–4, tension–1, cavitation–3. A gas-filled conduit after cavitation is said to be embolised.





3.3
Typical water potentials in a transpiring plant are listed. Arrange them in the order water passes and state what drives the flow.
Leaf cells: −0.8 MPa. Soil: −0.1 MPa. Atmosphere (50 % relative humidity): −95 MPa. Root xylem: −0.4 MPa.






Answer





Soil (−0.1) → root xylem (−0.4) → leaf cells (−0.8) → atmosphere (−95 MPa). Water moves passively down this gradient of decreasing water potential. The energy comes from evaporation at the leaf (ultimately solar energy); the plant does not pump water.





3.4
Four pots are weighed over 4 h. Unplanted soil controls lose 4 g per pot over the same time.



Pot

Leaf area (m²)

Calculate the mean rate.
Convert the rate of pot 1 to mmol H₂O m⁻² s⁻¹ (M(H₂O) = 18 g mol⁻¹).







Answer

3.5
State whether each change increases or decreases the transpiration rate when stomatal conductance stays the same.

Lower air humidity
Higher leaf temperature
Stronger wind removing the boundary layer
Smaller total leaf area







Answer






Increases (larger vapour pressure difference between leaf and air).
Increases (higher vapour pressure inside the leaf).
Increases (thinner boundary layer, lower resistance).
Decreases (less evaporating surface per plant).

title: P2 exercises — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Stomata

4.1
Put the steps of light-induced stomatal opening in order:

guard-cell water potential falls
blue light activates the guard-cell plasma-membrane H⁺-ATPase
turgor rises and the guard cells bow apart, opening the pore
K⁺ enters through inward-rectifying channels, with Cl⁻ uptake and malate synthesis
the membrane hyperpolarises
water enters the guard cells







Answer





b → e → d → a → f → c.





4.2
State whether each condition causes stomata to open or close.

Blue light at dawn
High intercellular CO₂ concentration
Increased ABA in the leaf
Low intercellular CO₂ concentration
Low leaf water potential (drought)







Answer






Open. b. Close. c. Close. d. Open. e. Close.






4.3
How does abscisic acid (ABA) close stomata? Give the sequence from ABA perception to pore closure.






Answer





ABA binds receptors in the guard cells → anion channels open and anions leave → the membrane depolarises → K⁺ leaves through outward-rectifying channels → guard-cell Ψs and Ψ rise → water leaves → turgor falls → the pore closes. ABA acts as a signal; it does not plug the pore.

title: P2 exercises — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Mineral nutrition

5.1
Define an essential element.






Answer





An element without which the plant cannot complete its life cycle, or which is part of an essential molecule or structure of the plant; its function cannot be replaced by another element.





5.2
Classify each element as a macronutrient or a micronutrient: N, Fe, K, Zn, Mg, Mo, P, Mn, S, Cu, Ca, B.






Answer





Macronutrients: N, K, Mg, P, S, Ca. Micronutrients: Fe, Zn, Mo, Mn, Cu, B. The classification refers to the amount required, not to importance.





5.3
Match each element to one role.




Element




A
Nitrogen


B
Phosphorus


C
Potassium


D
Magnesium


E
Iron



Roles: (1) central atom of chlorophyll; (2) main cation for osmotic regulation, e.g. in guard cells; (3) component of amino acids, proteins and nucleotides; (4) component of cytochromes and Fe–S proteins in electron transport; (5) component of ATP, nucleic acids and phospholipids.






Answer





A–3, B–5, C–2, D–1, E–4.





5.4
Deficiency of nitrogen first causes yellowing of the older leaves, whereas iron deficiency first causes yellowing of the young leaves. Explain the difference.






Answer





Nitrogen is mobile in the phloem: it is remobilised from old leaves to new growth, so old leaves show symptoms first. Iron is relatively immobile and cannot be withdrawn from old leaves, so new leaves, which depend on current uptake, show symptoms first.





5.5
What does each partner gain in an arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis?






Answer





The plant gains mineral nutrients, especially phosphate, and water taken up by the fungal hyphae from a larger soil volume. The fungus gains carbon (sugars and lipids) from the plant.

title: P2 exercises — Water, minerals and transport
section: Explore: A plant cell in a solution
text:
Explore: A plant cell in a solution
A flaccid plant cell is placed in a solution and exchanges water until its water potential Ψ = Ψs + Ψp equals that of the solution. Choose a preset or set the cell sap Ψs (at the flaccid volume), the solution Ψ and the wall stiffness; the bars and the readout give Ψs, Ψp and Ψ at equilibrium, and the label under the cell gives its state and protoplast volume.




E1.1
Click “Pure water” (cell sap Ψs −0.60 MPa, solution 0 MPa, wall stiffness 10 MPa). In which direction does water move, and what are Ψs, Ψp and Ψ of the cell at equilibrium?






Answer





Water moves into the cell. At equilibrium Ψ = 0 MPa, with Ψp = +0.57 MPa and Ψs = −0.57 MPa (the sap is slightly diluted as the protoplast swells to 1.06 × V₀). The cell is turgid.





E1.2
Click “−0.6 MPa” and then “−0.8 MPa”. Give the state of the cell (turgid, flaccid or plasmolysed) and its Ψp in each case.






Answer





−0.6 MPa: flaccid, Ψp = 0, no net water flow (the solution equals the cell sap). −0.8 MPa: plasmolysed, Ψp = 0; water leaves until Ψs has fallen to −0.80 MPa, at a protoplast volume of 0.75 × V₀.





E1.3
Click “Saline soil”: a root cell with Ψs = −0.40 MPa in a soil solution of −0.60 MPa. Does the cell gain or lose water, and what is its protoplast volume at equilibrium?






Answer





It loses water (−0.40 > −0.60) and plasmolyses; the protoplast shrinks to 0.67 × V₀ so that Ψs reaches −0.60 MPa. Even in wet soil, salt can lower the soil Ψ enough to draw water out of the root.





E1.4
Return to pure water (Ψs −0.60, solution 0) and compare wall stiffness 40 MPa with 2 MPa. Which wall gives the higher Ψp at equilibrium, and which cell swells more?






Answer





The stiff wall (40 MPa) gives the higher Ψp, +0.59 MPa, with almost no swelling (1.01 × V₀). The soft wall (2 MPa) swells to 1.24 × V₀, which dilutes the sap to −0.48 MPa, so Ψp is only +0.48 MPa.





E1.5
Keep the cell sap at −0.60 MPa and the wall at 10 MPa, and lower the solution Ψ slowly from 0. Below which solution Ψ does plasmolysis begin?






Answer





Below −0.60 MPa, i.e. when the solution Ψ is lower than the Ψs of the cell sap at the flaccid volume (incipient plasmolysis).

title: P2 exercises — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Explore: The soil–plant–air continuum
Steady-state transpiration through the chain soil → root → stem → leaf → air. The vapour pressure deficit and stomatal opening set the flux; each resistance along the path then lowers Ψ in proportion to it. Set humidity, soil Ψ, plant height and stomatal opening, or click a preset; the plot shows Ψ at each point, and the panel gives the transpiration rate.




E2.1
Click “Lecture” (50 % humidity, soil −0.10 MPa, 1 m, stomata fully open). Give the transpiration rate, Ψ of the leaf cells and Ψ of the air. Where along the path is the largest drop in water potential?






Answer





Transpiration 6.3 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹, leaf cells −0.83 MPa, air −95 MPa. The largest drop is between the leaf and the air (about 94 MPa), in the vapour phase, far larger than any drop in the liquid path.





E2.2
Click “Humid” (90 % humidity). Does transpiration increase or decrease, and is the leaf Ψ higher or lower than at 50 %? What happens at 100 % humidity?






Answer





Transpiration decreases to 1.3 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹ (the vapour pressure deficit falls from 1.58 to 0.32 kPa), and the leaf Ψ is higher, −0.25 MPa. At 100 % humidity the deficit is zero, transpiration stops and the profile is flat at the soil value.





E2.3
Click “Dry soil” (soil −0.80 MPa, stomata do not respond), then “Dry soil + ABA”. Give the transpiration rate and the leaf Ψ in each case.






Answer





Dry soil: 6.3 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹ and leaf Ψ −5.47 MPa, far below the wilting line; the xylem would cavitate. Dry soil + ABA: stomata partly close (conductance 89 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹), transpiration falls to 1.4 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹ and the leaf stays at −1.85 MPa. The plant saves water at the cost of CO₂ uptake.





E2.4
Use the “Lecture” settings and halve stomatal opening to 50 %. By what factor does transpiration change, and does the leaf Ψ rise or fall?






Answer





Transpiration halves, from 6.3 to 3.1 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹; the leaf Ψ rises from −0.83 to −0.47 MPa because less water flows through the resistances.





E2.5
Click “Redwood” (100 m tall). How much water potential does gravity alone cost over that height, according to the panel?






Answer





0.98 MPa (0.0098 MPa per metre × 100 m), before any loss due to flow.



Continue with the self-check quiz.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
text:
About this lecture
The tallest living tree, a coast redwood, is 115 m high. Water climbs from its roots to its top leaves every day, and there is no heart anywhere in the tree. Yet a tomato plant standing in wet, salty soil can wilt as if the soil were dry. What moves water through a plant, and why does wet soil not guarantee water? In P1 we built the plant: walled cells with turgor, apoplast and symplast, root hairs and endodermis, xylem and stomata. Today we make water and minerals flow through it.

Water potential: one quantity, Ψ, that predicts the direction of water movement, and how to calculate it.
Into the root: three routes, the endodermis, and the energy cost of taking up ions.
Up the xylem: cohesion–tension, driven by evaporation from the leaf.
Out of the leaf: measuring transpiration, and how stomata regulate it.
Minerals: which elements a plant needs, what they do, and partners in the soil.


The running example is the path of one water molecule from the soil to the air: soil, root, xylem, leaf, stomatal pore, atmosphere. Every section of the lecture is one stage of that path, plus the minerals that travel with the water. The salty-soil question is answered with a water-potential calculation halfway through, and the redwood question with cohesion–tension.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
section: The problem: water in, water out
text:
The problem: water in, water out



A plant loses ~500 water molecules for every CO₂ molecule it fixes. Of the water taken up, ~97 % evaporates from the leaves.
A maize plant transpires ~200 L over a growing season.
Water travels up to 100 m from soil to leaf, far beyond the reach of diffusion (A1: ~7 h for 1 cm).
So, as in an animal, long distances need bulk flow. But the plant has no pump.



Photo: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Before asking how water moves, we need a rule for which way it moves.

Start with the numbers so students see that water transport in a plant is a huge flux, not a trickle. The water loss is the price of opening stomata to let CO₂ in (P1, leaf slide). Link back to the A1 diffusion table: bulk flow is required. The puzzle is the energy source. The next slides give the rule for direction: water potential.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
section: Water potential: which way water moves
text:
Water potential: which way water moves



Water potential (Ψ): the free energy of water per unit volume, relative to pure water at atmospheric pressure, which has Ψ = 0.
Unit: megapascal (MPa). 1 MPa = 10 bar ≈ 10 atm.
Water moves passively from higher to lower Ψ.
In plants Ψ is almost always negative, so “higher” means less negative.


Highest to lowest:



Ψ (MPa)





0
pure water


−0.2
wet soil


−0.8
leaf cell


−1.5
dry soil



Water flows down this list.

What makes Ψ negative, and what can make it rise?

Exercises 1.1 and 1.2. The sign convention trips students up: −0.2 is higher than −0.8. Use the analogy of water flowing downhill, where “downhill” means towards more negative Ψ. The table is a preview of the soil-to-leaf gradient that we build up across the lecture.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
text:
The components of Ψ
\Psi = \Psi_s + \Psi_p \quad (+\,\Psi_g)



\Psi_s, solute (osmotic) potential: always ≤ 0; solutes lower the free energy of water.
\Psi_p, pressure potential: + in turgid cells (turgor, P1), − in transpiring xylem (tension).
\Psi_g, gravitational: +0.01 MPa per metre. Negligible in a cell; lifting water 100 m costs 1 MPa.
In dry soil, binding to surfaces (matric potential) also lowers Ψ.




How negative is Ψs for a real solution?

Two components do almost all the work in cells: solutes pull Ψ down, pressure pushes it up. Read the bars group by group: in a turgid cell a positive Ψp cancels part of Ψs; in a flaccid cell Ψp is zero and Ψ = Ψs; in the xylem of a transpiring plant the sap is almost pure water (Ψs near zero) but under tension, so Ψp itself is strongly negative. Turgor from P1 is now a number: Ψp. Point out that Ψp can be negative too, in the xylem of a transpiring plant, which is the key to cohesion–tension later. Gravity is introduced so students know when it can be dropped. Matric potential is mentioned only so students recognise the term.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Solute potential: Ψs = −cRT
\Psi_s = -cRT \qquad R = 0.008314\ \text{L MPa mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}
c is the osmolar concentration: count every dissolved particle.



Solution (25 °C, 298 K)

At 25 °C, RT \approx 2.48 L MPa mol⁻¹: each 0.1 osmol L⁻¹ lowers Ψs by ~0.25 MPa.
A salt that splits into two ions has twice the effect of a sugar at the same molarity.

Now we can predict what happens to a cell placed in a solution.

Exercise 1.4 is the first two rows. Carry the units through on the board: mol L⁻¹ × L MPa mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ × K = MPa. The rule of thumb (0.1 osmol per litre ≈ −0.25 MPa) helps students check answers. Sea water shows why most crop plants cannot use it: their cells would need a Ψ below −2.7 MPa just to take up water.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
section: Two cells in the same solution
text:
Two cells in the same solution
Both cells are placed in a solution with Ψ = −0.4 MPa.










Cell

Ψp (MPa)

Cell B’s Ψs (−0.7) is far below the solution’s Ψ (−0.4), yet it loses water: its high turgor raises its total Ψ.
Total Ψ decides the direction, not solute concentration alone.
As water moves, Ψp and Ψs change until Ψ inside equals Ψ outside: equilibrium, no net flow.

What happens to turgor as a cell gains or loses water?

Exercise 1.3. The trap is to compare only solute potentials. Cell B is the instructive case: plenty of solute, but the wall is already pushing hard, so water leaves. Emphasise that the numbers are initial values; they change as water moves. This sets up the next slide, where we follow one cell to equilibrium.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
text:
One cell, three solutions
A flaccid cell: Ψs = −0.6 MPa, Ψp = 0, so Ψ = −0.6 MPa (assume Ψs stays constant).

Turgor (P1) is the pressure that builds up until the cell’s Ψ matches its surroundings.
Ψp cannot fall far below zero in a living cell: the wall cannot pull, so the protoplast pulls away instead.

What does this look like if Ψs is allowed to change as the cell swells or shrinks?

Exercise 1.5. In pure water the cell takes up water until turgor exactly cancels the solute potential. In a more concentrated solution the cell loses water, turgor falls to zero and the membrane separates from the wall: plasmolysis, visible in onion epidermis in the practical. Transition: the table assumed Ψs is fixed; the next slide drops that simplification.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
section: Turgor and volume: the Höfler diagram
text:
Turgor and volume: the Höfler diagram


The same cell (Ψs = −0.6 MPa when flaccid), plotted against its protoplast volume:

Below the flaccid volume, Ψp = 0 and Ψ = Ψs: the protoplast shrinks away from the wall.
Above it, the stretched wall pushes back: Ψp rises steeply, and Ψs rises a little as the sap is diluted.
In pure water the cell stops at Ψ = 0, only a few % larger than when flaccid.




A root cell is exactly such a cell, sitting in the soil solution.

The Höfler diagram is the standard way to show how the components change together. The x-axis is protoplast volume relative to the volume at incipient plasmolysis. To the left, the protoplast has pulled away from the wall, Ψp is zero and Ψ equals Ψs, which becomes more negative as the cell loses water (Ψs = −0.6 / V). To the right, the wall is stretched elastically (here with a modulus of 6 MPa), so Ψp rises quickly. Full turgor in pure water is reached at Ψ = 0, where Ψp ≈ +0.55 MPa rather than the +0.6 of the previous slide: the cell swelled by about 9 % and diluted its sap a little. With a stiffer wall the difference shrinks, which is why the fixed-Ψs approximation works well. The three dots are the three rows of the previous table.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
section: Try it: a cell in a solution
text:
Try it: a cell in a solution




The cell from the last two slides, placed in a beaker. The cell always starts flaccid (Ψp = 0); its sap Ψs is set at that volume. The bars show the cell’s Ψs, Ψp and Ψ, and the red dashed line the solution’s Ψ; the arrows show the direction of water flow. Click “Pure water”: arrows point inwards, the cell swells, Ψp rises until the blue Ψ bar reaches the dashed line at zero, and the state reads turgid. Ask the room to predict before each click. “−0.6 MPa”: no flow, the cell stays flaccid. “−0.8 MPa”: water leaves, the protoplast shrinks away from the wall and Ψs falls to −0.8 (plasmolysis). “Saline soil” is the next slide: a root cell with Ψs −0.4 in a −0.6 MPa soil solution loses water. Then drag the wall-stiffness slider: a stiff wall (40 MPa) reaches full turgor with almost no swelling and Ψp ≈ +0.6 (the fixed-Ψs table), a soft wall (2 MPa) swells more and dilutes its sap. Finally drag the solution slider slowly and ask when plasmolysis starts: exactly when the solution Ψ drops below the cell sap Ψs. “Place a flaccid cell in the solution” replays the current case from the start.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
section: Wet but salty soil: the opening problem
text:
Wet but salty soil: the opening problem


A root cell has Ψ = −0.4 MPa.



Soil solution
Ψ
Water moves




Moist
−0.1
soil → root


Moist, saline
−0.6
root → soil




Salt lowers the Ψs of soil water: the soil is wet, but its Ψ is below the root’s.
To take up water again the plant must accumulate solutes (osmotic adjustment). This costs energy, and Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are toxic inside cells.



Photo: Mnolf, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Water is available in the soil. How does it cross the root to reach the xylem?

Exercise 1.6, and the answer to the second question in the introduction: wet soil can behave like dry soil for the plant. Work the comparisons: −0.1 > −0.4, so water enters; −0.4 > −0.6, so water leaves. The photo shows the extreme case, the −0.8 MPa row two slides back: in a strong solution the coloured protoplasts have shrunk away from the walls. You will see the same in onion epidermis in the practical. About 20 % of irrigated land is affected by salinity, so this is a major crop problem; P5 returns to salt stress. Transition: follow water inward across the root tissues we met in P1.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
section: Into the root: three routes and one barrier
text:
Into the root: three routes and one barrier



Apoplastic: through cell walls and spaces; crosses no membrane.
Symplastic: cytoplasm to cytoplasm through plasmodesmata.
Transmembrane: across the plasma membrane (and tonoplast) of each successive cell.

At the endodermis, the Casparian strip (suberin, with lignin) in the radial and transverse walls blocks the apoplast.



Every water molecule and ion entering the xylem has passed a membrane at least once. That membrane decides what gets in.

Exercises 2.1 and 2.2. These are the apoplast, symplast and endodermis from P1, now carrying water. The Casparian strip is the root’s checkpoint: without it, soil solution including toxic ions could flow through the walls straight into the xylem. Water crosses membranes passively; ions need transport proteins, and some need energy, which is the next slide.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
section: Crossing the membrane: water is passive, ions cost energy
text:
Crossing the membrane: water is passive, ions cost energy


Water

Moves through aquaporins: channels that raise membrane permeability.
Always passive, down the Ψ gradient. No ATP pumps water.

Ions

Plasma-membrane H⁺-ATPase uses ATP to pump H⁺ out: apoplast pH ~5.5, cytosol ~7.3, membrane potential −120 to −200 mV.
Channels let ions move down this gradient (K⁺ in).
H⁺-coupled carriers use H⁺ flowing back in to move ions against their own gradient (NO₃⁻, H₂PO₄⁻): secondary active transport.


Waterlogged roots: wet but starving

Water fills the soil pores.
Little O₂ reaches the roots.
Aerobic respiration falls: less ATP.
H⁺-ATPase slows; the H⁺ gradient declines.
Less H⁺-coupled uptake of mineral ions.


Now the water is in the xylem. What lifts it 100 m?

Exercises 2.3 and 2.4. Keep water and ions separate: aquaporins change how fast water moves, never the direction. The H⁺-ATPase is the plant’s primary pump, playing the role that the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase plays in animal cells (A4). The waterlogging chain shows that mineral uptake depends on root respiration, which links forward to P3 (respiration and fermentation in flooded roots).

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
section: Soil to air: a gradient of Ψ
text:
Soil to air: a gradient of Ψ



Soil → root → xylem → leaf cells → evaporation from mesophyll walls → air through the stomata.
Each step is downhill in Ψ: water moves passively the whole way.
The biggest drop is from leaf to air: air at 50 % relative humidity has Ψ ≈ −95 MPa.
The energy comes from evaporation at the leaf, ultimately from the sun. The plant spends no ATP moving water.




How does evaporation in a leaf pull on water in the roots?

Exercises 3.1 (order of steps) and 3.3 (order of Ψ values). This is the running example of the lecture in one picture. The air value comes from Ψ = (RT/V̄w) ln(RH): at 50 % humidity it is about −95 MPa, a hundred times more negative than the leaf, which is why evaporation is so powerful. The plant’s job is to control the last step (stomata), not to drive the flow.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Cohesion–tension



Water evaporates from mesophyll walls; the curved water surfaces in the wall pores pull on the water behind them.
This tension (−1 to −2 MPa in a tall tree) is transmitted down the continuous water column by cohesion (hydrogen bonds between water molecules) and adhesion to the conduit walls.
Lignified wall thickenings stop the conduits collapsing under tension (P1).



Photo: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

The leaf pulls, cohesion transmits the pull, rigid walls resist it.

The mechanism needs no pump at any height: the leaf pulls, cohesion transmits, the rigid walls resist. The section shows the xylem vessels as P1 described them: dead, empty tubes whose walls are reinforced by rings and spirals of lignified secondary wall. These thickenings work like the wire in a vacuum-cleaner hose: they stop the tube collapsing when the water inside is under tension. Recall that a tension of −1 MPa is a negative pressure ten times larger in magnitude than atmospheric pressure.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
section: When the column breaks; when the root pushes
text:
When the column breaks; when the root pushes





Term
Meaning




Cohesion
water molecules attract each other


Adhesion
water attracts the conduit walls


Tension
negative pressure in the xylem water


Cavitation
the column breaks; a gas bubble forms


Embolism
the conduit is gas-filled and blocked




Pits between conduits limit the spread of embolism.
Root pressure (≤ ~0.2 MPa) pushes sap up at night and causes guttation, but cannot lift water to the top of a tree.



Photo: Schnobby, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

If evaporation drives the flow, what sets how fast a plant loses water?

Exercise 3.2 matches these terms. Cavitation is the cost of working under tension: drought increases tension and risks embolism, and an embolised vessel no longer conducts. The photo shows the other force: on humid nights, when transpiration stops, roots keep loading ions into the xylem, water follows osmotically and the positive pressure pushes drops out of hydathodes at the leaf margin. The drops are xylem sap, not dew. Root pressure is real but at most about 0.2 MPa, enough for about 20 m in theory and far less in practice, and it is absent in many trees, so it cannot explain transport in tall trees.

Measuring transpiration: rate and units

Convert pot 1 to the standard unit, mmol H₂O m⁻² s⁻¹:
\frac{50\ \text{g m}^{-2}\,\text{h}^{-1}}{18\ \text{g mol}^{-1}} = 2.78\ \text{mol m}^{-2}\,\text{h}^{-1}
\frac{2.78}{3600\ \text{s h}^{-1}} = 7.7\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol m}^{-2}\,\text{s}^{-1} = 0.77\ \text{mmol m}^{-2}\,\text{s}^{-1}

Divide by leaf area so plants of different size can be compared.



Exercise 3.4. Work the conversion step by step: grams to moles, hours to seconds. Gas-exchange instruments report transpiration in mmol m⁻² s⁻¹ and photosynthesis in µmol m⁻² s⁻¹, which students meet again in P3. The two bullets are the experimental logic: a control for the non-plant water loss, and normalisation by the evaporating surface.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
text:
What sets the transpiration rate
Transpiration ≈ conductance × (vapour pressure in leaf − vapour pressure in air)


With stomatal conductance unchanged:

Lower air humidity → more: larger vapour pressure difference.
Warmer leaf → more: higher vapour pressure inside the leaf.
Stronger wind → more: thinner boundary layer.
Smaller leaf area → less: less evaporating surface.

Inside the leaf the air is saturated (~100 % humidity). The plant cannot control the weather; it controls the stomata.


Photo: Arlo James Barnes, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

So how do guard cells open and close the pore?

Exercise 3.5. The formula is Fick’s law from A1 in another form: flux = conductance × concentration difference. Humidity and temperature change the driving difference, wind and stomata change the conductance. The plant’s one fast control is the stomatal pore, which leads into the next slide.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
section: Stomatal opening: ion transport makes turgor
text:
Stomatal opening: ion transport makes turgor



Blue light activates the guard-cell H⁺-ATPase.
H⁺ is pumped out; the membrane hyperpolarises.
K⁺ enters through inward-rectifying channels; Cl⁻ is taken up and malate made, balancing the charge.
Guard-cell Ψs and Ψ fall.
Water enters by osmosis.
Turgor rises; radial microfibrils make the guard cells bow apart and the pore opens.




Guard-cell K⁺ can rise from ~100 to ~400–800 mM during opening.
Opening is the default in light. What makes stomata close?

Exercise 4.1 asks for this order. Each step uses an earlier idea: the H⁺-ATPase from the root slide, Ψs = −cRT (a few hundred millimolar of KCl lowers Ψs by about 1–2 MPa), turgor from P1, and microfibril orientation from the P1 wall slide controlling the direction of swelling. Stomata are hydraulic valves run by ion transport.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
section: Signals that open and close stomata
text:
Signals that open and close stomata





Signal
Response




Blue light at dawn
open


Low intercellular CO₂
open


High intercellular CO₂
close


Increased ABA
close


Low leaf Ψ (drought)
close




Abscisic acid (ABA), the drought hormone, made in roots and leaves:

ABA binds receptors in the guard cells.
Anion channels open; Cl⁻ and malate leave.
The membrane depolarises.
K⁺ leaves through outward-rectifying channels.
Guard-cell Ψs and Ψ rise; water leaves.
Turgor falls and the pore closes.


ABA is a signal: it changes ion channels, it does not plug the pore. Closing saves water but stops CO₂ uptake.

Exercises 4.2 and 4.3. The closing sequence is the opening sequence run in reverse, triggered by a hormone instead of light. The CO₂ responses make sense: if CO₂ inside the leaf is high, the pore need not be open. The last line is the trade-off of the whole plant: closing protects water status but halts photosynthesis, which P3 picks up (photorespiration and CAM). Before minerals, the next slide puts the whole water path together.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Try it: soil to air




The whole water path in one steady-state model. Transpiration is set in the vapour phase, conductance × vapour pressure deficit (leaf and air at 25 °C), and the same flux has to flow through soil, root, stem and leaf, losing Ψ in each in proportion to its resistance. The curve on the right is the soil-to-air gradient slide, now live; the blue dashes in the stem move at a speed proportional to the flux. Start with “Lecture” (50 % humidity, wet soil): about 6 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹, root xylem −0.4 and leaf −0.8 MPa as on that slide. “Humid”: the flux falls and the profile flattens towards the soil value; at 100 % nothing moves. Drag humidity down: the flux rises and the leaf Ψ falls, but the air (top right) is always tens of MPa below the leaf. “Dry soil” (−0.8 MPa) with stomata that do not respond: drying soil conducts poorly, so the leaf is dragged below −4 MPa and the xylem would cavitate. “Dry soil + ABA”: stomata partly close, transpiration drops to about a fifth and the leaf stays near −1.8 MPa; the plant trades CO₂ uptake for water. “Redwood”: 100 m of height costs about 1 MPa by gravity alone, before any flow. Ask which slider the plant itself controls: only stomatal opening. The resistances are illustrative, chosen to reproduce the lecture values.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport

Essential elements


An element is essential if the plant cannot complete its life cycle without it, or it is part of an essential molecule, and no other element can replace it.

Photo: Rasbak, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons


“Macro” and “micro” refer to the amount needed, not to importance: without 0.1 mg kg⁻¹ of Mo the plant dies just as surely.
C, H and O come from CO₂ and water.

What does each element do, and how do you recognise a deficiency?

Exercises 5.1 and 5.2. The concentrations are the standard values from Epstein, as quoted in Taiz & Zeiger: nitrogen is needed at about 10⁵ times the concentration of molybdenum. Students should be able to sort the twelve elements into the two groups. Essentiality is tested by growing plants in hydroponic solutions lacking one element. The photo shows what lack of the most-needed element looks like: a nitrogen-starved bean plant is pale yellow-green all over, compared with the dark green healthy plants at the edges. Nitrogen is in chlorophyll and in every protein, so the whole plant pales and grows slowly; the next two slides explain which leaves go first.

Exercises 5.3 (roles) and 5.4 (old versus young leaves). Read the table by columns: the role explains the symptom (N and Mg are in chlorophyll, so their lack yellows leaves), and the mobility column explains where it shows first, which is the next slide. Mobility is phloem mobility, so this links forward to P3, where the phloem moves sugar from sources to sinks.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
section: Reading a deficiency: old or young leaves?
text:
Reading a deficiency: old or young leaves?



A mobile element (N, P, K, Mg) is withdrawn from old leaves to supply new growth, so old leaves show symptoms first.
An immobile element (Fe, Ca) stays where it was deposited, so young leaves, which depend on current uptake, show symptoms first.
The photo: Mg deficiency in maize. Yellow stripes between the veins of older leaves; the veins stay green longest.



Photo: Alandmanson, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Roots do not take up all of this alone.

The mobility rule turns a symptom pattern into a diagnosis: where the yellowing appears tells you which group the missing element belongs to. Magnesium is the central atom of chlorophyll, so its lack shows as chlorosis; it is phloem-mobile, so the plant strips it from old leaves to supply young ones, and the old leaves go yellow first, between the veins. Iron deficiency also gives interveinal yellowing, but on the youngest leaves, because Fe is not remobilised. Ask: a tomato plant has yellowing confined to its top leaves; which group of elements do you suspect?

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Mycorrhizas: fungi extend the root



Fungal hyphae enter the root cortex and form arbuscules inside cells: tree-like branches that give a huge exchange surface.
Formed by ~70–80 % of land plant species.
Hyphae (~2–10 µm) reach far beyond the depletion zone around a root.
Plant gains: mineral nutrients, especially phosphate, and water.
Fungus gains: carbon (sugars and lipids), up to ~20 % of the plant’s photosynthate.



Photo: Msturmel, public domain, Wikimedia Commons


Exercise 5.5. Phosphate diffuses very slowly in soil, so a zone around each root is quickly depleted; fine hyphae extend the absorbing surface far beyond it, the A1 surface-area solution again. In the photo the fungus is stained; each dark tuft is an arbuscule inside a living cortical cell, where the plant and fungus exchange phosphate for carbon across the plant plasma membrane, which folds around the arbuscule. The fungus never crosses that membrane.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Root nodules: bacteria fix nitrogen



Rhizobia live in root nodules of legumes (pea, bean, clover).
They convert N₂ to NH₃ with nitrogenase, at a cost of ~16 ATP per N₂.
The plant supplies sugars; the bacteria supply ammonium.

Both symbioses trade carbon from the leaves for nutrients from the soil.


Photo: Bwiltz, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Carbon pays for water and mineral uptake. Where does that carbon come from?

Exercise 5.5. Nodules that are actively fixing are pink inside, from leghaemoglobin, which keeps O₂ low around the oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase while still supplying respiration. Both partnerships cost the plant carbon, as does all active ion uptake (respiration in roots). This sets up P3: how light becomes the carbon that pays for everything.

title: P2 — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Water potential
Ψ = Ψs + Ψp; pure water = 0 MPa; water moves to lower (more negative) Ψ


Solute potential
Ψs = −cRT, c in osmol L⁻¹; 0.1 M NaCl → −0.50 MPa at 25 °C


Turgor and plasmolysis
water enters until Ψ inside = Ψ outside; Ψp ≥ 0 in living cells


Saline soil
low soil Ψ can draw water out of roots in wet soil


Root routes
apoplastic, symplastic, transmembrane; Casparian strip blocks the apoplast


Ion uptake
H⁺-ATPase builds the gradient; channels and H⁺-coupled carriers use it


Cohesion–tension
evaporation creates tension; cohesion transmits it; no pump


Transpiration
units mmol H₂O m⁻² s⁻¹; rises with low humidity, heat, wind


Stomata
light → H⁺-ATPase → K⁺ in → water in → open; ABA → ions out → close


Minerals
macro/micro by amount; mobile elements show symptoms in old leaves



Next (P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget): the open stomata let CO₂ in. How does the leaf use light to turn CO₂ into sugar, how do some plants fix carbon while losing less water, and how does sugar reach the root?
Tutorial · Exercises · Quiz

Read the table in the order of the water path: the rule for direction, the calculation, uptake at the root, the xylem, loss from the leaf and its control, and the minerals carried with the water. P3 picks up the other gas passing through the stomata: every water molecule lost buys a share of CO₂, and P3 follows that CO₂ into sugar and out to the roots.

title: Practical: evidence for tissue identity and function
text:
What observations justify naming a tissue, and how does that tissue help an organ work? Work in pairs, then submit one individual observation sheet. You need paper and a pencil; the cases below supply textual observations. They are deliberately constructed descriptions, not microscope images or records of actual specimens. This activity practises reasoning before a specimen session; passing it does not establish visual identification or dissection skill. Those require the course’s actual slides, atlas and instructor-led practical.
Review the four broad tissue categories: epithelium forms linings and interfaces; connective tissue supports and links structures; muscle generates force; nervous tissue supports information processing and transmission. Actual organs contain several categories. A kidney section is not a single homogeneous tissue.

title: Practical: evidence for tissue identity and function

Those require the course’s actual slides, atlas and instructor-led practical.
